Global Coherence: When Every Agent Is Right and the Team Is Still Wrong
A Local-to-Global Semantic Foundation for Multi-Agent Collaboration

Xin Heng Affiliation: Tote AI Email: xin@tote.ai
October 1, 2026
Abstract

AI agents now work together on shared code, documents, tools, and scientific analyses, often alongside people. No participant sees the whole state. Every step can look right on its own while the combined result is wrong. We call this the global coherence problem, and we argue that it is a problem of state, not only of intelligence: a stronger model makes better local decisions, but it cannot see what is not in its context, and it cannot make locally valid pieces fit together when they do not. Intelligence alone cannot guarantee a solution. To our knowledge, this paper is the first to formulate this as a failure class of AI agent systems in its own right and to synthesize the relevant limits into specifications for two practices builders already use for reliability, context engineering and the agent harness: what each agent’s context must contain, and what the harness around the agents must own and check.

Our first result, the Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem, makes the missing-information case precise. A policy can guarantee a valid action from its context exactly when every world consistent with that context allows a common action. When two worlds look identical but require different actions, no amount of reasoning, deliberation, role decomposition, messaging, or randomization can guarantee the right choice. The best randomized policy succeeds with probability exactly 1/k1/k when kk indistinguishable worlds have disjoint valid actions, and a bb-bit hint raises this to at most 1/⌈k/2b⌉1/\lceil k/2^{b}\rceil. This is a theorem about context engineering: it says exactly what a context must contain. Choosing the smallest such context is NP-hard: putting everything in every window is rarely feasible, and finding the least that suffices is hard.

The second failure survives full information. Three agents can each use a locally valid, inverse-consistent translation between neighboring units while the loop through all three does not close; three roles can each make a legal spend while the total breaks the budget. No local check identifies the global error, because it lives in how the pieces fit, not in any one piece. Checking harder locally does not solve this in general: pairwise checks suffice when overlaps are tree-like, cycles can defeat them, and no fixed locality bound works universally across unrestricted constraint semantics. The two failures are linked, and the link is the paper’s central construction. The impossibility theorem says which distinctions a harness must keep; the second failure is what happens when those distinctions are lost on the way, as state is split into local views, re-encoded between participants, or changed by actions. We give a principled synthesis for guarding all three steps: a topology of where things meet, sheaves for whether local states glue into one world, groupoids for which encodings mean the same thing, and categories for how actions compose over time. These structures are not uniquely forced machinery. Under explicit assumptions on local views, lossless translations, and state updates, each realizes a property that exact validation requires, and each becomes unnecessary when its corresponding map is absent. Version checks, dependency engines, ledgers, and escrow quotas are domain-specific realizations of the same requirements. The same language also prices the problem. Agreement across representations can be certified in linear time, yet finding the smallest repair can be NP-hard, and a shared budget cannot be protected by independent local checks at all: it must be enforced at commit or split into quotas. The design these two failures lead to goes further than a manager agent, which is one more participant with one more view and is bound by the same theorem: models propose, and a harness built on this framework decides what is allowed. The framework tells that harness its job: which distinctions it must own, where overlaps can hide global inconsistency, which loops of translation must close, and which changes must wait for commit.

We test the theory in nine studies. A frontier LLM solves all 40 tasks of a revision benchmark when it can see the deciding event. With that event hidden, observed accuracy across tested reasoning, role, voting, and tool conditions is statistically compatible with guessing among three options (1/31/3); one sentence restoring the missing fact brings it to 40/40. On a preregistered 60-run TeamBench panel, ordinary agent teams overspend a shared 20-call budget in 5/5 runs, showing them the live count still leaves 4/5, and enforcing the budget at commit leaves 0/5; observed mean task progress does not fall in this five-seed comparison. A follow-up on the same task shows that fixed per-role escrow quotas also reach 0/5 violations, while an information-only counter still overspends in 4/5; progress comparisons between escrow and the ledger are descriptive because their attestation gates differ. Under an explicit unique-name diagnostic, public ontology-alignment networks contain pairwise-invisible same-ontology identity collisions in 23 of 45 networks from 2018–2024. Agents given split views reproduce such collisions in 9 of 40 merges, and a network-level check detects and removes all nine, although the send-to-all repair lowers mean F1 from 0.796 to 0.774. In a preregistered 222-episode τ2\tau^{2}-bench Telecom panel, ordinary policy checks tie our coherence harness where the injected change breaks a policy rule, as predicted; where a committed change is silently undone, agents with those checks score 0.07 on the benchmark’s own grader and agents with the harness score 1.00. Where a conventional tool already holds the relevant state—a dependency engine, a coupled solver—it matches our harness exactly, as the theory predicts. Across all nine studies the pattern is the one the theory draws: the harness wins where the deciding state is missing or unowned, and ties where a conventional tool already owns it. The proofs are complete and given in the appendices; the agent evidence uses one model family and modest panels, and scale is the next step.

1 Introduction: every step looks right, and the result is still wrong

Consider a three-agent team on a TeamBench task [51]: a Planner writes the plan, an Executor runs commands, and a Verifier checks the result, with 20 command runs allowed for the whole team. Each agent spends runs for good reasons, and no single run is a mistake. But the limit belongs to the team, no agent owns it, and the team spends about three times the budget. This is the failure this paper is about: every step is locally justified, and together they break a rule that belongs to no one. Showing the team the running total did not fix it. When the harness itself held the count and refused the 21st run, the violations disappeared; observed mean task progress did not fall in that five-run panel (Study IV).

The pattern is general. In τ2\tau^{2}-bench Telecom, a user and an assistant change different parts of one environment under different permissions [12]; in BixBench3, several scientific artifacts must stay derived from one evolving analysis [25]. The participants act on local views, each step can be locally correct, and the combined result need not be:

local validity⇏global coherence.\boxed{\text{local validity}\;\not\Rightarrow\;\text{global coherence}.}
Two ways to fail.

Figure 1 sketches both. The first is observation aliasing: two situations look the same to every participant but need different actions, as when two revision histories produce the same log once one event is hidden. Our first result, the Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem (Theorem 2.1), says exactly when this is fatal: a policy can guarantee a valid action from what it observes—for an LLM agent, its context—if and only if every world consistent with that observation allows a common action. When that fails, no amount of reasoning, deliberation, role decomposition, messaging, or sampling recovers the difference; with kk look-alike worlds whose admissible-action sets are pairwise disjoint, the best randomized worst-case success is exactly 1/k1/k (Theorem 2.3). A stronger model searches better within its context; it cannot see past it. Context engineering helps exactly when it puts the missing distinction into the window, and longer reasoning over the same window does not. This separates intelligence from identifiability, for human, AI, and mixed teams alike. In Study I, a frontier LLM solves all 40 tasks when it can see the deciding event; when that event is hidden, observed accuracy across the tested inference strategies is compatible with chance (1/31/3), and one sentence of added context stating the missing fact brings it back to 40/40.

The second failure concerns information the participants do have. Everyone can pass the checks available in their local scope while the whole is not coherent, because locally consistent pieces need not fit together into any single global state. Three pairwise translations can each be well formed, inverse-consistent, and locally plausible while the loop through all three does not return to where it started; three roles can each make a legal spend while the total breaks the budget, as in the TeamBench team above.

Four questions.

The paper asks what can be said about these failures before choosing any particular agent design. We separate four questions:

  • •

    Observation. Do the local views contain enough information for globally valid behavior?

  • •

    Realization. Do locally compatible pieces correspond to any global state?

  • •

    Transition. Do local actions combine into a valid global change?

  • •

    Semantic state. What is the least information that must be kept to decide which futures remain valid?

Cost cuts across all four: how much state must be observed, how hard global checking is, how hard it is to design the smallest sufficient set of observables, and whether repairing an inconsistency is harder than detecting it.

The framework.

The first question has a sharp answer, the impossibility theorem, and it says what the harness must keep and every decision’s context must reach: every distinction that changes which actions are valid (Proposition 2.4). The rest of the paper answers how. In a team the state is never in one place and never still. It is split into local views, re-encoded between participants, and changed by actions, and each of these steps can silently lose a distinction the theorem says must be kept. Mathematics already has a precise structure for each step. Together they form the paper’s central construction,

𝔛=(H,𝒞,𝒢,ℱ,D).\boxed{\mathfrak{X}=(H,\mathcal{C},\mathcal{G},\mathcal{F};D).}

Figure 2 shows all five on one example: a Design agent, a Fabrication agent, and a Cost agent share one beam, and each records its length in its own unit.

  • •

    A topology HH: where things meet. HH records which participants’ scopes overlap, and on which shared state. Here all three agents hold the beam length, so HH is a triangle. In general it is a hypergraph, because one field can be shared by many participants at once. Its shape helps decide when local checks are enough: on join trees pairwise agreement suffices, while cycles can hide inconsistency from pairwise checks.

  • •

    A groupoid 𝒢\mathcal{G}: what only looks changed. The objects are the encodings of one thing (11 m, 10001000 mm, 39.3739.37 in) and the arrows are the translations between them (×1000\times 1000, ÷25.4\div 25.4, ×0.0254\times 0.0254). Every translation can be undone; that is what makes this a groupoid, which is like a group except that two arrows compose only when one ends where the other starts. The check that matters is that translations composed around any loop return the identity. A single wrong factor, ÷25\div 25 instead of ÷25.4\div 25.4, looks plausible on its own edge and brings 11 m back as 1.0161.016 m around the loop.

  • •

    A sheaf condition ℱ\mathcal{F}: whether one world glues. Each agent holds a local piece of data: 11 m, 10001000 mm, 39.3739.37 in. The sheaf condition asks whether pieces that agree on every overlap come from exactly one world, here exactly one beam. When it holds, local agreement is enough; when it fails, the pieces agree everywhere and come from no world at all. This is where “every agent is right and the team is wrong” becomes a condition a harness can check.

  • •

    A category 𝒞\mathcal{C}: what can change. The objects are versions of the shared state and the arrows are actions that really change it: revise the beam to 1.21.2 m, then order $720 of steel. Arrows compose into histories, most cannot be undone, and order matters, so this is a category rather than a groupoid. The line between the two is the line between 1​m→1000​mm1\,\mathrm{m}\to 1000\,\mathrm{mm}, which only re-expresses the beam, and 1​m→1.2​m1\,\mathrm{m}\to 1.2\,\mathrm{m}, which changes it. Only changes are checked at commit.

  • •

    A history state DD: what still matters. This is the theory of agent memory. Of the whole past, the harness keeps only what changes which future actions are legal: here the budget left and the version each agent last read. That is enough to refuse an order priced from the v3 quote once the beam is revised in v4. The rest of the log can be dropped.

This is a principled synthesis, not the only possible implementation. Corollary 4.2 shows that exact validation requires particular properties under explicit assumptions: realizable gluing for distributed views, reversible loop-consistent translations for lossless formats, and self-updating semantic state for actions and history. The named structures are standard, compositional realizations of those properties, and each drops out when its corresponding map is absent. The framework also absorbs what practitioners already use: version checks, dependency engines, ledgers, escrow quotas, and residual solvers are domain-specific realizations, and in our experiments each one matches the general harness exactly where it already owns the relevant state. Other routes exist—weakening the goal, restructuring state, accepting probabilistic success—and we price each one (Appendix F.4). Sections 3–4 develop the synthesis in the language of agent systems, and Section 4.3 derives the required properties and shows how these structures realize them; no category theory is needed to follow the argument.

What the theory says.

Beyond the impossibility theorem itself, we give the exact success rate of the best randomized policy in general (Theorem B.2) and the number of bits of new information needed to raise it (Corollary B.3). Choosing the smallest set of fields or sensors that makes validation exact is NP-hard (Theorem 2.5). For the second failure, classical database results say local agreement is enough on tree-like overlap structures (Theorem 3.1), while cycles can make pairwise agreement insufficient. More generally, no fixed locality order works universally across unrestricted constraint semantics (Proposition 3.2), although structured cyclic classes can admit bounded tests. Agreement across different representations reduces to a cycle check that a spanning forest certifies in linear time (Theorem 3.4, Corollary 3.5), but repairing a disagreement at minimum cost is NP-hard (Proposition 3.6). Actions that change state are different from actions that only re-express it: re-expressions preserve global consistency automatically, while individually valid spends against a shared budget can jointly break it (Propositions F.4 and 3.3). So consistency must be checked when changes are committed, and version checks with atomic commit give the usual serializability guarantee, provided every value a change depends on is recorded (Proposition 4.1).

Why “just give everyone all the information” is not the answer.

A natural reply is that the impossibility theorem is correct but easy to escape: share all the context, and every agent will be right about the whole. We claim more than the theorem. Its corollaries are correct, and global coherence stays hard even in principle, for five separate reasons.

  • •

    Sharing everything is rarely an option, and sharing the least is hard. Context windows, bandwidth, privacy, and authority limit what each participant can see. So the real question is what to share, and removing aliasing requires exposing every distinction that changes which actions are valid. Finding the smallest context—the fewest fields, sensors, or log entries—that does this is NP-hard, and greedy selection is essentially the best polynomial-time approximation (Theorem 2.5). Also, in a team each decision is made on the acting participant’s own information set, not on the union of everyone’s views (Corollary 2.2).

  • •

    Local agreement does not always add up. Pairwise checks are enough when the overlaps form a join tree. Cycles can defeat pairwise checks, and no fixed locality bound is universal across unrestricted constraint semantics; structured cyclic classes can nevertheless admit bounded tests (Theorem 3.1, Proposition 3.2). Exact global checking costs time exponential in the width of the interaction structure in the general finite-domain case (Section 3.4).

  • •

    Finding an error is easier than fixing it. A spanning forest certifies that representations agree in linear time, but finding the fewest labels to change is Max-Cut-hard (Proposition 3.6).

  • •

    Shared constraints need coordination. Spends that are each legal on their own can merge into an illegal total (Proposition 3.3). The ways out are coordination at commit or a redesign such as escrow quotas, and each has a price (Appendix F.4).

  • •

    Change and time add their own conditions. Re-expressing state preserves gluing, but changing state does not (Proposition F.4). A long-running process must carry exactly the history that still matters (Theorem F.3), and a commit is safe only if everything it read is still current (Proposition 4.1).

The theory also says when coherence is easy: when one participant can hold and act on the whole exact state, the extra structure should add little (Section 5.11, Prediction 1). The hard case is ordinary multi-party work, where authority, views, and shared resources are split. Sections 3 and 4 prove these points. Section 5 shows them in agent runs. Showing the live budget to every agent still leaves overspending in 4 of 5 runs, and only ownership at commit or escrow stops it (Study IV). A single agent with the full view keeps an alignment network coherent, but agents with split views leave conflicts that only a network-level check finds (Study IX). And checks on the current state miss what changed since the agent read it: in τ2\tau^{2}-bench Telecom they commit on a stale quote in 10 of 10 episodes, and they never notice when a committed change is silently undone (Study V).

Hardness results for decentralized decisions are known in pieces, from team decision theory to decentralized POMDPs (Section 6), and software and systems research has long supplied related compositional structures. This paper’s contribution is to synthesize those conditions for AI agent harnesses: one framework organizes missing distinctions, cycles, shared invariants, repair, and time, helps diagnose which conditions a system faces, and names standard structures that realize the required properties. The nine studies test these pieces, the central ones on agent benchmarks under a fixed model.

What this means for building agent systems.

The theory separates two jobs, and they map directly onto how agents are built today. The model supplies proposal intelligence: interpreting intent, planning, choosing tools, and drafting changes. The harness supplies state, admissibility, and commit: it decides what enters each agent’s context, holds the distinctions that matter, checks each proposed tool call against them, and accepts, repairs, or rejects it. Context engineering and harness design are usually practiced as craft; the theory turns them into specifications. The impossibility theorem says what a context must contain, and the framework says what the harness must own and check. The model can stay as flexible and stochastic as it likes; what must be fixed is the shared record of facts that decide what is allowed. Stronger models improve the first job. They cannot replace the second when the needed distinction is missing from what they see. The limits bind every layer. No matter how capable the model or how well engineered its context, a constraint that several agents act on needs an owner (Proposition 3.3, Study IV). And no matter how carefully the harness is built, it guarantees only what its own state can tell apart (Proposition 2.4), catches a contradiction around a loop only if some check spans the loop (Proposition 3.2), and catches a stale read only if it remembers what each proposal read, since against the current state alone a stale proposal and a fresh one look the same (Theorem 2.1 applied to the harness itself, Study V). The harness is also a different thing from a manager or orchestrator agent. A manager is a model too: it proposes from its own view, so Corollary 2.2 binds it like any other role, and in Study IV a team with a dedicated Planner and Verifier still overspent its budget when shown the live count. Where an orchestrator does work, the framework says why: a hub that holds the shared fields makes the overlaps a tree, and on trees local checks are enough (Section 3.1). The harness is not a smarter participant. It owns the state, and the framework tells it which state to own, what to put in context, and which checks to run. The same results answer the team-design questions practitioners usually settle by intuition: who should own a decision, which roles can work in parallel, and who must wait for whom (Section 4.5).

What the evidence shows.

The studies follow the two failure modes;11 1 The code and run records for all nine studies will be released. Figure 3 shows four causal results. A frontier LLM solves all 40 aliasing-probe tasks when it can see the deciding event; with that event hidden, all tested arms are statistically compatible with chance (1/31/3), and one sentence stating the missing fact restores 40/40 (Study I, Section 5.2). The finite panel supports the predicted contrast but does not establish empirical equivalence to chance. When actions change shared state, ordinary TeamBench teams overspend a shared budget in 5/5 runs, exposure leaves 4/5, and commit enforcement leaves 0/5; observed mean progress does not fall in the five-run enforced comparison (Study IV, Section 5.5). On the same budgeted task, per-role escrow quotas also reach 0/5 violations while an information-only counter still overspends in 4/5; progress differences between escrow and the ledger are descriptive because their attestation gates differ. Under an explicit unique-name diagnostic, public OAEI ontology-alignment networks [66] carry pairwise-invisible same-ontology identity collisions in 23 of 45 networks across seven years (Study VIII, Section 5.9). Agents given split views reproduce them in 9 of 40 merges, a single full-view agent leaves none, and a network-level check removes them all; the current send-to-all repair lowers mean F1 from 0.796 to 0.774, so detection succeeds while repair routing remains open (Study IX, Section 5.10). When state changes under a user and an assistant in τ2\tau^{2}-bench Telecom, ordinary policy checks tie the coherence harness where the change breaks a policy rule, as predicted; but they commit on a stale quote in 10 of 10 episodes, and when a committed change is silently undone they score 0.07 on the benchmark’s own grader while the harness scores 1.00 (Study V, Section 5.6). Where a conventional mechanism already owns the relevant state—dependency closure for stale derivations, a residual solver for coupled design—it matches the general harness exactly (Studies III and VI). The theory predicts that equality; the studies above test the boundaries where no such mechanism exists.

What is new.

This paper’s novelty is the agent-facing synthesis and operationalization. To our knowledge, it is the first work to formulate global coherence as a failure class of agent systems in its own right, separate identifiability and commit semantics from model capability, and assemble the relevant information-theoretic and local-to-global conditions into a framework that says what each agent’s context must contain and what the harness must enforce. The mathematical ingredients have important precedents, credited below; the contribution is connecting their guarantees and limits to agent harness design and testing the resulting boundary. The experiments probe its counterintuitive parts:

  • •

    A stronger model is not the fix for missing information. A model that solves every task when it can see the deciding fact produces accuracy statistically compatible with chance when that fact is hidden across the tested reasoning, deliberation, and voting conditions; one added sentence stating the fact solves every task again (Study I). The theorem supplies the general impossibility statement; the finite panel is consistent with it.

  • •

    More context is not the fix for shared state. Context fixes missing information, as Study I shows, but agents who have the live budget in their context still overspend it. A shared invariant needs an owner: enforcement at commit, or quotas that split it (Study IV).

  • •

    Checking every handoff is not the fix. Every pairwise review can pass while the integrated result is impossible, in public benchmark data and in agent runs alike (Studies VIII and IX).

  • •

    Checking the current state is not the fix. A commit can rest on a stale read, and a committed change can be silently undone, while every check on the current state passes (Study V).

The mathematics is deliberately borrowed, and that is a strength. Acyclic database schemes, group synchronization, sheaves, treewidth, Myhill–Nerode minimization, and optimistic concurrency control are each battle-tested in their own field, and we credit each where it appears. What was missing is the bridge to AI agents: identifying the validation properties distributed agent systems require, showing how these classical structures realize them under explicit assumptions, and telling builders when each property matters and when it does not. The new formal results serve that bridge: the admissibility form of the aliasing theorem with its exact randomized value and bit bounds, and the hardness of choosing the smallest state to expose, a close relative of minimal reducts in rough-set theory (Appendix A sorts every result by origin). The contribution is the bridge, not new mathematics. The empirical claims are deliberately narrower than the theory. They use one model family, a synthetic aliasing probe, five seeds per arm on three TeamBench tasks, and failures that we inject into τ2\tau^{2}-bench tasks. Within that scope the result is that the predicted failures occur, the tested inference variations do not remove them, and owning the missing state does. How often these failures dominate on broad agent benchmarks is the next question, and the theory says where to look.

Contributions of this paper.
  • •

    A limit on what reasoning can fix. The Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem and its quantitative forms: the exact success rate of the best randomized policy, the number of bits of new state needed, and extensions to multi-agent protocols and tool use. For AI systems the message is direct: more reasoning, more agents, more messages, and more samples cannot recover a distinction that none of them can see. Adding the missing state to context can, and the smallest such context is exactly the one that keeps apart worlds allowing different actions.

  • •

    One framework for local-to-global coherence. A topology says where things meet, sheaves ask whether local views glue into one world, groupoids record which encodings mean the same thing, and categories describe how actions compose over time. Under explicit assumptions, we derive the properties exact validation requires and use these standard structures as a compositional realization of them. This turns “every agent passes its local checks and the team is wrong” from an anecdote into a condition a harness can check, and it explains why familiar tools work exactly where they do.

  • •

    The price of coherence. Local checks suffice on join-tree overlap structures; cycles can defeat pairwise checks, and no fixed locality bound works universally across unrestricted constraint semantics. Agreement across encodings can be certified in linear time, while the smallest repair can be NP-hard. A shared budget cannot be protected by independent local checks, and choosing the smallest state to expose is NP-hard. The cost depends on how the parts interact, not on how many agents there are.

  • •

    A specification for agent harnesses. Models propose; a harness that owns the state decides what is allowed, and the framework specifies exactly what it must hold, what it must put into context, and what it must check. This goes beyond a manager agent, which proposes from its own view like any other role. The model can stay stochastic. Version checks, dependency engines, ledgers, and escrow quotas are special cases, and the theory says when each is enough. For builders this gives a concrete rule: when a multi-agent system fails, first ask which distinction no one owns, before asking for a bigger model or more agents.

  • •

    Evidence that the theory predicts where the harness helps and where it does not. Nine studies, four of them causal agent experiments frozen before scoring: a controlled aliasing probe, TeamBench, τ2\tau^{2}-bench Telecom, and ontology alignment. The harness removes the targeted failures without a stronger model, and it ties conventional tools exactly where those tools already own the state.

2 Model and the limit of reasoning

This section states the result everything else rests on: no amount of reasoning recovers a distinction that is not in view. We keep only what later sections use. The quantitative refinements, and all proofs, are in Appendix B.

2.1 What participants see and what they may do

The model needs three ingredients: the worlds that could be true, what each participant sees, and which actions are allowed in each world. Let XX be the set of possible global states and 𝒜\mathcal{A} the set of actions. For each state xx, let C⁡(x)⊆𝒜C(x)\subseteq\mathcal{A} be the actions allowed there. CC can encode anything that decides legality: authority, budgets, invariants, freshness, or required artifacts. A participant does not see xx itself; it sees an observation y=Ω⁡(x)y=\Omega(x). In a team, Ω⁡(x)\Omega(x) can be the tuple of everyone’s local views (Ω1​(x),…,Ωm​(x))(\Omega_{1}(x),\ldots,\Omega_{m}(x)). A runtime, in turn, remembers some summary ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) of the state. So Ω\Omega is what a decision-maker can see, and ϕ\phi is what the runtime keeps. In agent-engineering terms, Ωi\Omega_{i} is agent ii’s context—its prompt, retrieved documents, tool results, and memory—and the runtime is the agent harness, the code around the model that assembles that context, executes tool calls, and decides which of them take effect. We use “runtime” and “harness” interchangeably.

For the local-to-global part we need one more object. Split a scope UU into local scopes U1,…,UnU_{1},\ldots,U_{n}: participants’ views, subsystems, or artifacts. Write X⁡(U)X(U) for global states and Match⁡({Ui})\mathrm{Match}(\{U_{i}\}) for tuples of local states that agree wherever scopes overlap. Restricting a global state to its local pieces gives a map

ρ:X⁡(U)→Match⁡({Ui}).\rho:X(U)\rightarrow\mathrm{Match}(\{U_{i}\}).

Both failures from the introduction are properties of this one map. In aliasing, ρ\rho is not one-to-one: two different worlds give the same local views. In non-realizability, ρ\rho is not onto: locally matching pieces come from no world at all. A coherent system needs ρ\rho to be a bijection. That is exactly the sheaf condition; with representations identified up to equivalence, it becomes the descent condition [76, 77, 78]. This section is about the first failure; Section 3 develops the second.

2.2 The impossibility theorem

The central result makes a simple point exact: no policy can act on a distinction it cannot see. The idea has a long history, as perceptual aliasing in reinforcement learning [82] and as indistinguishability arguments in distributed computing [29]. What we add is the exact condition for choosing a valid action, and what it implies for teams, randomness, tools, and hints.

In words: a policy can always pick a valid action exactly when, for every observation, all the worlds that could be behind it share at least one valid action.

Theorem 2.1 (Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem).

Let Ω:X→Y\Omega:X\to Y and C:X→2𝒜C:X\to 2^{\mathcal{A}}. There exists a deterministic policy π:Y→𝒜\pi:Y\to\mathcal{A} satisfying

π⁡(Ω⁡(x))∈C⁡(x)∀x∈X\pi(\Omega(x))\in C(x)\qquad\forall x\in X

if and only if every observation fiber has a common admissible action:

∀y∈Ω⁡(X),⋂x∈Ω−1​(y)C⁡(x)≠∅.\forall y\in\Omega(X),\qquad\bigcap_{x\in\Omega^{-1}(y)}C(x)\neq\varnothing.

Proof sketch. If a universally valid policy exists, its action π⁡(y)\pi(y) must be admissible for every state in the fiber Ω−1​(y)\Omega^{-1}(y), hence lies in the intersection. Conversely, choose one action from each nonempty intersection. Appendix B gives the full proof.

The typical case has two worlds that look identical, Ω⁡(x)=Ω⁡(x′)\Omega(x)=\Omega(x^{\prime}), but allow disjoint actions, C⁡(x)∩C⁡(x′)=∅C(x)\cap C(x^{\prime})=\varnothing. Then no policy that acts on the observation can be right in both.

What this means.

If two different realities give a group the same evidence but need different decisions, the group cannot guarantee the right decision from that evidence, and this holds for any decision process whose complete available information is Ω⁡(x)\Omega(x): one AI agent, a team of agents, a human organization, or a human–AI collaboration. Take the revision log from the introduction. Three teams commit, revert, and re-apply changes to one shared parameter, and before writing, an agent must name the current head; if the last event is hidden, three different histories produce the same log but leave three different heads. Whatever head the agent names, it is wrong in two of the three worlds, and only recovering the hidden event changes that, which is exactly what Study I tests.

More agents do not help.

The same holds for any team that only talks among itself.

Corollary 2.2 (Reasoning and role decomposition do not create missing state information).

Consider any deterministic multi-round protocol whose agents begin with local observations Ω1​(x),…,Ωm​(x)\Omega_{1}(x),\ldots,\Omega_{m}(x) and thereafter exchange messages computed only from those observations and prior messages. If no new external observation is introduced, the complete transcript and final action are functions only of the joint initial observation Ω⁡(x)\Omega(x). Therefore states aliased by the joint observation remain indistinguishable regardless of the number of agents, roles, reasoning rounds, or messages.

The proof is an induction over communication rounds: every message is computed from what the agents saw, so the whole transcript is too. Randomness does not help either; it changes which answer is chosen, not which worlds can be told apart. The corollary also has a positive reading. When a team fails on a distinction that its joint observation does contain, the failure is one of protocol—who sends what, and who owns which decision—not an impossibility. And the theorem applies at every single decision: an action taken by one role is limited by what that role has seen and been told, not by the union of everyone’s views.

How much can randomness, tools, and hints buy?

The impossibility theorem answers a yes-or-no question: can a policy always pick a valid action? When the answer is no, two questions remain: how often can a policy still be right, and what would it take to do better? The table answers each in one line:

Question Answer Result
Can randomizing help? With kk look-alike worlds whose admissible-action sets are pairwise disjoint, no randomized policy or team does better than 1/k1/k in the worst case. Theorem 2.3
Exactly how well, in general? The best guaranteed success is 1/τ∗1/\tau^{*}, the value of a small linear program over the look-alike worlds. Randomizing helps only when valid actions partly overlap. Theorem B.2
How much new state fixes it? A bb-bit hint gives at most 1/⌈k/2b⌉1/\lceil k/2^{b}\rceil in the worst case. Anything short of ⌈log2⁡k⌉\lceil\log_{2}k\rceil bits leaves it at a coin flip or worse. Corollary B.3
When do tools help? A tool result is a new observation. Tools help exactly when some sequence of queries splits the look-alike worlds into groups that each share a valid action. Theorem B.4
Does “good enough” escape it? No. The same condition holds with “valid” replaced by “within ε\varepsilon of optimal.” Proposition B.5

We state the first in full, because it is the one the experiments test most directly.

Theorem 2.3 (Randomized aliasing bound).

Let x1,…,xkx_{1},\ldots,x_{k} be states that are indistinguishable to the base observation and whose nonempty admissible-action sets C⁡(xi)C(x_{i}) are pairwise disjoint. Then any randomized policy using no additional semantic state has worst-case success probability at most

1k.\frac{1}{k}.

The bound applies equally to one stochastic agent or to a randomized multi-agent protocol that receives no new external observation of which state is present.

Proof sketch. All kk worlds induce the same output distribution. Because their valid-action sets are disjoint, the kk success probabilities sum to at most one, so at least one is at most 1/k1/k. Conditioning on the internal random seed gives the same conclusion for randomized multi-agent protocols. Appendix B gives the full proof.

Example.

Suppose a shared project dashboard makes ten globally different situations look identical, while each situation requires a different intervention. A stochastic agent may randomize, debate, self-critique, or sample many chains of thought, but without new state information it must use the same output distribution in all ten worlds. Its worst-case success therefore cannot exceed 10%10\%. This is directly relevant to agent benchmarks: more inference-time compute can improve reasoning inside one observed world, but it cannot identify which member of an aliased family is actually present.

Two lessons follow for AI. Inference compute and semantic state are different resources, and one cannot pay for the other. And new information can be counted: extra roles, tokens, or rounds help exactly when they bring in a distinction that splits look-alike worlds. Study I tests this directly, comparing more reasoning with the same observation against the same reasoning with one added distinction (Section 5.2).

2.3 What the runtime must keep

The fix follows. Coherence should not depend on every participant rebuilding the whole world in its head. The runtime should hold the distinctions that change which actions are valid, and check proposals against them. How much must it hold?

A runtime that rejects everything is perfectly safe and perfectly useless, so we separate soundness (never accept an invalid action), progress (accept something when possible), and completeness (accept every valid action). If the runtime remembers only z=ϕ⁡(x)z=\phi(x), let XzX_{z} be the worlds that share that summary. The most it can safely accept is

Csafe​(z)=⋂x∈XzC⁡(x).C_{\mathrm{safe}}(z)=\bigcap_{x\in X_{z}}C(x).
Proposition 2.4 (Maximal sound abstraction).

Any sound validator based only on zz must accept a subset of Csafe​(z)C_{\mathrm{safe}}(z). Hence nonblocking progress at zz is possible if and only if Csafe​(z)≠∅C_{\mathrm{safe}}(z)\neq\varnothing. Exact validation of arbitrary proposals is possible if and only if

ϕ⁡(x)=ϕ⁡(x′)⟹C⁡(x)=C⁡(x′).\phi(x)=\phi(x^{\prime})\Longrightarrow C(x)=C(x^{\prime}).

In words: the runtime can safely accept exactly what is valid in every world it cannot tell apart, and it can judge every proposal correctly only if it never merges two worlds that allow different actions. The smallest such state is the quotient

x∼Cx′⇔C(x)=C(x′).x\sim_{C}x^{\prime}\iff C(x)=C(x^{\prime}).

The “authoritative semantic state” means: not a copy of the whole world, but every distinction that can change whether a proposal is valid. The model does not need the whole world in its prompt. Instead, the harness can hold that state outside the model and put into each decision’s context only what it needs. For context engineering this is the exact target: a context is sufficient precisely when it never merges two worlds that allow different actions.

However, knowing what must be kept does not make it easy to find. Suppose a designer has candidate fields, sensors, or log entries and wants the fewest that make validation exact.

Theorem 2.5 (Minimum exact instrumentation is NP-hard).

Given a finite state set, admissibility profiles, and candidate observables, finding a minimum-cardinality subset of observables sufficient for exact proposal validation is NP-hard.

The proof reduces Set Cover (Appendix B.3). Greedy selection is essentially the best polynomial-time approximation, and the problem is a close relative of finding minimal reducts in rough-set theory [72]. This is a hardness result about design, not about running the system: checking a proposal against a chosen state can be cheap even when finding the smallest sufficient state is hard. It is the first reason that “just share everything” is not an answer.

3 When every agent is right and the team is still wrong

Section 2 was about information that no one has. This section is about information that everyone has, but in pieces. Each agent’s piece passes every check the agent can run, and the pieces still add up to no possible world. It happens in three ways in agent systems—pieces compared pairwise, a budget no one owns, and translations between formats—and each is a place where the framework earns its keep. For each, a sharp result says exactly when local checks are enough and what it costs when they are not, and each turns into a design rule. Proofs are in Appendices C and D.

3.1 Pairwise checks miss loops

Consider three agents that each own one variable and each reconcile with a neighbor. The A–B check requires A=BA=B, the B–C check requires B=CB=C, and the A–C check requires A≠CA\neq C. Each check can be satisfied, and so can any two of them together. No assignment satisfies all three: the first two force A=CA=C, and the third forbids it. Replace the Booleans with “uses schema v2,” “the deadline moved,” or “these two records are the same customer,” and this is a familiar failure of multi-agent pipelines: every handoff review passes, and the integrated result is impossible (Figure 1b).

The question underneath is whether local states that agree on every overlap come from one global state; in the notation of Section 2.1, whether ρ\rho is onto. An assignment of states to scopes for which the answer is always yes, and uniquely so, is called a sheaf [67, 6]. That is the right name for it: the sheaf condition is precisely the statement that local agreement implies one global state, so it gives a runtime an exact target to check. A sheaf specifies what coherence means; search and repair are separate steps.

One detail matters for agent design. The false pass happens when agents compare what each considers possible—constraints, plans, ranges—rather than what each has committed to. If every agent commits to a concrete value, comparing committed values on overlaps catches the triangle. Agents usually exchange the former. (This is the possibilistic contextuality of Abramsky and Brandenburger [2]; Appendix C.)

When are pairwise checks enough? Database theory has a sharp answer, and it depends only on the shape of who overlaps with whom.

Theorem 3.1 (Tree-shaped overlaps suffice; Beeri, Fagin, Maier, and Yannakakis [14, 15]).

If the overlap structure of the local constraints is acyclic (formally, α\alpha-acyclic: it has a join tree), then local constraints that agree pairwise are globally consistent. If it has a cycle, some pairwise-consistent family of local constraints is not.

A planner–coder–tester chain is a tree. So is a hub-and-spoke team in which every agent reconciles only with an orchestrator that holds the shared fields. A review loop, or three teams that each share an interface with the other two, is a cycle. Cycles remove the pairwise guarantee, and increasing the checked group size has no universal fixed bound across unrestricted constraint families:

Proposition 3.2 (No fixed-size check is enough).

For every kk, there is a finite set of local constraints in which every kk of them can be satisfied together, but all of them cannot.

The construction is a parity puzzle on a ring of more than kk agents. Any proper subset of the constraints can be satisfied, and only the sum of all of them exposes the contradiction (Appendix C.2). Algorithms that propagate derived constraints, rather than check groups in isolation, do solve rings, but on expander-shaped interaction graphs they too fail at every fixed level. Some structured problems do have a fixed check size—Helly’s theorem gives d+1d+1 for convex constraints in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} [58]—so the useful question for a given system is which structure it has.

Design rule. If the agents’ overlaps form a join tree, pairwise reconciliation is enough. Cycles remove that guarantee: use a global method appropriate to the constraint class, or restructure the overlaps into a join tree. For translation networks, Section 3.3 gives the exact loop check.

3.2 A shared budget needs an owner

A different failure arises when a constraint lives in no agent’s scope. Give mm agents a shared budget BB of tool calls, test runs, or dollars, and let each track its own spend sis_{i}. Each spend is legal on its own, and the agents share no variables, so there is nothing to compare: every local check passes. Nothing stops ∑isi>B\sum_{i}s_{i}>B. More checking between agents cannot help, because no agent’s view contains the total. This is the TeamBench failure of Study IV.

Proposition 3.3 (A shared budget cannot be protected by independent checks).

For m≥2m\geq 2 agents and B≥1B\geq 1, two agents can each make a spend that is legal from a common valid state, while the two spends together exceed the budget. In database terms, the spend transactions are not invariant-confluent [9], so protecting the budget requires coordination or a restructured budget.

Two fixes work. An authoritative ledger that checks the total at commit adds a scope that contains the constraint. Escrow quotas BiB_{i} with ∑iBi=B\sum_{i}B_{i}=B split the constraint into local ones, at the cost of flexibility: one agent cannot borrow another’s unused share. Locks and reservations are further options. Study IV runs both fixes against an information-only alternative; Appendix F.4 compares them.

Design rule. Name an owner for every constraint that spans agents. Showing the number to everyone is not ownership.

3.3 Translations that each look right can fail around a loop

Agents translate constantly. One reports meters and another feet; one emits a JSON schema and another a SQL table; a matcher says class XX in one ontology is class YY in another; a refactor renames a function. Call two descriptions equivalent when a meaning-preserving translation connects them and can be undone. A collection of such reversible translations is a groupoid, or a group when the same translations apply to everything. The name carries real content, because it says what to keep: not just the fact that two things are equivalent, but the translation itself.

Here is why. Put agents on the nodes of a graph, and let each edge carry a translation gi​jg_{ij} from agent ii’s format to agent jj’s, with gj​i=gi​j−1g_{ji}=g_{ij}^{-1}. The system is globally consistent if one underlying object explains every agent’s description: there are frames hih_{i} with gi​j=hi​hj−1g_{ij}=h_{i}h_{j}^{-1}. This is the noiseless group-synchronization problem [54].

Theorem 3.4 (Loops decide consistency).

The translations are globally consistent exactly when following them around every loop returns to the identity.

One direction is a telescoping product; the other builds frames along a spanning tree. That construction is also the practical algorithm:

Corollary 3.5 (A linear-time consistency check).

Pick a spanning forest of the agent graph, fix one frame per tree, and propagate frames along the trees. Then check each remaining edge against the frames at its two ends. The translations are consistent exactly when every such check passes. With |V||V| agents, |E||E| translation edges, and cc connected components, this takes β1=|E|−|V|+c\beta_{1}=|E|-|V|+c edge checks and O⁡(|V|+|E|)O(|V|+|E|) compose-and-compare operations, although the graph can contain exponentially many loops.

Each edge beyond the forest adds one independent constraint; for a finite group, a uniformly random labeling is consistent with probability |G|−β1|G|^{-\beta_{1}} (Appendix D). A loop whose translations do not compose to the identity is said to have nontrivial holonomy. The triangle of Section 3.1 is the smallest example: write “same” as 00 and “opposite” as 11, and the loop sums to 0+0+1=1≠00+0+1=1\neq 0. In ontology matching the same structure appears as a chain of “same as” links that joins two distinct classes of one ontology. No single link looks wrong; only the loop shows the conflict (Studies VIII and IX).

Why canonical IDs are not enough.

A tempting shortcut is to map every description to a canonical form—a canonical ID, an embedding, a normalized schema—and compare those. That keeps whether two things are equivalent and throws away how. It can hide exactly the failure above: every description looks the same after canonicalization while the loop of translations still does not close (Study VII; Appendix F.1). Edits that change the object, such as revising a beam from 1​m1\,\mathrm{m} to 1.2​m1.2\,\mathrm{m}, are not translations at all. They are state changes, treated in Section 4.2.

Design rule. Keep the translations, not just the equivalence classes, and check every loop. A spanning forest does this in linear time.

3.4 Structure, not agent count, sets the price

How expensive is coherence? Three results say the answer depends on how agents interact, not on how many there are.

Exact checking is exponential only in width.

For finite-domain constraints, dynamic programming over a tree decomposition checks global consistency in time roughly O⁡(n​dw+1)O(nd^{w+1}) for nn variables of domain size dd and treewidth ww [33]. For general constraint problems the exponential dependence on width cannot be substantially removed [40, 57] (Appendix D.2). A hundred agents in a pipeline can be cheap to keep coherent; five densely coupled agents can be expensive.

A small signature can track a large constraint.

For linear constraints, whether the pieces fit is decided by one short vector, the syndrome, computed from the local specifications by linear algebra. When updates can shift it arbitrarily, the syndrome is also the least a monitor must remember to track coherence over time (Theorem D.3). The ring puzzle that defeats every fixed-size check has a one-bit syndrome. Needing a global witness is not the same as being expensive to monitor.

Finding a conflict is cheap; fixing it optimally is not.
Proposition 3.6 (Minimum repair is Max-Cut-hard).

For “same/opposite” labels on a graph, Corollary 3.5 decides consistency in linear time, but finding the fewest labels whose change makes the graph consistent is NP-hard.

With every label set to “opposite,” the fewest changes equals the number of edges minus the maximum cut, so the problem contains Max-Cut [50, 34] (Appendix D.3). The same gap holds for general linear constraints, where minimum repair is syndrome decoding [17].

Design rule. Check before commit rather than repair afterward. Detecting an inconsistency at commit is cheap; deciding afterward which agent’s output to change can be the hard part.

4 From theory to a coherence harness

Sections 2 and 3 say what can go wrong. This section proposes a runtime, the coherence harness: how it sits next to the model, what it checks when a proposal would change the world, what it remembers, and why the structures from the introduction—a topology, a category, a groupoid, and a sheaf condition—are the ones it needs. It closes with what the same results say about organizing the team around the harness.

4.1 The harness loop

The results hold for any decision process, but LLM agents make them urgent. An LLM policy is useful because it is flexible: it infers intent, plans, chooses tools, and adapts. The same flexibility makes its proposals stochastic and hard to certify end to end. The runtime therefore splits the work. Agent ii proposes from its context,

a~t∼πθ(⋅∣Ωi(xt),mt,𝒯i),\widetilde{a}_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\Omega_{i}(x_{t}),m_{t},\mathcal{T}_{i}),

where mtm_{t} is its memory and 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} its tools. The runtime checks the proposal against its authoritative state zt=ϕ⁡(xt)z_{t}=\phi(x_{t}),

V⁡(zt,a~t)∈{accept,repair,reject},V(z_{t},\widetilde{a}_{t})\in\{\operatorname{accept},\operatorname{repair},\operatorname{reject}\},

and only accepted changes produce xt+1x_{t+1}. The checks can cover identity, authority, freshness, budgets, format compatibility, and required artifacts. The model stays stochastic; the rule for what may change does not have to be. Figure 4 shows the split.

The split separates three questions that agent research usually blurs. Capability asks whether the model can propose a useful action. Identifiability asks whether the available state contains enough information to determine which actions are valid. Commit correctness asks whether accepted local actions keep the whole system consistent. Agent benchmarks usually score all three at once. The theory predicts cases where scaling capability saturates because the bottleneck is identifiability or commit semantics, not reasoning strength.

4.2 What the runtime checks at commit

Re-expressing state is safe; changing it is not.

Two kinds of action look alike in an agent log but behave differently. A re-expression—converting units, translating a schema, re-encoding a record—leaves the underlying object unchanged. A state change—spending budget, editing a design, overwriting a file—does not. If every agent only re-expresses its state and the translations agree where scopes overlap, the result is automatically globally consistent. If agents change state, each change can be locally legal and every overlap can agree while the combination is still no valid world; the shared budget of Section 3.2 is the example. So re-expressions need no commit-time check, and state changes do. Proposition F.4 (Appendix F.6) states this precisely. By induction, a trajectory in which every committed step is a re-expression or was checked at commit stays coherent. This is why the framework keeps re-expressions in the groupoid 𝒢\mathcal{G} and changes in the category 𝒞\mathcal{C}: the split is exactly the line between what needs no check and what does.

Keep only the history that changes the future.

Agent memory grows without bound, and most of it does not affect what is legal next. Two histories can share one memory state exactly when every possible continuation is legal after one if and only if it is legal after the other. This is the Myhill–Nerode theorem [46]: the smallest exact monitor has one state per such class. For a budget BB and kk obligations that must be done before finish, the smallest state is the obvious pair, remaining budget and completed obligations: (B+1)​2k+2(B+1)2^{k}+2 states, but only ⌈log2⁡(B+1)⌉+k\lceil\log_{2}(B+1)\rceil+k bits plus a terminal flag (Appendix E). Provenance, such as which version an artifact was derived from, belongs in memory exactly when it changes which futures are legal. A stale derivation is the standard case (Study III).

Stale reads and atomic commit.

An agent reads state, thinks for several turns, and proposes a change. By then the state may have moved. The classical fix is optimistic concurrency control [52]: record the version of everything the proposal depended on, and at commit atomically check that none of it has changed before applying the change.

Proposition 4.1 (Version checks give one-at-a-time semantics).

Suppose every proposal records every state item it depended on, every write advances the written item’s version, and the version check and the writes happen atomically. Then the committed changes are equivalent to running them one at a time in commit order.

For an LLM agent the first condition is the hard one. The read set is every authoritative item that entered the model’s context and influenced the proposal, not only the items the final tool call touches. A quote the agent read five turns ago belongs to the read set of the order it places now; this is what ordinary τ2\tau^{2}-bench checks miss (Study V). The model’s sampled output is part of the transaction, so the equivalence is to serial execution with the same samples (Appendix E.2).

4.3 Why sheaves, groupoids, and categories

The impossibility theorem says only that the runtime must keep every distinction that changes which actions are valid (Proposition 2.4), and in a simple system one ledger field does that. The structures appear because in a multi-agent system that state is never in one place and never still. It passes through maps, and each map can lose a distinction the theorem says must be kept. Each structure is the condition that its map loses nothing.

Map What goes wrong in an agent system What the runtime must guarantee Structure Studies
world →\to agents’ views two worlds look the same to every agent; or views fit pairwise but match no world views jointly separate worlds that allow different actions; committed views glue sheaf (HH, ℱ\mathcal{F}) I, IV, IX
format →\to format a lossy translation merges objects; translations disagree around a loop translations are reversible and close around every loop groupoid (𝒢\mathcal{G}) VII–IX
state →\to next state the runtime must re-read the world after each step to know what is legal its state updates itself, and updates compose category (𝒞\mathcal{C}) IV, V
history →\to memory memory forgets what still matters, or keeps what never will keep history exactly when it changes legal futures history (DD) III, V
Splitting state into views needs gluing.

A runtime that reads only the agents’ local views can be exact only if the views jointly tell apart every two worlds that allow different actions; this is the impossibility theorem applied to the map from the world to the views. And it commits only states that some real world produces exactly when it rejects every combination of views that matches pairwise but comes from no world. These are the two conditions that define a sheaf, with one weakening that matters in practice: the views need to separate worlds only by which actions they allow, not in every detail (Proposition F.1). Section 3 showed both failures.

Translating between formats needs a groupoid.

A translation cannot restore a distinction its source format already lost: if agent ii’s format merges two objects, every format translated from it merges them too. When every format is lossless, the translations between them are forced: each can be undone, and composing them around any loop returns the identity. Conversely, any family of reversible translations that closes around every loop comes from lossless encodings of one object (Proposition F.2). That is exactly a groupoid with consistent loops, and Corollary 3.5 checks it.

Acting needs a self-updating state.

A runtime that must re-read the world after every action to know what is now legal is not keeping state; it is polling. For the runtime to update its own state, the state must keep apart any two worlds that some future sequence of actions would tell apart. A budget shows the difference. With one or two units left, the same actions are legal now, but after one spend they are not. “May spend now” is exact for one step; the remaining count is the smallest state that updates itself (Theorem F.3, the Myhill–Nerode construction applied to valid actions [46, 60]). Because the updates compose—updating for aa and then for bb is updating for a​bab—actions act on the runtime’s state as a category. The history state DD is the same construction indexed by histories.

Corollary 4.2 (Where each structure is needed).

Consider a runtime that must accept exactly the valid actions and commit only realizable states. If it accepts arbitrary combinations of local views at commit, it needs the gluing check. If agents use several lossless formats, it needs reversible, loop-consistent translations. If it must update its state under actions without re-reading the world, it needs the self-updating state. Conversely, with one scope there is nothing to glue, with one format there is nothing to translate, and when no action changes the state the self-updating state reduces to the exact state of Proposition 2.4.

This is the sense in which the framework is principled rather than arbitrary. Remove a map and its corresponding property drops out; add the map under the assumptions above and exact validation requires that property. The named mathematical structure is a standard compositional realization, not the only possible implementation.

Appendix F.3 gives the precise conditions and proofs. The corollary is what the predictions of Section 5.11 test: each structure should help where its map can lose information, and add only overhead elsewhere. It also explains the ties in Studies III and VI. The corollary constrains properties, not machinery. A version counter, a dependency engine, or a residual solver meets the relevant condition in its own domain, and there it should match the general runtime. The structures are the general way to meet the conditions across boundaries where no such mechanism exists.

The same pattern—first a requirement for sufficient information, then a structure chosen to preserve it as it is distributed—appears in team decision theory, in atlases of charts in geometry, in sufficient statistics and filtering, and in version control, where a merge conflict is a gluing failure (Appendix F.3). The impossibility theorem does not force this design on its own. Weakening the goal, querying for the information, restructuring the state, or accepting probabilistic success are legitimate alternatives, each with a cost (Appendix F.4).

4.4 The framework assembled: 𝔛=(H,𝒞,𝒢,ℱ,D)\mathfrak{X}=(H,\mathcal{C},\mathcal{G},\mathcal{F};D)

Putting the pieces together gives the framework of the introduction as five runtime components: HH, where things meet; 𝒞\mathcal{C}, what can change; 𝒢\mathcal{G}, what only looks changed; ℱ\mathcal{F}, whether one world glues; and DD, what still matters. Figure 2 shows them on one example; the table says what each does and what fails without it.

Question Component What it does What fails without it
What is local? dependency graph HH scope, authority, impact, dependencies a missed dependency, or a change that propagates unchecked
What do actions do? action semantics 𝒞\mathcal{C} preconditions, effects, and how actions compose an invalid order, or results that depend on the path taken
What is the same? translations 𝒢\mathcal{G} identity and format translation duplicated objects, or a loop of translations that does not close
What fits together? gluing check ℱ\mathcal{F} overlap and realization checks at commit locally compatible pieces with no global state
What still matters? history state DD versions, invalidation, obligations, resources a stale derivation, or a forgotten obligation

For readers who know the categorical form: the translations 𝒢\mathcal{G} make the assignment of states to the scopes of HH a groupoid-valued presheaf 𝒮\mathcal{S}, the gluing check ℱ\mathcal{F} is its descent condition, and 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a category-valued prestack whose groupoid core is 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Appendix F.3 spells this out. The experiments use only the concrete checks; the formalism is what guarantees that those checks are the right ones.

The architecture in one sentence.

A model supplies proposals; an authoritative state holds the distinctions that matter; a governed commit decides which proposals change the world. The model can remain stochastic. The runtime need not reproduce its chain of thought and need not replace domain solvers. It must own the distinctions required by Theorem 2.1 and Proposition 2.4, check global consistency where local checks are not enough, and check state changes at commit.

Each component catches failures the others cannot see, so none of them is redundant. Two systems can agree on every other component and still differ on the one in question. The same dependency graph HH can carry different action semantics 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The same local actions can pass every local check and still fail the gluing check ℱ\mathcal{F}. Two records with identical fields can be different objects, and two with different schemas can be the same one; only 𝒢\mathcal{G} tells them apart. Identical current values can differ in whether they are still valid; only DD tells them apart. Appendix F.2 gives a small countermodel for each.

4.5 Designing the team: owners, dependencies, and parallel work

Multi-agent systems today are organized by job title. A tech lead oversees the project, engineers do the work, and the pricing role waits until the design is done. These choices are made by human intuition. They are often right, but nothing says when they are necessary or what else would work. The framework turns each of them into a question about state, and each question has an answer among the results above. Fix the roles 1,…,m1,\ldots,m. For role ii, let WiW_{i} be the items of authoritative state its proposals write, and let RiR_{i} be every item whose value can change whether its proposals are valid. RiR_{i} therefore includes the scope of every constraint the proposal must respect, not only the fields the tool call touches. In the beam example of Figure 2, the Cost agent’s quote has Rcost∋beam lengthR_{\mathrm{cost}}\ni\text{beam length}, which the Design agent writes, and both agents’ spends read the shared budget.

  1. 1.

    Give each role the distinctions its decisions need. The harness can reject an invalid proposal, but it cannot make a role propose a valid one. Role ii can always propose an admissible action exactly when every fiber of its own context Ωi\Omega_{i} has a common admissible action for that role (Theorem 2.1); otherwise the harness keeps rejecting it. Its information set is its own: a decision taken by role ii is bounded by Ωi\Omega_{i} and the messages it has received, not by the union of all views (Corollary 2.2). A context that never merges two worlds allowing that role different actions is always sufficient (Proposition 2.4). Finding the smallest one is NP-hard (Theorem 2.5), so in practice it is chosen greedily.

  2. 2.

    Give every cross-role constraint an owner. A constraint whose scope lies in no single role’s WiW_{i}, and whose actions are not invariant-confluent, cannot be protected by the roles checking independently (Proposition 3.3 for a budget; Bailis et al. [9] in general). It needs either a scope that contains it and is checked at commit (a ledger), or a split into local constraints (escrow, ∑iBi=B\sum_{i}B_{i}=B); locks, reservations, and conservative stopping are costlier alternatives (Appendix F.4). In the formal sense this is what leading means: the lead for a constraint is whichever component holds its whole scope and refuses violating commits. A person or an agent can lead in this sense only by holding that state authoritatively and controlling the commit, which is the harness’s job. A lead agent that receives only summaries is one more Ωi\Omega_{i}, and Corollary 2.2 binds it like any other role. Study IV shows the difference: a team with a Planner and a Verifier overspent when shown the live count, and both an owning ledger and escrow quotas stopped it.

  3. 3.

    Decide parallel or sequential from read and write sets. If Wi∩Rj=Wj∩Ri=Wi∩Wj=∅W_{i}\cap R_{j}=W_{j}\cap R_{i}=W_{i}\cap W_{j}=\varnothing, neither role can invalidate the other. Committing them in either order gives the same state, and the version check of Proposition 4.1 never fires, so parallel work is free. These are Bernstein’s conditions for parallel execution [18], with RiR_{i} widened to everything that bears on validity. When Wi∩Rj≠∅W_{i}\cap R_{j}\neq\varnothing, as when Design writes the length that Cost reads, there are three correct options, each with a price:

    • •

      Sequence jj after ii, which is a lock. This is “pricing waits for engineering,” and it costs latency.

    • •

      Run in parallel with a check at commit. Role jj records the versions of RjR_{j}, and the harness rejects or reruns jj’s proposal if ii has since written. This is correct by Proposition 4.1 and costs rework in proportion to how often the two actually conflict.

    • •

      Restructure the dependency. Cost quotes a named version, and the history state DD records that provenance, so a later design change invalidates the quote instead of silently outdating it (Theorem F.3, Study III). Escrow is the same move applied to a budget: it shrinks each RiR_{i} to the role’s own share, which makes the roles independent.

    The common-sense rule is therefore one point on a trade-off, not the only correct design.

  4. 4.

    Shape who must reconcile with whom. Let HH record which roles’ scopes overlap and on which state, as in Section 1; two roles overlap when (Ri∪Wi)∩(Rj∪Wj)≠∅(R_{i}\cup W_{i})\cap(R_{j}\cup W_{j})\neq\varnothing, or when a translation must hold between their encodings. If HH is acyclic in the sense of Theorem 3.1 (it has a join tree), checking each handoff is enough. Cycles remove that general guarantee, and no fixed locality bound works universally across unrestricted constraint semantics (Proposition 3.2). For translation handoffs, either the whole cycle space is certified, at a cost of β1=|E|−|V|+c\beta_{1}=|E|-|V|+c checks (Corollary 3.5), or a hub that owns the shared fields makes every other role overlap only with the hub, so HH becomes a star, which is a tree. This is why hub-and-spoke orchestration often works, and it says what the hub must hold. Exact finite-domain checking can cost time exponential in the treewidth of HH (Section 3.4), so the design target is low width rather than few agents.

  5. 5.

    Make translations between role vocabularies explicit. Wherever two roles encode the same object differently, such as engineering units and pricing SKUs, the handoff carries an explicit reversible translation, and the loops are certified by Corollary 3.5 (Theorem 3.4, Studies VII–IX).

Each step rests on the result it cites, and together they address the failure modes of Sections 2 and 3. Like the framework itself (Corollary 4.2), a step matters only where its condition is present: a team with one encoding needs no translations, and roles with disjoint read and write sets need no schedule. The steps do not give the optimal team. They do not say which role does the work best, which is a matter of capability. And the cheapest design meeting the conditions involves problems that are hard in general: the smallest sufficient context is NP-hard to find (Theorem 2.5), and exact checking grows exponentially with the width of HH (Section 3.4). What they replace is the guesswork. “Should this be led by the tech lead?” becomes “which constraint spans these roles, and who holds its scope?” “Should pricing wait?” becomes “does WdesignW_{\mathrm{design}} meet RcostR_{\mathrm{cost}}, and which of the three options is cheapest here?” Individual steps have direct evidence: ownership and escrow in Study IV, commit-time version checks in Study V, provenance invalidation in Study III, and loop checks and full versus split views in Studies VII–IX. Testing the procedure as a whole is an open experiment (Section 5.12).

5 Empirical program

5.1 Overview: nine studies, three kinds of evidence

Each study targets one claim of the theory. The agent studies and the real-data study could have come out the other way; the deterministic studies confirm that a mechanism behaves as proved. The table lists them in paper order; the text below says how much weight each can bear.

One model, held fixed.

All agent studies use one LLM, gpt-6-sol, with the reasoning effort stated in each study. The conclusions are designed to hold for any model, for three reasons. The impossibility theorem binds every policy however capable, so no model can lift Study I’s aliased tasks above chance. Each causal study holds the model fixed and changes only what state the agents see or what the runtime enforces, so every comparison measures the state, not the model. And Study I shows the model is competent: it solves every task whose deciding event it can see. A stronger model improves what agents do with the information they have; the theory says it cannot recover information they lack. Repeating the frozen designs with other model families is a direct replication and the natural next test. Every agent panel was frozen before its first scored call and ran under a spending cap fixed in its preregistration, so no panel could be extended, or stopped early, after its results were seen.

Study Claim tested Evidence Result
I. Aliasing probe more reasoning cannot recover a hidden distinction (Thms. 2.1, 2.3, B.4) agent, 40 paired tasks, frozen design observed 12–17/40 across aliased arms; none significantly above 1/31/3; one authoritative sentence gives 40/40
II. TeamBench roles role decomposition can help under information asymmetry reanalysis of released runs, 164 matched cells removing Planner or Verifier costs 11–14 pass-rate points; team vs. fully informed solo not significant; descriptive, not causal
III. Stale derivations current values alias fresh and stale state; a dependency engine that keeps provenance equals the runtime (Thm. F.3, Prediction 4) deterministic synthetic pipeline, 8 seeded cases unsafe commits: local checks 8/8; dependency closure and runtime both 0/8
IV. TeamBench budget a shared invariant needs ownership; escrow can restructure it (Prop. 3.3) agent, three panels: 27 + 60 + 15 runs violations 5/5 ordinary, 4/5 visible/query, 0/5 ledger or escrow
V. τ2\tau^{2}-bench Telecom distributed state is common; ordinary checks tie where they own the invariant, and stale reads and silent reverts need the runtime structural audit, 114 tasks; agent, preregistered, 222 episodes 97/114 initialize both actors’ state; predicted-tie tasks: both guards 0 violations (unguarded 14/34); other tasks: conventional 24/25, coherence 0/25; silent-revert reward 0.07 vs 1.00
VI. Sobieski classical solvers equal the runtime on their home ground (Prediction 4) deterministic, 86 + 40 cases ties with Gauss–Seidel and version-aware restart
VII. Cycle suite a spanning forest certifies representation coherence (Cor. 3.5) deterministic, 1,800 instances forest 100% at β1\beta_{1} checks; local, pairwise, canonical-ID 0%; short loops ≤\leq66%; random loops 94.5%
VIII. OAEI networks pairwise-invisible identity collisions occur under a unique-name diagnostic public matcher outputs, preregistered replication 23 of 45 networks, 2018–2024; 5 of 7 systems in 2025
IX. Split views split views need a network-level check agent, frozen, 60 tasks split views 9/40 hidden collisions; network check 0/40, but repair lowers mean F1 to 0.774
How to read the evidence.

Read together, the nine studies trace the boundary the theory draws. The runtime wins where the deciding state is missing or unowned (Studies I, IV, V, and IX), and it ties where a conventional mechanism already owns that state (Studies III and VI, and the predicted-tie half of Study V). Both halves matter: a theory that only predicted wins could not be wrong. Studies I, IV, IX, and the Study V revision panel are the causal agent experiments: each holds the model fixed and changes only what state the agents see or what the runtime enforces. Study VIII shows that the failure Study IX isolates is common in real matching systems. Studies III, VI, and VII are deterministic checks: VII confirms that the certificate works as proved, and III and VI confirm that conventional mechanisms match the runtime where they already own the relevant state. Study II and the Study V structural audit are descriptive; they show that the structures the theory is about are present in public benchmarks, not that a coherence mechanism improves them. Every result is backed by recorded run data and, for the deterministic studies, an executable reproduction.

5.2 Study I: more reasoning versus one authoritative distinction

Theorem 2.1 and its quantitative forms predict a sharp contrast. On an aliased fiber with pairwise-disjoint admissible sets, no policy that reasons, samples, or deliberates on the same observation can succeed with probability above 1/k1/k (Theorem 2.3); one added authoritative distinction resolves the task; and a tool query helps exactly when it splits the fiber (Theorem B.4). Study I tests all three directly, on a synthetic benchmark we built so that the aliasing is exact by construction. Each task is a 60-event revision log in which three teams commit, revert, or re-apply changes to one shared parameter. The agent must name the current head, and the commit server rejects any other parent. The final event is one of three operations that leave three different heads, and the options are exactly those three. In the identifiable version the final event is visible; in the aliased version it is redacted, so the prompt is identical across all three truths, chance is 1/31/3, and there is no fallback action. Forty paired tasks were frozen before any scored call; every arm uses gpt-6-sol.

Arm Identifiable Aliased
Low / medium / high reasoning effort 40/40 each 12 / 17 / 14 of 40
Planner + verifier 40/40 13/40
Five-sample majority vote 40/40 13/39
Query tool that cannot reveal the event 40/40 13/40
Query tool that can read any event 40/40 40/40
One authoritative fact (“the current head is XX”) 40/40 40/40

Every arm solves every identifiable task, so the model has the competence the task requires. On aliased tasks, observed accuracy ranges from 12/40 to 17/40, and no arm that keeps the same observation significantly exceeds 1/31/3 (best one-sided binomial p=0.14p=0.14), whether it reasons longer, deliberates in two roles, or votes over five samples. This failure to reject does not establish empirical equivalence to chance; the exact impossibility result comes from the task construction and Theorem 2.3. Model-stated confidence is 1.0 on identifiable tasks and 0.35–0.45 on aliased single-agent arms; the majority arm’s 0.58 is its five-sample vote share, not stated confidence.
