The single sentence naming the current head raises accuracy to 40/40 (23 tasks gained over medium effort, none lost; McNemar p=1.2×10−7p=1.2\times 10^{-7}). A query tool that can read the redacted event also reaches 40/40 and read that event in all 40 runs, while a matched tool that returns only visible team notes stays at 13/40 (27 tasks gained, none lost; p=7.5×10−9p=7.5\times 10^{-9}). All four preregistered hypotheses hold; the frozen report is marked incomplete because one majority-vote cell failed on a transient API error, which cannot change the outcome.

This is the paper’s central claim in its cleanest form. Across the tested arms, more reasoning, more roles, and more samples on the same observation leave observed accuracy statistically compatible with the information-theoretic value of 1/31/3; one authoritative distinction, supplied directly or through a query that splits the fiber, raises the observed result to 40/40. The theorem, not a null result from forty tasks, supplies the general limit.

5.3 Study II: TeamBench role structure

TeamBench structurally separates Planner, Executor, and Verifier permissions and provides deterministic artifact graders [51]. In its Restricted condition a single agent works without the full specification, so the requirements reach the work only if a teammate relays them; this is the information asymmetry the theory is about. We recomputed five-condition summaries from the six cross-model result files released with TeamBench (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, Gemini 3 Flash, GPT-5 mini, GPT-5 nano, Claude Haiku 4.5, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 on 28 tasks); no new model runs are involved. Requiring all five conditions for the same model–task pair leaves 164 matched cells, representing 820 condition records at seed 0.

TeamBench’s default grader fails any run that lacks a valid attestation file, the Verifier’s sign-off, even when every task check passes. Its own leaderboard counts such attestation-only failures as passes. We report pass rate both ways.

Pass rate
Condition Default Attestation-only Mean partial Mean elapsed (s)
grader failures pass
Single agent, full access 15.9% 31.1% 0.709 97
Single agent, Executor access 12.2% 22.6% 0.640 80
Planner + Executor + Verifier 35.4% 36.0% 0.764 789
Executor + Verifier 21.3% 25.0% 0.697 269
Planner + Executor 24.4% 24.4% 0.713 372
Roles inside the team.

Each role carries weight under either grading. Removing the Planner lowers pass rate by 14.0 points with the default grader and by 11.0 points with attestation-only failures counted as passes (the full team wins 26 matched cells and loses 8; two-sided sign test p=0.003p=0.003); mean partial score falls by 0.068. Removing the Verifier lowers pass rate by 11.0 and 11.6 points (22 wins, 3 losses; p=0.0002p=0.0002), and mean partial by 0.051. Task-cluster bootstrap intervals for the two partial-score differences are [0.029,0.115][0.029,0.115] and [0.016,0.086][0.016,0.086], and under the default grader every model loses pass rate when either role is removed. Against the single agent that lacks the specification, the full team gains 13.4 points even with attestation-only failures counted as passes (25 wins, 3 losses).

Team versus a fully informed single agent.

TeamBench reports that its Full Team is not significantly better than Solo on average (a +0.5+0.5-point uplift on its 155-task reference ablation with Gemini 3 Flash) [51]. The large gap in our default-grader column, 35.4% versus 15.9%, does not contradict that result; it is mostly an attestation effect. Without a Verifier, a single agent often never writes the sign-off: 102 of 164 single-agent runs fail the attestation check, against 26 of 164 full-team runs. Once attestation-only failures count as passes, the gap shrinks to 36.0% versus 31.1%. The team wins 18 cells and loses 10, which is not significant (sign test p=0.18p=0.18) and agrees with TeamBench’s null. The team keeps a modest edge in mean partial score (0.764 versus 0.709; task-cluster interval [0.017,0.093][0.017,0.093]). That edge is consistent with TeamBench’s finding that teams help most where single-agent performance is low, which describes these six models: on its leaderboard, for example, Sonnet 4.6 and Haiku 4.5 gain 20.0 and 16.7 points from the team.

What it shows.

When the specification is split across roles, the Planner and the Verifier each carry weight, and a team recovers much of what the uninformed single agent loses. Whether a team beats a fully informed single agent is not established here; it depends on how the attestation is graded. Because the panel varies structure together with inference budget and opportunities for correction, isolating the state-semantics hypothesis is left to the fixed-budget intervention of Study IV.

5.4 Study III: stale derivations, where history is the missing state

What it tests.

The theory makes two claims about memory that this study checks directly. First, two states with identical current values can differ in whether they are still valid, so a check that sees only current values is aliased: by Theorem 2.1 applied to the checker, it cannot tell a fresh derivation from a stale one. The distinction lives in the history state DD, here the provenance of which input revision each artifact was built from (Theorem F.3). Second, a conventional mechanism that already tracks that provenance should match the general runtime exactly (Prediction 4). It is the smallest executable form of both claims.

Setup.

The instrument is a synthetic, deterministic pipeline that we built for this test; no public benchmark and no LLM are involved. Eight source inputs each feed a chain of three derived artifacts, as an analysis pipeline turns datasets into cleaned tables, fitted results, and report figures. Every artifact records its value and the revision of each source it was derived from. One source changes before planning, and the plan recomputes its chain. Then, between planning and commit, a second source is reissued as a new revision with the same value, as when an input is re-approved or re-signed. The three artifacts derived from it now cite a superseded revision. Their values are numerically correct and every artifact is well formed, so every local check passes, including one that recomputes the values and compares only the numbers. A commit is unsafe if the committed pipeline contains any artifact derived from a superseded revision. The eight cases, one per seed, vary the coefficients and which chains are involved, not the failure.

We compare four guards, each run on all eight cases:

Guard What it checks before commit Unsafe commits
Local checks only each artifact is well formed and readable 8/8
Changed-source closure recomputes everything downstream of the source known to have changed at planning time 8/8
Dependency-closure guard rereads all sources at commit and recomputes every artifact whose recorded inputs no longer match 0/8
Coherence harness rereads at commit, compares each artifact’s provenance with current revisions, invalidates stale descendants, and recomputes them 0/8

In this instrument a guard commits unsafely exactly when it misses the late revision, so the column also reads as detection: the first two guards detect 0 of 8 late revisions, and the last two detect 8 of 8.

What it shows.

The two failing guards fail for different reasons, and each reason is a result of the theory. Local checks fail because the stale state and the fresh state look identical artifact by artifact: an aliasing failure, not a reasoning failure. Changed-source closure fails although it is a correct dependency engine, because it checks against the state as it was at planning time; this is the stale-read condition of Proposition 4.1, which requires validation against everything read, at commit. The two passing guards both keep provenance and both validate at commit, and they tie exactly. That tie is the prediction, not a disappointment: where a conventional mechanism already owns the relevant history, the general runtime should add nothing (Prediction 4, Corollary 4.2).

Limits.

Because the instrument is built so that the stale state is invisible to local checks, the 8/8 and 0/8 entries confirm the mechanism; they do not estimate how often stale derivations occur or how agents behave. Study V measures the agent-level counterpart on a public benchmark, where the agent commits on a stale quote in 10 of 10 episodes under current-state checks. Studies V and IX test the runtime where no conventional check owns the relevant state.

5.5 Study IV: who owns a shared budget on TeamBench

The question and the answer.

Proposition 3.3 predicts that a budget shared by several agents cannot be protected by the agents themselves, however well informed, and that two remedies work: an owner that refuses the violating commit, or a split into per-role quotas. Study IV tests this on TeamBench [51] in three panels, each frozen before scoring, with one model held fixed (gpt-6-sol at medium reasoning effort) on the same three hard tasks: a budgeted workflow (LH2), specification-to-tests (TEST1), and leader election (DIST5, a control). The prediction holds on every safety count. Ordinary teams overspend the 20-call budget in 5 of 5 runs. Showing them the live count still leaves 4 of 5. Enforcing the budget at commit leaves 0 of 5, and so do per-role escrow quotas. Mean task progress does not fall in the five-run enforced comparison; the panel is too small for a noninferiority claim. How we got there is itself evidence: the first panel’s guard made no difference because it owned a different variable from the one the task and grader counted, and once ownership was aligned, the guard removed the failure.

Panel 1: a guard on the wrong variable.

The 27-run panel compared an ordinary Planner–Executor–Verifier team, TeamBench’s budget-matched solo agent, and a coherent_full team with a ledger guard and attestation gate. Their strict passes were 1/9, 0/9, and 1/9, with mean partial scores 0.856, 0.833, and 0.856. The arms did not separate because the guard, task, and grader measured different state. The generator drew workspace limits from 15 to 30 while the specification and grader fixed 20; the guard counted an internal script ledger that the task already self-limited; and the attestation gate enforced presence rather than the truth of the attested claim. A post-scoring audit found the actual shared-budget failure: ordinary teams issued 55–67 shell commands and guarded teams 22–57 against the stated limit of 20, while solo agents issued 4–6. This is the ownership condition of Proposition 2.4: a guard constrains the state it owns and nothing else.

Panel 2: the aligned intervention.

Before a second panel, the budget was pinned at 20; the task defined calls to TeamBench’s shell-command tool, run, summed across the team, as the authoritative unit; the guard rejected a call before execution once the aggregate reached 20; the evaluator counted that same unit from saved logs; and the attestation gate required both a pass verdict and a successful rerun of the task’s visible check. A fourth arm, visible_state, exposed exactly the same live budget and attestation state without enforcing either. Across the three team arms, model, prompts, tools, turn and remediation caps, tasks, and graders were held fixed; the budget-matched solo arm is a non-causal efficiency reference. All five preregistered seed blocks completed within the spending cap: three tasks, four arms, 60 runs.

Arm (15 runs) Strict Mean partial LH2 over 20 TEST1 bad attestation
Ordinary team 0/15 0.820 5/5 5/5
Budget-matched solo 0/15 0.873 0/5 5/5
visible_state 0/15 0.860 4/5 3/5
coherent_full 2/15 0.865 0/5 2/5

On LH2, every enforced run stopped at exactly 20 executed calls, rejecting 1–32 surplus attempts (mean 10.4). Ordinary teams issued 57–72 calls; showing the live count lowered the median from 70 to 29 but still left 4/5 violations. Enforcement therefore removed the targeted failure while exposure alone did not. Progress did not collapse: on LH2, coherent_full scored 0.874 mean partial with 2/5 strict passes versus 0.860 and 0/5 for the ordinary team; on TEST1 it scored 0.820 versus 0.740; and on the DIST5 control both guarded arms scored 0.900 versus 0.860. TEST1 showed the same ordering on missing-or-false attestations—2/5 under enforcement, 3/5 with exposure, 5/5 ordinarily—although hidden mutant misses remained outside the visible check the gate owned.

Panel 3: other ways to protect the budget.

Appendix F.4 lists classical alternatives to a shared ledger: expose a counter without refusing, stop conservatively when remaining budget is uncertain, or restructure the invariant into fixed per-role escrow quotas. A third, separately frozen panel held the second panel’s LH2 task, model, seeds, and grader fixed, reused the ordinary and ledger arms, and ran three new arms (15 cells): query_counter (live count, no refuse), conservative_stop (refuse once remaining would fall below slack 5), and quota_escrow (executor 14 + verifier 6). Attestation gates were off on the new arms so the contrast isolates the budget escape.

LH2 arm (5 seeds) Violations (>20>20) Mean partial Strict
Ordinary team (reuse) 5/5 0.860 0/5
query_counter 4/5 0.860 1/5
conservative_stop 0/5 (stops at 15) 0.828 1/5
quota_escrow 0/5 0.960 4/5
coherent_full (reuse) 0/5 0.874 2/5

Information alone still fails: the query counter overspends in 4/5 runs, matching the visible_state finding. Both ownership mechanisms succeed on safety. Escrow matches the ledger at 0/5 violations and has higher observed progress on this panel (mean partial 0.960 versus 0.874; strict 4/5 versus 2/5). That progress gap is descriptive, not a causal ledger-versus-escrow contrast: there are only five seeds, and the reused ledger arm still carries the attestation gate that the escape arms turned off. The safety result is unambiguous: for this additive shared budget, splitting into local quotas is enough. Conservative stopping also prevents overspend by construction, at the cost of unused slack (every run stops at 15). The frozen decision is therefore restructuring suffices for this invariant: a unique shared-ledger claim is not required on LH2. The general runtime remains warranted where no such restructuring is available a priori, as in Study IX’s split-view conflicts.

What the three panels show together.

Each panel isolates one claim of the theory.

  • •

    Information is not ownership. The visible_state and query_counter arms gave every agent the exact live count, and the teams still overspent in 4 of 5 runs. The agents were not missing the fact, and the team already had a dedicated Planner and Verifier, so neither more context nor more roles closes the gap (Proposition 3.3, Corollary 2.2). Visibility lowered the median spend from 70 to 29 calls, but not below the limit: it changes behavior without guaranteeing the invariant.

  • •

    Ownership works, in either of its two forms. Refusal at commit and per-role escrow both reach 0 of 5, the two remedies Proposition 3.3 names. Observed mean progress is not lower in either five-run panel. This rules out collapse in these runs, not a general safety–progress trade-off; the escrow–ledger progress contrast is additionally confounded by different attestation gates.

  • •

    A guard is only as good as the state it owns. The first panel’s guard was active and still changed nothing, because it counted a different quantity from the task’s limit (Proposition 2.4, Prediction 7). For harness builders this is the most practical lesson: before asking whether a guard works, check that it guards the variable the task is scored on.

Within each comparison the model, prompts, tools, tasks, and graders were fixed, so the differences come from what the harness owns, not from the model. The limits are those of a small panel: three tasks, five seeds per cell, and one model family.

5.6 Study V: τ2\tau^{2}-bench Telecom, structural audit and revision panel

τ2\tau^{2}-bench is unusually well matched to the coherence hypothesis because the benchmark itself makes global state distributed. The user controls device-side actions, the assistant controls carrier-side actions, and the environment evaluates the joint result [12].

We audited the 114 public base tasks in the pinned τ2\tau^{2}-bench v0.2.0 Telecom corpus, containing 803 initialization actions, 516 declared golden actions, and 209 terminal environment assertions:

  • •

    97 of 114 initialize both user/device and assistant/carrier state;

  • •

    71 declare golden actions for both requestors;

  • •

    59 assert postconditions in both environments;

  • •

    94 declare at least two golden actions and 82 declare at least three;

  • •

    98 contain at least eight initialization, golden-action, and assertion items.

The counts show that dual-control global state is central to the benchmark. The golden actions describe benchmark solutions rather than observed trajectories or uniquely required action sequences; all 71 dual-requestor cases are graded through terminal environment assertions rather than exact action matching. The 114 generated cases are not independent real-world samples. Thus the audit establishes prevalent two-actor structure, not model performance; it contains structures relevant to typed locality, transformation semantics, compatibility, and dynamics without testing a coherence intervention. Representation equivalence is exercised less, so 𝒢\mathcal{G} is predicted to add little marginal value unless the task construction is extended.

Revision panel.

The audit shows where the structure is; the panel tests whether owning it matters. We injected three kinds of coherence failure into public Telecom tasks. In a stale read, a carrier fact the assistant already read changes before it writes. In an authority change, an action that was allowed becomes forbidden during the conversation. In a silent revert, a carrier change the assistant already committed is undone. There are 12 injected tasks on 7 public base tasks, plus the 7 bases uninjected as controls. Task labels give the kind of injection: S1–S4 inject a stale read, A1–A4 an authority change, and P1–P4 a change after a committed step (in P1 a payment fails to post; P2–P4 are silent reverts). The τ2\tau^{2} agent, user simulator, conversation loop, and evaluator are unmodified; the agent is gpt-6-sol at medium effort and the simulated user is gpt-6-sol at low effort. Three arms differ only in how the assistant’s write calls are handled. The unguarded arm uses the stock tools. The conventional arm adds three policy preconditions from the Telecom policy, checked on the current carrier state at call time. The coherence arm adds two things on top: read-set validation, which rejects a write when a fact it depends on has changed since the agent read it (Proposition 4.1), and a committed-effect monitor, which sends one notice if a postcondition of an earlier committed write stops holding.

The theory predicts a split, not a blanket win, and the split was frozen before any scored episode. When the injected change breaks a policy precondition, an ordinary current-state check already catches it, so conventional and coherence should tie (Prediction 4). When no current precondition fails—the fact behind a legal write went stale, or a committed change stopped holding—only a runtime that remembers what was read and what was committed can see the problem. All 222 episodes completed, with no infrastructure failures.

Target violations / exposed τ2\tau^{2} reward
Tasks Unguarded Conventional Coherence Unguarded Conventional Coherence
Predicted tie (7 tasks) 14/34 0/35 0/34 0.63 0.86 0.86
Predicted coherence (5 tasks) 25/25 24/25 0/25 0.28 0.44 1.00
   stale read (S3, S4) 10/10 10/10 0/10 0.70 1.00 1.00
   silent revert (P2–P4) 15/15 14/15 0/15 0.00 0.07 1.00
Uninjected controls (7 bases) — — — 0.93 1.00 1.00

The frozen decision rules are all met: the split is confirmed. Three readings follow, in increasing order of strength.

Where an ordinary check owns the invariant, it is enough. When a contract ends mid-call or a second overdue bill posts, the unguarded agent resumes the line anyway (14 of 34 exposed episodes), and both guarded arms stop every such write with the same reward. This is the same predicted tie as in Studies III and VI: where a conventional mechanism owns the invariant, the runtime adds nothing.

Stale reads are invisible to current-state checks. When a price or bill amount changed after the agent quoted it, the conventional arm committed on the old figure in 10 of 10 episodes; every one of those writes was legal at call time. The coherence arm’s zero is guaranteed by the definition of its check, so it is not the informative number. The informative numbers are that the agent never re-read on its own, and that after one rejection it re-read, re-quoted, and lost no reward. The τ2\tau^{2} grader itself does not penalize these stale commits (the conventional arm scores 1.00 on them), so this violation is one the benchmark does not see.

Silent reverts are the strongest result, and it is behavioral. When a line activation, a roaming change, or a data refuel was quietly undone after the agent committed it, the unguarded and conventional arms scored 0.00 and 0.07 on τ2\tau^{2}’s own grader: they believed the job was done. The coherence arm scored 1.00 in 15 of 15 episodes. It received one notice each time, and the agent redid the change. Nothing in the design forces this outcome; the agent had to act on the notice. This is the transition layer in practice: a runtime that keeps committed postconditions as part of its state turns an invisible reversal into a visible one.

The guard was cheap. No correct action was rejected in any uninjected control, and coherence episodes on injected tasks were shorter (44 messages versus 51) and cheaper. The panel has weak spots, recorded rather than fixed because the design was frozen. In two tasks (S1 and A3) the agent re-reads the changed fact before acting, so no arm, including unguarded, ever acts on stale data. In one task (P1) the frozen success criterion was too narrow: when a payment failed to post, agents in every arm handed the customer to a human instead of requesting payment again, so its reward is 0 in every arm, though its violation count remains valid. One unguarded control episode failed through an ordinary agent error. The panel has five runs per injected cell, uses one model family for both agent and simulated user, and injects the failures itself; it measures what the mechanism does when these failures occur, not how often they occur naturally.

5.7 Study VI: Sobieski, where a classical solver already owns the state

What it tests.

Prediction 4 says that where a conventional mechanism already owns the relevant state, the general runtime should do exactly as well as that mechanism, no better and no worse. Study III checked this on a pipeline we built. This study checks it on a public engineering benchmark whose classical tools are decades old: iterate coupled equations until they converge, and restart when the design version changes. A tie is the expected result. A runtime win here would mean the classical tools were broken; a loss would mean the general semantics costs more than they do.

Setup.

The Sobieski Supersonic Business Jet (SSBJ) is a standard multidisciplinary design benchmark with exact public equations [35, 36, 71]. Four disciplines play the role of agents, each a deterministic function; no LLM is involved. Structure computes weights from the lift and the engine weight. Aerodynamics computes lift and drag from those weights and the engine scale factor. Propulsion computes engine weight, scale factor, and fuel consumption from the drag. Mission computes the aircraft’s range from all of them. The first three form a cycle: three feedback values (lift, engine weight, and engine scale factor) must equal what each consumer assumed when it ran. In the paper’s terms, the coupling graph is HH, and the gluing condition ℱ\mathcal{F} is that every shared value equals the value its consumer used, so that the four disciplines describe one aircraft. We use GEMSEO’s public implementation of the equations; our independent reconstruction of the Propulsion and Mission submodels matches published values to within 7×10−87\times 10^{-8} (Appendix G.3).

Three terms recur below. An update call is one execution of one discipline. A sweep runs all four once, in order from Structure to Mission, and so costs four calls. Because the disciplines form a cycle, one sweep does not settle the values: each sweep feeds its outputs back as the next sweep’s inputs, and the values approach a consistent solution only gradually. A case is coherent when one further sweep, run as an independent audit, changes no feedback value by more than 10−710^{-7} of its scale; at that point the disciplines agree on one aircraft. We also report the error in computed range against an exact root-finder solution of the coupled equations.

Panel 1: when to stop iterating.

The 86 cases are 43 designs (the benchmark’s initial, feasible, and near-optimal designs, and 40 designs drawn between the feasible and optimal designs with small perturbations), each started from two different initial guesses for the feedback values. Four schedulers decide when to stop. One sweep and three sweeps stop after a fixed budget of 4 or 12 calls. Residual-converged Gauss–Seidel, the classical method, sweeps until the feedback values stop changing. The coherence guard, the runtime’s commit rule, commits only when every shared value agrees with what its consumer used, and otherwise sweeps again.

Scheduler Coherent cases Mean update calls Mean relative range error
One sweep 0/86 4.00 4.68×10−34.68\times 10^{-3}
Three sweeps 0/86 12.00 5.08×10−55.08\times 10^{-5}
Residual-converged Gauss–Seidel 86/86 35.53 1.40×10−101.40\times 10^{-10}
Coherence guard 86/86 35.53 1.40×10−101.40\times 10^{-10}

Every fixed-budget run stops at an aircraft whose disciplines disagree: Structure was sized for a lift that Aerodynamics no longer produces. After one sweep the computed range is off by about 0.5% on average; after three, by about 0.005%. Nothing inside a sweep reports that the system has not settled, and the number of sweeps needed varies from 8 to 10 across cases, so no fixed budget is safe in advance. The difference between 4 and 35.5 mean calls is the price of being right: about nine times the cost of a single sweep, spent on reaching agreement rather than wasted. The converged scheduler and the guard make exactly the same calls because, on this system, the guard’s agreement check is the same test Gauss–Seidel uses to stop. A converged residual is the gluing condition ℱ\mathcal{F} in numerical form, so the tie is exact by construction.

Panel 2: a revision during a sweep.

In each of 40 cases the design is revised from the feasible design to a new one partway toward the optimum, and the revision lands mid-sweep: Structure has already run on the old design, while Aerodynamics, Propulsion, and Mission run on the new one. The result has mixed provenance. It blends two aircraft and describes neither. Four revision policies respond. Accept mixed revision keeps that result as it is (4 calls). Continue for two sweeps keeps it and iterates two more sweeps on the new design (12 calls). The provenance guard and restart, the runtime’s rule, uses the history state DD to record which design revision each output came from, discards outputs from a superseded revision, and iterates to agreement. The conventional version-aware restart, the classical rule, discards in-progress work whenever the design’s version number changes and solves again.

Revision policy Coherent cases Mean update calls Worst range error
Accept mixed revision 0/40 4 8.87×10−38.87\times 10^{-3}
Continue for two sweeps 0/40 12 1.17×10−41.17\times 10^{-4}
Provenance guard and restart 40/40 40 1.04×10−101.04\times 10^{-10}
Conventional version-aware restart 40/40 40 1.04×10−101.04\times 10^{-10}

Accepting the mixed result fails every case, with range off by up to 0.9%. Two more sweeps wash out the old design but stop before the values settle, so they also fail every case. Both restart policies succeed in all 40 at 40 calls, 4 of them on the discarded sweep, and they make identical calls: here the version number is the provenance the runtime keeps, DD in its simplest form.

What it shows.

The study supports the theory in two ways, neither of which is a runtime advantage. The 0/86 and 0/40 rows show that the failure the theory describes occurs in classical engineering too: every discipline computes correctly and every stopping rule is reasonable, yet the committed aircraft is incoherent unless something checks the global condition. The 86/86 and 40/40 rows, at identical cost, show that the runtime adds nothing where a classical tool already owns the state. A converged residual is a specialized compatibility check, and a version counter is a specialized history state, so the general semantics reduces to them, as Prediction 4 requires. The runtime is needed where shared state has no common numerical residual or single version counter, such as agents with split views (Study IX) or a stale read under dual control (Study V). There the same semantics apply and no classical tool supplies them.

5.8 Study VII: checking that translations agree around every loop

What it tests.

Section 3.3 makes three claims about translations between agents’ formats. A translation error can be invisible to every check that looks at one agent or one edge, including canonical IDs. Checking short loops is not enough. And checking every loop, which sounds infeasible because a graph can have exponentially many, costs only β1=|E|−|V|+c\beta_{1}=|E|-|V|+c comparisons along a spanning forest (Theorem 3.4, Corollary 3.5). This study runs those claims as code. It is deterministic and model-free, and its decision rules were frozen before any score was computed.

Setup.

Each instance is the simplest translation problem: sign synchronization. Agents sit on the nodes of a graph and each holds the same axis, but each may orient it either way. Each edge records whether two neighbors’ orientations are the “same” or “opposite”. The instance is coherent when one choice of orientations explains every edge label, which by Theorem 3.4 means every loop has an even number of “opposite” labels. We used twenty graphs: rings of 3 to 12 nodes, two complete graphs, two grids, the Petersen graph, a pair of disjoint rings, and four random graphs, with β1\beta_{1} (the number of independent loops) ranging from 1 to 25. Each graph carries 90 instances, 1,800 in all. On each graph, 30 are coherent and 30 carry the primary corruption, a flipped label on one edge that lies on a loop. That flip leaves every node valid and every edge self-consistent; only the loops through that edge stop closing. The other 30 carry one of three control corruptions that simpler validators can see: a malformed node, a node describing a different object, or an edge whose two directions do not undo each other.

The validators.

Seven validators run on every instance, ordered by how much of the loop structure they examine:

  • •

    Local only checks that each node’s data is well formed.

  • •

    Pairwise only also checks every edge: its two directions undo each other, and it carries one neighbor’s description to the other’s.

  • •

    Quotient-first is the canonical-ID approach: map every node’s description to a canonical form, confirm that all forms match, and discard the translations.

  • •

    Bounded cycles adds a check of every loop of length at most kk, for k=3k=3, 4, and 6.

  • •

    Sampled cycles checks β1\beta_{1} randomly chosen loops, the same budget as the forest but without its choice of loops.

  • •

    Spanning forest is Corollary 3.5: fix orientations along a spanning tree, then check each of the β1\beta_{1} leftover edges against them.

  • •

    Groupoid descent is an independent implementation of the same decision by a different algorithm (union-find), included as a cross-check. It re-examines each translation in both directions, so it reports more checks.

Validator Flipped-edge errors caught Mean loop checks (coherent)
Local / pairwise / quotient-first 0% 0
Bounded cycles (k=3/4/6k=3/4/6) 18.3% / 43.8% / 66.2% 1.1 / 4.0 / 14.6
Sampled cycles (budget β1\beta_{1}) 94.5% 4.2
Spanning forest / groupoid descent 100% 4.2 / 18.5
Reading the table.

No validator raised a false alarm on any coherent instance, so the table measures only how many real errors each catches and at what cost.

  • •

    Checks that never look at a loop catch nothing. Local, pairwise, and canonical-ID validators miss every flipped edge. They are blind to this error class, not weak: each catches the control corruption it can see. Quotient-first is the important case, because canonical IDs are the common engineering shortcut. Every description maps to the same canonical form, so the check passes while the loop does not close. This is the failure Section 3.3 predicts.

  • •

    Checking short loops catches only errors on short loops. A bounded-cycle check catches a flipped edge exactly when that edge lies on a loop of length at most kk, matching the frozen prediction on every instance. Raising kk from 3 to 6 multiplies the checks thirteenfold and still misses a third of the errors, including every error on rings longer than six. This is Proposition 3.2 in executable form: no fixed loop length is enough.

  • •

    Random loops do well on average but carry no guarantee. With the same budget as the forest, random loops catch 94.5% overall but only 76.7% on the hardest graph, and nothing in the result tells the user which errors were missed.

  • •

    The spanning forest catches every error at the minimum cost. It catches all 600 flipped edges and uses exactly β1\beta_{1} checks on every coherent instance, 4.2 on average, slightly more than the k=4k=4 short-loop check spends while catching 43.8%, and under a third of what k=6k=6 spends while catching 66.2%. The independent union-find implementation agrees with it on all 1,800 instances.

The suite also confirms the counting law behind that cost: a random labeling is coherent with probability exactly 2−β12^{-\beta_{1}} on every graph small enough to enumerate. Each independent loop is therefore a separate constraint, so β1\beta_{1} loop checks are necessary as well as sufficient: any smaller set of loops leaves some loop unconstrained (Appendix D).

What it shows.

The spanning forest is the only validator here that is both complete and cheap. It needs one comparison per independent loop, a number set by the graph’s shape and not by its exponentially many loops, and it misses nothing. Every other strategy either cannot see this error or catches it only sometimes, and the most common shortcut, canonical IDs, is among those that cannot see it. For a harness builder, the rule of Section 3.3 is therefore practical as well as correct: keep the translations, and check β1\beta_{1} edges against a spanning forest.

Limits.

The errors are planted, and the instance is built so that local checks cannot see them, so the zeros confirm the theorem as stated rather than estimate how often such errors occur. Study VIII supplies that estimate from real data, where hidden loop conflicts appear in 23 of 45 ontology-alignment networks and a triangle check catches a median of only 80% of them per network, the same short-loop gap seen here. The suite uses one simple group and noise-free labels; non-commuting translations and noisy data are left for future work.

5.9 Study VIII: holonomy in OAEI Conference alignment networks

Particular instances of this obstruction have been studied in data integration: cycles of schema mappings used to detect erroneous mappings among peers [1], chains of owl:sameAs links that join two distinct identifiers of one dataset [23], and alignments that are pairwise consistent but globally inconsistent across three ontologies [53]. Each addresses one setting. Here the same obstruction is one case of the general local-to-global problem of Section 3, certified by the spanning-forest check of Section 3.3, and measured systematically, under a preregistered design, on an established matching benchmark. On the OAEI 2025 Conference track [66], seven matching systems each produce twenty-one pairwise equivalence alignments among seven ontologies of the public OntoFarm collection of conference-organization ontologies [87]. Treating each system’s alignments as an undirected equality network, we apply an explicit unique-name diagnostic: a chain of “same as” links is flagged when it identifies two distinct identifiers inside one ontology even though every individual alignment can look locally one-to-one. We call that flagged pattern a same-ontology identity collision, or “conflict” below for brevity. It is not, by itself, an OWL logical contradiction, because OWL does not generally impose a unique-name assumption; it is a structural warning whose relation to curated reference alignments is measured rather than assumed.

Six of the seven systems’ networks contain such conflicts, and five contain conflicts that no pairwise check can see: fifty conflict pairs have shortest witness chains of length L≥3L\geq 3 and are therefore invisible to a per-alignment one-to-one check (LSMatch has no conflicts; LogMapLt’s are all L=2L=2). Correspondences on those invisible chains are absent from the public curated reference alignment (OAEI’s ra1) at 60/144=41.7%60/144=41.7\%, versus 420/1555=27.0%420/1555=27.0\% for the remaining correspondences (one-sided Fisher p=2.1×10−4p=2.1\times 10^{-4}; optimistic, because overlapping chains make units dependent). Fifty-five non-reference correspondences are flagged only by the whole-network check. A triangle-only check catches 78%78\% of the invisible conflicts; the rest need chains of length 44–77. Typical audited cases merge a class with its own subclass or neighbour—for example sigkdd#Author≡sigkdd#Author_of_paper\texttt{sigkdd\#Author}\equiv\texttt{sigkdd\#Author\_of\_paper} in five systems. The curated reference itself has fifteen conflict pairs, thirteen pairwise-invisible (e.g. ekaw#Paper≡ekaw#Regular_Paper\texttt{ekaw\#Paper}\equiv\texttt{ekaw\#Regular\_Paper} at L=4L=4), consistent with OAEI’s note that transitive closure of ra1 surfaced conflicts later addressed in ra2.

Replication across 2018–2024.

To test whether 2025 is a one-campaign artifact, we froze a second design before scoring and applied it to every complete Conference participant network from 2018 to 2024. Many submissions are byte-identical resubmissions across years, so the unit is the distinct network: 72 system-years reduce to 48 distinct networks, and removing three identical to networks already scored above leaves 45 new ones. Because overlapping chains make correspondences dependent, the frozen tests are network-level rather than pooled.

Preregistered quantity (45 new distinct networks) Result
Networks with a pairwise-invisible conflict 23/45 (51%; 95% CI 37–65%)
Years in which such a network occurs 7/7
Networks where chain correspondences are more often absent from ra1 21 vs 2 (sign test p=3.3×10−5p=3.3\times 10^{-5})
Same, one network per system (33 systems) 18 vs 2 (p=2.0×10−4p=2.0\times 10^{-4})
Spearman(invisible conflicts per 100 correspondences, share in ra1) −0.63-0.63

The outcome is replicates under the frozen rule. Across all distinct networks from 2018 to 2025, 28 of 52 contain a pairwise-invisible collision under the unique-name diagnostic. The negative rank correlation makes collision density a candidate reference-free quality signal: networks with more hidden holonomy per correspondence agree less with the curated answers, without implying that every flagged collision is an error. Different systems repeat the same merges: sigkdd#Author≡sigkdd#Author_of_paper\texttt{sigkdd\#Author}\equiv\texttt{sigkdd\#Author\_of\_paper} and ekaw#Session≡ekaw#Conference_Session\texttt{ekaw\#Session}\equiv\texttt{ekaw\#Conference\_Session} each occur in ten distinct networks, and edas#ConferenceChair≡edas#SessionChair\texttt{edas\#ConferenceChair}\equiv\texttt{edas\#SessionChair} in eight—again mostly a class merged with a subclass or sibling. One observation was made after scoring and is not a frozen result: two unusually large outputs form giant components that contain 99% of the 31,245 invisible collision pairs, so pooled pair-level figures describe mainly those two networks. The per-network median share caught by a triangle check is 80%, close to the 2025 figure of 78%; the network-level tests above are unaffected by the outliers.

The panel covers the Conference track, and absence from the reference is an upper bound on error because the reference is incomplete. Within that scope, the evidence is consistent across eight campaigns and dozens of independently built systems: informal multi-view “sameness” routinely produces same-ontology identity collisions that pairwise checks cannot see, and the correspondences on those witness chains are absent from the curated reference more often than other correspondences. The diagnostic is therefore associated with alignment quality; it does not declare every collision a logical error.

5.10 Study IX: agents curating mappings, with full and split views

Study VIII shows the failure in systems that match one pair of ontologies at a time. The agent test asks when a language model curating such mappings reproduces the failure, and whether a runtime check removes it. Two frozen experiments share one task set and one model; they differ in what each agent sees. We built 40 conflict tasks from real OAEI Conference components containing a pairwise-invisible conflict, plus 20 conflict-free controls (median 19 candidate correspondences per conflict task), and froze the design before any scored call. Each task shows the agent every candidate correspondence with entity names and parents, states the transitivity and unique-name rules, and asks it to select the correspondences to keep. Four arms use gpt-6-sol at medium reasoning effort with identical instructions and differ only in the runtime check applied before commit: none, pairwise one-to-one, triangle, or full-network. A fifth, non-LLM arm repairs by repeatedly cutting the weakest link on a shortest conflict chain, in the manner of de Melo’s repair [23]. All 280 episodes completed.

The agent resolved every conflict on its first submission. The unguarded agent left a pairwise-invisible conflict on 0 of 40 conflict tasks (95% CI 0–8.8%), and no runtime check ever rejected a submission, so all four LLM arms received the same treatment. The frozen decision rule labels the outcome harm, because the network-guarded arm scored slightly lower F1 than the unguarded arm on clean tasks (−0.038-0.038). Since the guard never intervened, that difference is sampling variation between independent runs rather than an effect of the guard; the decision rule did not anticipate an arm with zero interventions. Two further findings are clear. The agent beats the non-LLM repair on 26 of 40 conflict tasks versus 10 (4 ties; two-sided sign test p=0.011p=0.011), mainly through precision (0.75 versus 0.64). On a metamorphic subset of ten tasks, the agent dropped a correspondence whose target was swapped for its superclass in 10 of 10 cases, but its kept set was less stable under presentation changes than under plain resampling: an identical re-prompt reproduced it in 9 of 10 tasks, renumbered candidates in 7 of 10, and JSON formatting in 6 of 10.

This is the outcome the theory predicts for a full view: the agent saw every correspondence in each conflict and was told the rule, so a strong model performed the global check itself. The conflicts of Study VIII arise differently. Each matcher sees one pair of ontologies, and the outputs are combined afterward; Theorem 2.1 predicts that this split view is where a guard becomes necessary.

Split views.

The second experiment, frozen separately, tests that prediction on the same 60 tasks with the same model. Each ontology pair in a task is curated by its own agent call that sees only that pair’s candidates and the unique-name rule; the pair results are merged. Three split-view arms differ only in the check applied to the merged network: none, the pairwise one-to-one check, or the full-network check, which sends each flagged witness chain back to the pair agents on it. The full-view agent above serves as the reference. A scale arm gives a single full-view agent entire system networks of 186–300 candidates, with and without the network check. All 70 new episodes completed.

Arm (40 conflict tasks) Hidden conflict left Mean F1 Tasks with intervention
Full view, one agent 0/40 0.803 0
Split views, no check 9/40 (22.5%) 0.796 0
Split views, pairwise check 9/40 (22.5%) 0.796 0
Split views, network check 0/40 0.774 9

With the same model and the same candidates, splitting the view produces hidden collisions on 9 of 40 tasks (95% CI 12–38%), against none for the full-view agent. The pairwise check never fires, because these collisions never appear inside a single pair. The network check detects and removes all nine, with no case in the other direction (McNemar one-sided p=0.002p=0.002), and never fires on the 20 clean tasks, where F1 is unchanged. This is the preregistered safety outcome; the next paragraph reports the repair-quality cost. At scale, the full-view agent left a hidden collision on 1 of 10 whole networks, and the network check removed it with no loss of F1. The outcome is support under the frozen rule.

Detection and repair separate, as Proposition 3.6 anticipates. On 8 of the 9 repaired tasks, F1 against the reference fell (mean 0.774 versus 0.796), because the runtime sent each flagged chain to every pair agent on it and each dropped its own link: 47 correspondences were removed to resolve 9 conflicts, 34 of them in the reference. Every chain contained at least one reference-absent link, so a single well-chosen drop per conflict was available; this diagnosis was made after scoring. The check therefore detects exactly, and the accuracy of the repair depends on how the runtime assigns it; Section 5.12 describes the follow-up on repair routing.

Taken together, the two experiments locate the runtime’s role. With one model held fixed, a full view lets the agent keep the network coherent itself; split views—the way the systems of Study VIII actually work—produce hidden collisions, and a check that tracks translations across the whole network detects every one of them. Detection is exact in this panel; high-quality repair is not yet solved, as the 0.022 mean-F1 decrease under send-to-all routing shows.

5.11 Falsifiable predictions

A theory of coherence earns trust by predicting when extra structure should not help, not only when it should. The theory makes seven such predictions, and every one we have tested so far has held.

  1. 1.

    No distributed state, little value from descent. If one actor has one authoritative state and every action is locally validated, explicit local-to-global machinery should add overhead with little gain.

  2. 2.

    No representation multiplicity, little value from 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Representation-equivalence machinery should not improve tasks with one canonical encoding. Conversely, when one semantic object is distributed across reversible heterogeneous views, validators that retain explicit equivalence morphisms (cycle / descent checks) should detect global incoherence that local checks and quotient-first canonicalization miss. Studies VII and VIII support the converse on controlled graphs and on public multi-ontology alignments. Study IX confirms both sides at the agent level: with a full view the check has nothing to add, and with split views it detects every hidden collision the pairwise check leaves. Its send-to-all repair removes those collisions but lowers mean F1, separating detection from repair quality.

  3. 3.

    No revisions, little value from DD. A one-shot task with immutable inputs should not benefit materially from provenance and invalidation logic.

  4. 4.

    Known complete dependency closure can match the general runtime. A conventional dependency engine should equal the general semantics on tasks where HH, 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and freshness are fully captured by that engine. Studies III and VI support this: dependency closure matches the runtime on every stale derivation, and residual-converged Gauss–Seidel and version-aware restart match it on Sobieski. Study IV’s LH2 escape panel extends the same idea to resources: fixed per-role escrow quotas match the shared ledger on safety for an additive budget. Study V’s revision panel extends it to dual-control policy: where the injected change breaks a policy precondition, current-state checks tie the runtime with zero violations.

  5. 5.

    Role decomposition without state ownership can fail. Adding planners, verifiers, or more messages should not reliably fix global invariants that no component enforces at commit time. Study I shows the observation-level form: a planner–verifier pair does not significantly beat chance on aliased tasks. Study IV shows the commit-level form: a Planner–Executor–Verifier team shown the live budget still overspends in 4 of 5 runs.

  6. 6.

    Semantic guards should remove targeted failures without requiring a stronger model. Holding model and inference budget fixed, a guard that owns the missing invariant should reduce that invariant’s failure rate specifically rather than producing a diffuse benchmark-wide improvement. Study IV supports the safety prediction: aligned budget enforcement changes 5/5 violations to 0/5, observed mean progress does not fall in the five-run comparison, and the unrelated control is unchanged. The LH2 escape panel shows that per-role escrow does the same for safety while an information-only counter does not; its progress comparison with the ledger is descriptive because the attestation gates differ. Study V shows the same specificity across failure types: read-set validation and the committed-effect monitor remove stale-read and silent-revert violations that current-state checks leave (24/25 to 0/25), with no false rejections on uninjected controls.

  7. 7.

    Ownership miss looks like theory miss. A commit guard that enforces a nearby but non-identical state variable can leave the evaluation’s failure mode intact. That residual should be read as incomplete ownership of the graded invariant—the operational content of the aliasing theorem—not as evidence that stronger models or more roles were required. Study IV shows both sides: the first panel’s mismatched ledger does not separate, while the aligned second panel removes the targeted violation.

Predictions 1–3 are Corollary 4.2 with the corresponding map absent: no restriction to a nontrivial cover, no translation between encodings, and no state-changing history. These predictions distinguish the theory from the weaker claim that “more structure is good.” Sometimes more structure should do nothing; sometimes it should make the system slower; and specialized conventional mechanisms should often match the general formalism on their native problems—including escrow quotas for an additive shared budget. Prediction 7 is the evaluation counterpart of Predictions 5–6: the runtime must own the same distinction the test scores.

5.12 Next experiments

The escapes comparison on LH2 (Section 5.5) and the τ2\tau^{2}-bench revision panel (Section 5.6) were each run exactly as preregistered. The next experiments move toward natural failure rates and broader public benchmarks.

5.12.1 1. Natural rates on τ2\tau^{2}-bench

The revision panel measures what the runtime does when stale reads and silent reverts occur; it does not measure how often they occur on their own. The next step is uninjected frequency measurement on a larger model panel, with the two weak tasks and the narrow P1 criterion redesigned before a new freeze.

5.12.2 2. Broaden the 𝒢\mathcal{G} evidence

Studies VII–IX cover the certificate, real-data prevalence, and the agent-level split between full and split views. Two steps remain. The first is repair routing: comparing a single arbiter, the deterministic weakest-link rule, and send-to-all routing, so that the runtime keeps accuracy as well as coherence. The second is a broader metamorphic suite carrying the probes—known semantics-preserving transforms and non-equivalent near-neighbors, asking for invariance f⁡(g​x)=f⁡(x)f(gx)=f(x) or equivariance f⁡(g​x)∼g⁡(f⁡(x))f(gx)\sim g(f(x))—since Study IX already found the agent’s selections less stable under renumbering and reformatting than under plain resampling. Appendix G.2 expands the designs; the conditional prediction remains that of Section 5.11: one canonical encoding, little value from 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

5.12.3 3. Team design from state structure

Section 4.5 derives a team design from read sets, write sets, and constraint scopes. The direct test holds the model and the total budget fixed and compares three ways of organizing the same roles: a common-sense design (a lead agent, with pricing sequenced after engineering), the derived design (owners for cross-role constraints, parallel work under commit-time version checks, and a hub or loop check wherever HH has a cycle), and a fully sequential baseline. The prediction is that the derived design matches the sequential baseline on coherence violations, matches or beats the common-sense design on latency, and that the common-sense design fails exactly on the constraints it leaves without an owner.

6 Relation to prior work

The work sits at the intersection of agent evaluation, distributed/transactional state, constraint reasoning, compositional semantics, and local-to-global mathematics.

ReAct and Toolformer establish the modern pattern of interleaving language-model reasoning with external actions and tools [69, 86]. AgentBench, WebArena, GAIA, OSWorld, and SWE-bench extend evaluation into persistent interactive environments [48, 55, 59, 84, 88]. TeamBench adds OS-enforced role separation [51]; τ2\tau^{2}-bench distributes control between user and assistant [12]; and BixBench3 evaluates long computational-science trajectories [25]. These works provide the environments in which globally distributed state becomes operationally visible. In practice, reliability on such tasks is pursued through context engineering, memory, and agent harnesses that wrap the model with tools, guards, and checks; the present paper gives these practices a specification, saying what a context must contain and what a harness must own and check.

The mathematical ingredients predate agentic AI. Acyclic database schemes characterize when local relational consistency implies global consistency [15]; bounded-width constraint systems expose a structural tractability parameter [33]; optimistic concurrency control supplies serializable commit semantics under validation conditions [52]; Myhill–Nerode characterizes minimal deterministic state for future language behavior [46]; and group synchronization relates global frames to cycle consistency [54]. Set Cover supplies the hardness source for minimum instrumentation [50]; coding theory supplies the hardness of minimum syndrome repair [17]. Coordination-avoidance and escrow methods in databases [9, 65] and team decision theory in control [45] address closely related design questions; Appendices F.3 and F.4 compare them with the present architecture. In data integration, cycle-based detection of erroneous mappings [1], identity-constraint violations in linked data [23], and inconsistency propagation in connected alignments [53] study specific instances of the representation-layer obstruction; the present paper treats them as cases of one local-to-global semantics and measures the obstruction on a public benchmark (Studies VIII and IX).

Software and systems engineering have used these structures for collaborative development for three decades, each for one layer. Goguen gave concurrent interacting objects a sheaf semantics [38]; institutions made heterogeneous specification languages composable [39]; Specware composed and refined specifications by categorical colimits [75]; and Fiadeiro developed categorical methods for architectural design and connector composition independently of that line [27]. The viewpoints framework organized multi-stakeholder development around partial perspectives [28]; later work argued that inconsistency among those perspectives can be useful to retain rather than always eliminate [64]; and view merging computes their integration as a colimit [68]. Bidirectional lenses keep a pair of views synchronized under updates [32]; multi-model consistency management extends this to many models and observes that not every multi-ary relation factors into binary ones [80], which is the pairwise-invisible obstruction that Studies VIII and IX measure. Co-design and ologs bring categorical composition to multidisciplinary engineering design and knowledge representation [20, 74], and cycle-consistent map networks do the same for shape collections [47]. Read against 𝔛\mathfrak{X}, sheaf semantics, view merging, Specware colimits, and multi-model consistency sit in ℱ\mathcal{F}; lenses and cycle-consistent correspondences sit in 𝒢\mathcal{G}; and refinement morphisms that change the design sit in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The present framework places them in one semantics and adds what this line of work leaves open: whether the available views contain enough information for any valid action (Section 2), which minimal state must be carried forward in time (Section 4.2), and when a stochastic proposer may commit.

The aliasing theorem belongs to the tradition that treats what a distributed system can do as a function of what its participants know. Knowledge-based analysis shows that coordinated action requires common knowledge, which cannot be attained when communication is not guaranteed [42]; FLP and CAP give impossibility results for consensus and replicated state [29, 37]; and team decision theory and decentralized POMDPs make the information structure itself the object of control. Decentralized decision and detection problems are NP-complete even in simple static forms [11], and decentralized POMDPs are NEXP-complete in general [19, 45, 56, 83]. The aliasing theorem is the single-decision, admissibility-valued core of this tradition: it asks not what is optimal or agreed but whether any policy is guaranteed valid, and that question yields the exact minimax value, the semantic-bit bound, and the instrumentation hardness proved here.

Category theory provides a language for compositional transformations and effects [31, 63]; functorial data migration treats schema change as structure-preserving transformation [73]; hypergraph categories and structured cospans formalize wiring of open systems [7, 30]; groupoids formalize equivalence beyond one group action [81]; and sheaves provide a canonical language for integrating compatible local information [67]. Sites and stacks in groupoids provide the standard bridge between locality, equivalence, and descent [62, 76, 77, 78].

This paper brings these lines of work to AI agents as one theory. Acyclic schemes, group synchronization, sheaf semantics, view merging, lenses, version validation, and team decision theory each answer one of the four questions—observation, realization, transition, semantic state—for one kind of system, and none was written for agents. The paper states the four questions once, for any collaboration of AI or human participants; proves the results that connect them (observation-fiber admissibility and its minimax value, exact semantic abstraction, minimum-instrumentation hardness, and their temporal and obstruction consequences); derives the relevant classical structures under explicit assumptions on restriction, translation, and self-updating state; and measures the resulting obstructions on public agent benchmarks. Strong conventional mechanisms are special cases: a version guard, residual solver, transaction manager, or dependency engine matches the general semantics whenever it already captures the complete relevant state relation, as Studies III and VI confirm.

7 Conclusion

When every agent passes the checks available in its local scope and the team is still wrong, one possible cause is not model capability but distributed state: the information that decides correctness is spread across contexts, participants, artifacts, representations, and time, and no one holds it all. That is the global coherence problem. It is broader than any one engineering discipline, and narrower than a claim that all or even most agent failures are global.

The theory answers four questions. Observation: if the deciding distinction is not in context, no amount of reasoning can guarantee the right action, and we know exactly how well randomization can do and how many bits of new state close the gap. Realization: join-tree overlap makes pairwise checks enough; cycles remove that guarantee, and no fixed locality bound works universally across unrestricted constraint semantics; agreement across representations can nevertheless be certified in linear time. Transition: re-expressing state is safe, changing it is not, so changes must be checked at commit. Semantic state: the memory worth keeping is exactly the history that changes what can happen next. Two costs run through all four: designing the smallest sufficient context is NP-hard, and repairing an inconsistency can be much harder than detecting it. Together these answers motivate one principled synthesis: a topology of where things meet, categories for what can change, groupoids for what only looks changed, sheaves for whether one world glues, and a history state for what still matters. Under explicit assumptions, these structures realize the properties exact validation requires; familiar tools of practice are domain-specific realizations of the same requirements.

The evidence lands on the boundary the theory draws, on both sides. A model that solves every task when it can see the deciding event scores 12–17 of 40 across tested arms when that event is hidden, with no arm significantly above chance, and one sentence of added context stating the missing fact raises the result to 40/40 (Study I). The theorem supplies the general limit; the finite panel is consistent with it. On TeamBench, ordinary teams overspend a shared 20-call budget in 5/5 runs, showing them the live count leaves 4/5, and commit enforcement removes every violation; observed mean progress does not fall in the five-run enforced comparison. On the same task, per-role escrow also reaches zero violations while an information-only counter does not; escrow–ledger progress differences are descriptive because their attestation gates differ (Study IV). Under the stated unique-name diagnostic, matching systems that work one pair at a time produce pairwise-invisible identity collisions across eight OAEI campaigns (Study VIII). Agents given split views reproduce them, and a network-level check detects and removes every one, but the send-to-all repair lowers mean F1 from 0.796 to 0.774 (Study IX). In τ2\tau^{2}-bench Telecom, ordinary policy checks suffice where the injected change breaks a policy rule, but only a harness that remembers what was read and what was committed prevents stale-read commits and recovers silently undone changes, 15 of 15 (Study V). Where a conventional mechanism already owns the relevant state, it matches the general harness, exactly as predicted (Studies III and VI).

The limits are clear. The agent studies use one model family and modest samples, and the aliasing probe is synthetic by design. The studies show that the predicted failures occur, that the tested reasoning, role, and sampling variations do not eliminate them in these panels, and that owning the missing state removes the targeted failures; they do not establish empirical equivalence among inference strategies or measure how much of broad agent-benchmark failure these mechanisms explain. The theorem, rather than the finite panel, supplies the general impossibility result. Natural prevalence and broader replication are the next empirical questions, and the theory says where to look: shared invariants across roles, split views over one object, and state that changes while agents reason about it.

This matters most as agent systems move from single assistants to teams and swarms. There, views are split by design and no participant may hold the whole state, so the conditions that permit the studied failures become more common. Such systems need explicit semantics for shared state, equivalence, and commit. The lesson for the agent community runs against instinct: when a team of agents fails, the fix may be not a bigger model, a longer context, or more review, but a harness that owns the state no one holds and puts the right distinctions into each agent’s context. No model and no context, however good, removes the need for an owner of a genuinely shared invariant; and a harness helps only with the state it owns, at the scope it checks, over the history it remembers. The central claim is simple: local intelligence cannot substitute for missing global state, but stochastic local intelligence can act reliably inside an explicit shared state with a governed commit. The claim is proved where it can be proved and tested where it must be tested, and it does not depend on any one domain. Multi-agent AI does not need only bigger models. It also needs context engineering with a target and a harness with a specification, and this paper supplies both.

Appendix A Proof conventions and provenance of results

The appendices distinguish three kinds of mathematical statements.

  1. 1.

    Elementary formulations and derived results for the present model. These include the admissible-action form of the Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem, its minimax (fractional-transversal) value, its randomized and adaptive-query extensions and sharp semantic-bit bounds, exact semantic abstraction, the minimum-instrumentation reduction, the fixed-kk Tseitin counterfamily as used here, the prestack form of coherence preservation with its shared-budget counterexample, the bridging results of Section 4.3 (local sufficiency, the groupoid of translations, and the coarsest self-updating exact state), and several runtime-state corollaries, including the linear obstruction (syndrome/cokernel) monitor theorem, the task-dependent state counts, and the fixed-length versus mutual-information contrast. The minimax value is linear-programming duality applied to this setting, and the adaptive version is a decision-tree argument; both are elementary once stated. The underlying indistinguishability and perceptual-aliasing ideas have classical precedents; the paper’s contribution is the particular formulation, extensions, and integration into global-coherence semantics. Proofs of the stated results are given in full.

  2. 2.

    Specializations or direct consequences of classical mathematics. Cycle synchronization, Myhill–Nerode minimization, acyclic relational gluing, possibilistic contextuality, treewidth-based CSP algorithms and their lower bounds, bounded-width theory, graph and cellular-sheaf cohomology, Max-Cut hardness of signed-graph balancing, Helly-type local-to-global bounds, invariant confluence [9], and optimistic concurrency are established theories. We state the exact form used by the paper and prove the specialized corollaries needed for the AI semantics, while citing the underlying results.

  3. 3.

    Interpretive projections. Connections to sheaf/descent language, obstruction quotients, category-theoretic composition, and agent-runtime design organize the preceding results into one framework; their mathematical content is the classical and derived results listed above.

Throughout, a guarantee is worst-case unless a distribution is explicitly stated. A stochastic policy may use arbitrary internal computation and randomness. The impossibility statements concern missing information, not bounded model intelligence: if two worlds induce the same complete information available to the policy, unlimited internal reasoning cannot distinguish them.

Appendix B Observation aliasing, exact state, and instrumentation

B.1 Full Observation-Aliasing Impossibility and information-budget results

This subsection proves the results of Section 2.2 and states in full the refinements summarized there: how often a randomized policy can be right, how many extra bits close the gap, when tool queries suffice, and what changes for near-optimal behavior.

B.1.1 Deterministic action selection

Let XX be a state space, YY an observation space, Ω:X→Y\Omega:X\to Y, 𝒜\mathcal{A} an action space, and C⁡(x)⊆𝒜C(x)\subseteq\mathcal{A} the (possibly empty) set of admissible actions at xx. A deterministic policy is a function π:Y→𝒜\pi:Y\to\mathcal{A}.

Full proof of Theorem 2.1.

Assume first that a universally valid policy π\pi exists. Fix any y∈Ω⁡(X)y\in\Omega(X). For every x∈Ω−1​(y)x\in\Omega^{-1}(y),

π⁡(y)=π⁡(Ω⁡(x))∈C⁡(x).\pi(y)=\pi(\Omega(x))\in C(x).

Thus the same element π⁡(y)\pi(y) belongs to every admissibility set in the fiber, so

π⁡(y)∈⋂x∈Ω−1​(y)C⁡(x),\pi(y)\in\bigcap_{x\in\Omega^{-1}(y)}C(x),

and the intersection is nonempty.

Conversely, suppose every nonempty observation fiber has nonempty common admissibility intersection. For each y∈Ω⁡(X)y\in\Omega(X) choose one element

ay∈⋂x∈Ω−1​(y)C⁡(x).a_{y}\in\bigcap_{x\in\Omega^{-1}(y)}C(x).

Define π⁡(y)=ay\pi(y)=a_{y} on Ω⁡(X)\Omega(X) and arbitrarily elsewhere. For any x∈Xx\in X, the chosen action aΩ⁡(x)a_{\Omega(x)} belongs to C⁡(x)C(x) by construction. Hence π⁡(Ω⁡(x))∈C⁡(x)\pi(\Omega(x))\in C(x) for every state. This proves necessity and sufficiency. ∎

The result is stronger than the statement that two aliased states have different truth labels. Different labels alone do not force different behavior. The obstruction is behavioral: the fiber must lack a common admissible action. This distinction prevents a false impossibility claim when a conservative action is valid in every aliased world.

B.1.2 Multi-agent communication without new observation

Consider mm agents with initial local observations oi=Ωi​(x)o_{i}=\Omega_{i}(x). A deterministic TT-round protocol consists of message functions

mi,t=Fi,t​(oi,{mj,s:s<t})m_{i,t}=F_{i,t}\bigl(o_{i},\{m_{j,s}:s<t\}\bigr)

and a final decision function of the transcript. Let the joint initial observation be

Ω⁡(x)=(Ω1​(x),…,Ωm​(x)).\Omega(x)=(\Omega_{1}(x),\ldots,\Omega_{m}(x)).
Proof of Corollary 2.2.

We prove by induction on the round that every message is a deterministic function of the joint initial observation. At round 11, each message is a function of the sender’s initial observation and therefore of the joint tuple. Assume all messages before round tt are functions of the joint initial observation. Then each round-tt message is a function of one initial observation and earlier messages, hence again a function of the joint tuple. By induction, the complete transcript is a function of Ω⁡(x)\Omega(x), and so is any deterministic final action computed from that transcript.

Therefore if Ω⁡(x)=Ω⁡(x′)\Omega(x)=\Omega(x^{\prime}), the protocol produces identical transcripts and identical final actions in the two worlds. If no common admissible action exists for the aliased worlds, the protocol cannot be valid on both. The number of roles, rounds, tokens, or internal computations does not change the information partition unless some operation introduces a new observation of the external state. ∎

The statement allows arbitrarily sophisticated messages. An agent can send proofs, plans, summaries, intermediate code, or entire copies of its local observation. None of these can distinguish states already identified by the joint observation map.

B.1.3 Randomized policies

A randomized policy on observation yy is a probability distribution PyP_{y} over actions. Its success probability at state xx is

px=PΩ⁡(x)​(C⁡(x)).p_{x}=P_{\Omega(x)}(C(x)).
Lemma B.1 (Aliased disjoint-action bound).

Let x1,…,xsx_{1},\ldots,x_{s} share one observation yy and let the sets C⁡(xi)C(x_{i}) be pairwise disjoint. Then for every randomized policy,

∑i=1spxi≤1.\sum_{i=1}^{s}p_{x_{i}}\leq 1.

Consequently, mini⁡pxi≤1/s\min_{i}p_{x_{i}}\leq 1/s and the uniform average success is at most 1/s1/s.

Proof.

All states induce the same output distribution PyP_{y}. Pairwise disjointness gives

∑i=1spxi=∑i=1sPy​(C⁡(xi))=Py​(⨆i=1sC⁡(xi))≤1.\sum_{i=1}^{s}p_{x_{i}}=\sum_{i=1}^{s}P_{y}(C(x_{i}))=P_{y}\!\left(\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{s}C(x_{i})\right)\leq 1.

The average is therefore at most 1/s1/s, and at least one term cannot exceed the average. ∎

A randomized multi-agent protocol with no new external observations can be regarded as a deterministic function of the initial joint observation plus an internal random seed. Conditional on any seed, aliased states still induce the same transcript. After averaging over seeds they therefore induce the same transcript and output distributions. Randomness changes which common distribution is used; it does not refine the observational partition.

Full proof of Theorem 2.3.

Apply Lemma B.1 with s=ks=k. The kk states share one output distribution because they share one observation, and their admissible-action sets are pairwise disjoint. Hence the sum of their success probabilities is at most one, so at least one state has success probability at most 1/k1/k. The same output-distribution premise holds for randomized multi-agent protocols by conditioning on the internal random seed as described above. ∎

B.1.4 Minimax value and fractional transversals

Theorem B.2 (Minimax value of an aliased fiber).

Let F=Ω−1​(y)F=\Omega^{-1}(y) be a finite fiber and 𝒜\mathcal{A} finite. Define the fractional transversal number

τ∗(F)=min{∑a∈𝒜wa:w≥0,∑a∈C⁡(x)wa≥1∀x∈F},\tau^{*}(F)=\min\Bigl\{\textstyle\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}w_{a}:\ w\geq 0,\ \sum_{a\in C(x)}w_{a}\geq 1\ \ \forall x\in F\Bigr\},

with τ∗​(F)=∞\tau^{*}(F)=\infty if some C⁡(x)C(x) is empty. The best worst-case success probability of any randomized observation-only policy on FF is

v⁡(F)=maxP∈Δ⁡(𝒜)⁡minx∈F⁡P⁡(C⁡(x))=1τ∗​(F).v(F)=\max_{P\in\Delta(\mathcal{A})}\ \min_{x\in F}\ P(C(x))=\frac{1}{\tau^{*}(F)}.

By linear-programming duality, τ∗(F)=max{∑xμx:μ≥0,∑x∈F:a∈C⁡(x)μx≤1∀a}\tau^{*}(F)=\max\{\sum_{x}\mu_{x}:\mu\geq 0,\ \sum_{x\in F:\,a\in C(x)}\mu_{x}\leq 1\ \forall a\}. When τ∗​(F)<∞\tau^{*}(F)<\infty, the normalized dual optimum is a prior on FF under which no action succeeds with probability above v⁡(F)v(F).

Proof.

If some C⁡(x)C(x) with x∈Fx\in F is empty, every policy fails at xx, so v⁡(F)=0=1/τ∗​(F)v(F)=0=1/\tau^{*}(F). Otherwise v⁡(F)v(F) is the optimum of the linear program

max⁡ts.t.∑a∈C⁡(x)Pa≥t(x∈F),∑aPa=1,P≥0.\max\ t\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{a\in C(x)}P_{a}\geq t\ \ (x\in F),\qquad\sum_{a}P_{a}=1,\qquad P\geq 0.

The uniform distribution is feasible with t≥1/|𝒜|>0t\geq 1/|\mathcal{A}|>0, so the optimum is positive. If (P,t)(P,t) is feasible with t>0t>0, then w=P/tw=P/t satisfies every covering constraint and has total weight 1/t1/t. Conversely, if ww is a fractional transversal, then P=w/∑awaP=w/\sum_{a}w_{a} and t=1/∑awat=1/\sum_{a}w_{a} are feasible. Hence maxt=1/min∑awa=1/τ∗(F)\max t=1/\min\sum_{a}w_{a}=1/\tau^{*}(F).

Write Mx,a=𝟏[a∈C(x)]M_{x,a}=\mathbf{1}[a\in C(x)]. The covering program min{𝟏⊤w:Mw≥𝟏,w≥0}\min\{\mathbf{1}^{\top}w:Mw\geq\mathbf{1},\ w\geq 0\} and the packing program max{𝟏⊤μ:M⊤μ≤𝟏,μ≥0}\max\{\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mu:M^{\top}\mu\leq\mathbf{1},\ \mu\geq 0\} are both feasible and bounded, so strong duality makes their optima equal. Let μ∗\mu^{*} be a packing optimum and π=μ∗/τ∗​(F)\pi=\mu^{*}/\tau^{*}(F). For every action aa,

π({x∈F:a∈C(x)})=1τ∗​(F)∑x:a∈C⁡(x)μx∗≤1τ∗​(F),\pi\bigl(\{x\in F:a\in C(x)\}\bigr)=\frac{1}{\tau^{*}(F)}\sum_{x:\,a\in C(x)}\mu^{*}_{x}\leq\frac{1}{\tau^{*}(F)},

so under the prior π\pi every policy, randomized or not, succeeds with probability at most 1/τ∗​(F)1/\tau^{*}(F).

For the consequences: v⁡(F)=1v(F)=1 iff some PP has P⁡(C⁡(x))=1P(C(x))=1 for every x∈Fx\in F, iff the support of PP lies in ⋂x∈FC⁡(x)\bigcap_{x\in F}C(x), iff that finite intersection is nonempty. If the C⁡(x)C(x) are nonempty and pairwise disjoint, any fractional transversal places weight at least one on each of |F||F| disjoint sets, so τ∗​(F)≥|F|\tau^{*}(F)\geq|F|, and one unit on one action per set attains it. ∎

Three consequences follow. First, v⁡(F)=1v(F)=1 exactly when the fiber has a common admissible action, so Theorem 2.1 is the case τ∗=1\tau^{*}=1. Second, nonempty pairwise-disjoint admissible sets give τ∗​(F)=|F|\tau^{*}(F)=|F|, so the bound of Theorem 2.3 is attained by choosing uniformly among one admissible action per state. Third, randomization can help substantially when admissible sets overlap without a common element. With C⁡(x1)={a,b}C(x_{1})=\{a,b\}, C⁡(x2)={b,c}C(x_{2})=\{b,c\}, C⁡(x3)={a,c}C(x_{3})=\{a,c\}, every deterministic policy fails in some state, while the uniform distribution on {a,b,c}\{a,b,c\} succeeds with probability 2/3=1/τ∗2/3=1/\tau^{*} in every state. Randomness does not create information, but it can hedge across an aliased fiber, and τ∗\tau^{*} measures exactly how well.

The integral transversal number τ⁡(F)\tau(F), the fewest actions that together hit every C⁡(x)C(x), satisfies τ∗​(F)≤τ⁡(F)\tau^{*}(F)\leq\tau(F). A deterministic policy has worst-case success 11 when τ⁡(F)=1\tau(F)=1 and 00 otherwise, so the gap between the two is the value of randomization on that fiber.

B.1.5 Additional semantic bits

Suppose the kk states in Theorem 2.3 share the same base observation but the runtime may send a deterministic semantic label z=ϕ⁡(x)z=\phi(x) chosen from at most M=2bM=2^{b} labels. Partition the states into label classes F1,…,FqF_{1},\ldots,F_{q} with q≤Mq\leq M. Within a class, the policy receives identical information and therefore uses one output distribution.

Corollary B.3 (Semantic-information bounds).

Under the setting of Theorem 2.3, suppose the runtime provides a deterministic semantic label with at most M=2bM=2^{b} values, refining the kk aliased worlds into at most MM classes. Then

average success≤min⁡(1,2bk),worst-case success≤1⌈k/2b⌉,\text{average success}\leq\min\!\left(1,\frac{2^{b}}{k}\right),\qquad\text{worst-case success}\leq\frac{1}{\lceil k/2^{b}\rceil},

where the average is under the uniform distribution on the kk worlds, and both bounds are attained. Consequently, any worst-case success guarantee above 1/21/2 requires 2b≥k2^{b}\geq k, that is, b≥⌈log2⁡k⌉b\geq\lceil\log_{2}k\rceil for integer bb: short of exact discrimination, a lossy interface cannot guarantee better than a coin flip on its worst state.

Proof.

For each nonempty label class FjF_{j}, Lemma B.1 implies

∑xi∈Fjpxi≤1andminxi∈Fj⁡pxi≤1|Fj|.\sum_{x_{i}\in F_{j}}p_{x_{i}}\leq 1\qquad\text{and}\qquad\min_{x_{i}\in F_{j}}p_{x_{i}}\leq\frac{1}{|F_{j}|}.

Summing the first inequality over all classes gives ∑i=1kpxi≤q≤2b\sum_{i=1}^{k}p_{x_{i}}\leq q\leq 2^{b}, so uniform average success is at most 2b/k2^{b}/k, and of course at most one. For the worst case, the kk states occupy at most MM classes, so by pigeonhole some class has |Fj|≥⌈k/M⌉|F_{j}|\geq\lceil k/M\rceil, and the second inequality gives worst-case success at most 1/⌈k/M⌉1/\lceil k/M\rceil.
