For attainment, split the kk states into min⁡(M,k)\min(M,k) classes whose sizes differ by at most one, so every class has at most ⌈k/M⌉\lceil k/M\rceil states. In class FjF_{j} let the policy choose uniformly among one admissible action per state. Each state then succeeds with probability 1/|Fj|≥1/⌈k/M⌉1/|F_{j}|\geq 1/\lceil k/M\rceil, and each class contributes total success exactly one, so average success is min⁡(M,k)/k\min(M,k)/k.

Finally, if M<kM<k then ⌈k/M⌉≥2\lceil k/M\rceil\geq 2 and worst-case success is at most 1/21/2. A worst-case guarantee above 1/21/2 therefore requires M≥kM\geq k, that is, b≥log2⁡kb\geq\log_{2}k, or b≥⌈log2⁡k⌉b\geq\lceil\log_{2}k\rceil when bb counts whole bits. ∎

The requirement is targeted: the shared runtime must expose enough semantic distinctions to separate cases that demand different behavior, rather than the whole world. If four otherwise identical program states differ only in which of four mutually exclusive approvals is authoritative, at least two bits of authoritative state are needed to distinguish all four exactly, and with only one bit the worst case is a coin flip. Inference compute and semantic state are different resources, and one cannot pay for the other.

This is a sharp bound for an explicit family in which correct actions are pairwise disjoint. Its role is to demonstrate that inference compute and semantic information are distinct resources in the worst case. For overlapping admissible sets, the same argument applies class by class with 1/τ∗​(Fj)1/\tau^{*}(F_{j}) in place of 1/|Fj|1/|F_{j}|.

B.1.6 Fixed-length labels versus mutual information

Suppose instead that the label ZZ may be random, the prior on the kk states is uniform, and I⁡(X,Z)≤bI(X;Z)\leq b bits. Because the admissible sets are disjoint, each successful action identifies the state, so a policy with average success probability psp_{s} under the uniform prior yields an estimator X^\widehat{X} of XX from ZZ with Pr[X^=X]≥ps\Pr[\widehat{X}=X]\geq p_{s}. Fano’s inequality [21] gives

log2⁡k−b≤H⁡(X∣Z)≤1+(1−ps)​log2​k,henceps≤b+1log2⁡k.\log_{2}k-b\leq H(X\mid Z)\leq 1+(1-p_{s})\log_{2}k,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad p_{s}\leq\frac{b+1}{\log_{2}k}.

For b≤log2⁡kb\leq\log_{2}k, the label that equals XX with probability p=b/log2⁡kp=b/\log_{2}k and a blank symbol otherwise has I⁡(X,Z)=p​log2​k=bI(X;Z)=p\log_{2}k=b and achieves ps=p+(1−p)/kp_{s}=p+(1-p)/k, so the bound is nearly tight. Counting label values and counting bits of mutual information therefore give very different prices; the main-text corollary uses the former because it governs worst-case guarantees.

B.1.7 Adaptive queries

A dd-query deterministic protocol is a decision tree of depth at most dd. Each internal node is labeled by a query q∈Qq\in Q, chosen as a function of Ω⁡(x)\Omega(x) and the answers seen so far; each outgoing edge is labeled by an answer; each leaf is labeled by an action. The information set of a node reached from xx is the set of states that agree with xx on Ω\Omega and on every query answered along the path.

Theorem B.4 (Adaptive aliasing).

Let QQ be a finite set of side-effect-free queries q:X→Yqq:X\to Y_{q} available in addition to Ω\Omega. For I⊆XI\subseteq X define

Solv0​(I)⇔⋂x∈IC⁡(x)≠∅,Solvd​(I)⇔Solvd−1​(I)∨∃q∈Q​∀y∈q⁡(I):Solvd−1​(I∩q−1​(y)).\mathrm{Solv}_{0}(I)\iff\bigcap_{x\in I}C(x)\neq\varnothing,\qquad\mathrm{Solv}_{d}(I)\iff\mathrm{Solv}_{d-1}(I)\ \vee\ \exists q\in Q\ \forall y\in q(I):\ \mathrm{Solv}_{d-1}\bigl(I\cap q^{-1}(y)\bigr).

A deterministic protocol that issues at most dd adaptively chosen queries guarantees an admissible action in every state if and only if Solvd​(Ω−1​(y))\mathrm{Solv}_{d}(\Omega^{-1}(y)) holds for every y∈Ω⁡(X)y\in\Omega(X). With no bound on the number of queries, such a protocol exists if and only if every block of the joint partition generated by Ω\Omega and all q∈Qq\in Q has a common admissible action.

Proof.

We prove by induction on dd that, for any information set II, a protocol of depth at most dd that is admissible on every state of II exists iff Solvd​(I)\mathrm{Solv}_{d}(I). For d=0d=0 the protocol is a single action, which must lie in ⋂x∈IC⁡(x)\bigcap_{x\in I}C(x). For d≥1d\geq 1, a protocol of depth at most dd either is a single action, requiring Solv0​(I)\mathrm{Solv}_{0}(I) and hence Solvd−1​(I)\mathrm{Solv}_{d-1}(I) by monotonicity, or begins with some query qq and continues on each answer y∈q⁡(I)y\in q(I) with a protocol of depth at most d−1d-1 on I∩q−1​(y)I\cap q^{-1}(y). By the induction hypothesis, the latter exists iff Solvd−1​(I∩q−1​(y))\mathrm{Solv}_{d-1}(I\cap q^{-1}(y)) for every y∈q⁡(I)y\in q(I). This is the recursive definition of Solvd​(I)\mathrm{Solv}_{d}(I). Applying the claim to I=Ω−1​(y)I=\Omega^{-1}(y) for each base observation gives the first statement.

For the unbounded case, let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be the common refinement of the partitions induced by Ω\Omega and by every q∈Qq\in Q. If every block of 𝒫\mathcal{P} has a common admissible action, the protocol that issues every query and then plays such an action is admissible. Conversely, two states in the same block give the same base observation and the same answer to every query, so any protocol follows the same path on both and plays the same action at the same leaf. That action must therefore be admissible on the whole block. ∎

Query side effects are excluded in the theorem. When a query also spends a shared resource, the protocol must additionally keep the spend admissible, which bounds the usable depth dd.

B.1.8 Approximate decision quality

Proposition B.5 (Approximate-optimality impossibility).

Let L⁡(x,a)L(x,a) be global loss and L∗​(x)=infaL⁡(x,a)L^{*}(x)=\inf_{a}L(x,a), assumed finite. For tolerance ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0, define the ε\varepsilon-optimal action set

Cε​(x)={a:L⁡(x,a)≤L∗​(x)+ε}.C_{\varepsilon}(x)=\{a:L(x,a)\leq L^{*}(x)+\varepsilon\}.

An observation-only deterministic policy can guarantee global regret at most ε\varepsilon if and only if every observation fiber has a common ε\varepsilon-optimal action:

∀y∈Ω⁡(X),⋂x∈Ω−1​(y)Cε​(x)≠∅.\forall y\in\Omega(X),\qquad\bigcap_{x\in\Omega^{-1}(y)}C_{\varepsilon}(x)\neq\varnothing.

Hence if one aliased fiber has no action that is ε\varepsilon-optimal in every compatible global state, no amount of observation-preserving reasoning can guarantee ε\varepsilon-optimal global behavior.

Proof.

Fix ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 and define

Cε​(x)={a:L⁡(x,a)≤L∗​(x)+ε}.C_{\varepsilon}(x)=\{a:L(x,a)\leq L^{*}(x)+\varepsilon\}.

A policy has worst-case regret at most ε\varepsilon precisely when its selected action belongs to Cε​(x)C_{\varepsilon}(x) for every possible state xx. The statement is therefore exactly Theorem 2.1 applied to the admissibility correspondence CεC_{\varepsilon}. (For ε=0\varepsilon=0 the set C0​(x)C_{0}(x) may be empty when the infimum is not attained; the theorem then correctly reports that no guarantee exists.) If every observation fiber has a common ε\varepsilon-optimal action, choose one such action for each fiber and obtain the guarantee. If some fiber has empty intersection, any policy chooses the same action for every state in that fiber, and that action must fall outside Cε​(x)C_{\varepsilon}(x) for at least one compatible state, producing regret strictly greater than ε\varepsilon there. ∎

For intuition, imagine two operating conditions that look identical to a team: in one, plan AA is near-optimal and plan BB costly; in the other, the ranking reverses. If no single plan lies within tolerance in both worlds, the team cannot guarantee even an approximately optimal choice until the missing distinction becomes observable. This extension is intentionally conditional rather than a blanket claim that local reasoning cannot attain global optimality. If aliased states happen to share one ε\varepsilon-optimal action, then the information deficit does not prevent an ε\varepsilon-optimal guarantee. The obstruction arises only when the hidden distinction changes what counts as sufficiently good global behavior.

B.2 Exact semantic abstraction, soundness, progress, and completeness

Let ϕ:X→Z\phi:X\to Z be the runtime abstraction. A validator is a map

V:Z×𝒜→{0,1}.V:Z\times\mathcal{A}\to\{0,1\}.

It is sound if V⁡(ϕ⁡(x),a)=1V(\phi(x),a)=1 implies a∈C⁡(x)a\in C(x). It is complete if a∈C⁡(x)a\in C(x) implies V⁡(ϕ⁡(x),a)=1V(\phi(x),a)=1. Exactness means both.

Proof of Proposition 2.4.

Fix zz and let AV​(z)={a:V⁡(z,a)=1}A_{V}(z)=\{a:V(z,a)=1\}. If VV is sound, then for every x∈Xzx\in X_{z} and every a∈AV​(z)a\in A_{V}(z) we have a∈C⁡(x)a\in C(x). Hence

AV​(z)⊆⋂x∈XzC⁡(x)=Csafe​(z).A_{V}(z)\subseteq\bigcap_{x\in X_{z}}C(x)=C_{\mathrm{safe}}(z).

Therefore the intersection is the unique maximally permissive sound action set at that abstraction state. A sound nonblocking validator exists at zz iff this set is nonempty.

For exactness, suppose first that ϕ⁡(x)=ϕ⁡(x′)=z\phi(x)=\phi(x^{\prime})=z. If C⁡(x)≠C⁡(x′)C(x)\neq C(x^{\prime}), choose aa in the symmetric difference. Exact validation would require different values for V⁡(z,a)V(z,a) in the two states, impossible. Hence exactness implies identical admissibility profiles within every fiber.

Conversely, if all states in a fiber share one profile, define V⁡(z,a)=1V(z,a)=1 exactly when aa belongs to that common profile. This is well-defined and exact. Thus exact validation is possible iff ϕ\phi refines the equivalence relation x∼Cx′⇔C(x)=C(x′)x\sim_{C}x^{\prime}\iff C(x)=C(x^{\prime}). ∎

Corollary B.6 (Minimal exact state count).

Let

K=|{C⁡(x):x∈X}|.K=\bigl|\{C(x):x\in X\}\bigr|.

Every exact abstraction has at least KK reachable labels, and the quotient map x↦C⁡(x)x\mapsto C(x) has exactly KK. Therefore the minimum exact deterministic state count is KK, and any fixed-length binary code needs at least ⌈log2⁡K⌉\lceil\log_{2}K\rceil bits.

Proof.

States with different admissibility profiles cannot share an exact abstraction label by Proposition 2.4; hence at least one label per profile is necessary. Mapping to the profile itself attains the bound. The bit bound is the pigeonhole principle. ∎

Interpretation.

The quotient is task-relative. If the only operation is deciding whether a single fixed action a0a_{0} is legal, the semantic state may collapse to one bit even when the underlying world is enormous. If the runtime must validate arbitrary proposals, it must preserve the full admissibility profile. Thus “global state” in this paper means sufficient semantic state for the intended action interface, not necessarily a lossless copy of the physical world.

B.3 NP-hardness of minimum exact instrumentation

Choosing the fewest fields that make validation exact is a covering problem over pairs of states that must be told apart, and it inherits Set Cover’s hardness and approximability.

Define the decision problem Exact-Instrumentation: given a finite state set XX, profiles C⁡(x)C(x), candidate observables f1,…,fpf_{1},\ldots,f_{p}, and integer kk, is there a subset J⊆[p]J\subseteq[p] with |J|≤k|J|\leq k such that the joint map (fj)j∈J(f_{j})_{j\in J} never merges two states with different admissibility profiles?

Theorem B.7.

Exact-Instrumentation is NP-complete for explicitly represented finite instances; the corresponding minimum-cardinality optimization problem is NP-hard.

Proof.

Membership in NP follows because a proposed subset JJ can be checked by comparing the selected observable vectors for every pair of explicitly listed states with different profiles.

For NP-hardness reduce Set-Cover. Let the universe be U={u1,…,um}U=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{m}\}, candidate subsets S1,…,SpS_{1},\ldots,S_{p}, and cover budget kk. Construct one reference state x0x_{0} and one state xux_{u} for every u∈Uu\in U. Let

C⁡(x0)={a0},C⁡(xu)={a1}C(x_{0})=\{a_{0}\},\qquad C(x_{u})=\{a_{1}\}

for two distinct actions a0,a1a_{0},a_{1}. All states xux_{u} share one profile, so exact validation requires only that each xux_{u} be separated from x0x_{0}; no pair xu,xvx_{u},x_{v} needs separation.

For each set SjS_{j}, define Boolean observable

fj(x0)=0,fj(xu)=𝟏[u∈Sj].f_{j}(x_{0})=0,\qquad f_{j}(x_{u})=\mathbf{1}[u\in S_{j}].

A selected family JJ distinguishes x0x_{0} from a particular xux_{u} iff some selected set contains uu. Therefore the selected observables are exact iff the corresponding subsets cover every universe element. There is an exact instrumentation of size at most kk iff there is a set cover of size at most kk. Since Set-Cover is NP-complete [50], the decision problem is NP-complete and the optimization problem NP-hard. ∎

The reduction also shows why the problem is naturally a hitting/set-cover problem on conflicting state pairs. Let

P={{x,x′}:C⁡(x)≠C⁡(x′)}.P=\{\{x,x^{\prime}\}:C(x)\neq C(x^{\prime})\}.

Each observable covers the pairs it distinguishes. Exact instrumentation is precisely the problem of covering PP. Consequently the greedy Set Cover algorithm, which repeatedly selects the observable separating the most still-unseparated conflicting pairs, achieves an H⁡(|P|)≤ln⁡|P|+1H(|P|)\leq\ln|P|+1 approximation when the finite conflict universe is explicit. The bound cannot be improved much. In the reduction above the conflicting pairs are exactly {x0,xu}\{x_{0},x_{u}\} for u∈Uu\in U, so |P|=|U||P|=|U| and instrumentation size equals cover size. Any (1−ϵ)​ln⁡|P|(1-\epsilon)\ln|P| approximation for Exact-Instrumentation would therefore give a (1−ϵ)​ln⁡|U|(1-\epsilon)\ln|U| approximation for Set Cover, which is impossible in polynomial time unless P=NP\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP} [24]. The problem generalizes the Minimum Test Collection problem of Garey and Johnson [34], which is the special case in which all admissibility profiles are distinct and observables are binary. It is also closely related to finding a minimum decision-relative reduct in rough-set theory, where the conflicting pairs PP form the discernibility matrix and the decision attribute plays the role of the admissibility profile [72]. The hardness itself is therefore expected. What the admissibility form adds is its meaning: the attributes that must be kept are exactly those that separate worlds where different actions are valid.

Appendix C Realization, acyclicity, and local checking

C.1 Local-to-global realization and the two reconstruction failures

Let R:X⁡(U)→Match⁡({Ui})R:X(U)\to\mathrm{Match}(\{U_{i}\}) be the restriction-to-local-views map. In the set-valued case, two logically independent properties are:

separatedness:R​ is injective,gluing/existence:R​ is surjective.\begin{array}[]{ll}\text{separatedness:}&R\text{ is injective},\\ \text{gluing/existence:}&R\text{ is surjective}.\end{array}

A sheaf satisfies both for each declared cover. This decomposition is useful for agent semantics because failure of injectivity and failure of surjectivity have different operational meanings.

If RR is not injective, two distinct global states produce the same complete local family. If those states have incompatible action requirements, Theorem 2.1 turns the structural non-uniqueness into an action-selection impossibility. If RR is not surjective, a family of local states can pass all declared matching tests yet correspond to no global world at all.

C.1.1 Three-variable cyclic counterexample

Let local relation RA​BR_{AB} contain assignments satisfying A=BA=B, RB​CR_{BC} assignments satisfying B=CB=C, and RA​CR_{AC} assignments satisfying A≠CA\neq C, with Boolean variables. Each relation projects onto {0,1}\{0,1\} on its shared variable, so the pairwise projections agree. But a global assignment would imply A=B=CA=B=C from the first two relations and A≠CA\neq C from the third, contradiction. Hence pairwise matching does not imply a global realization on this cyclic scope pattern.

The same example can be written as a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} edge-label problem: equality is label 00, inequality is label 11, and the cycle sum is 0+0+1=1≠00+0+1=1\neq 0. The relational contradiction and nontrivial group holonomy are therefore two descriptions of the same obstruction in this case; general sheaf obstructions are richer than group holonomy.

The failure lives in the presheaf of relations, not of assignments. Let ℛ⁡(W)\mathcal{R}(W) be the set of relations on a variable set WW, with projection as restriction. The family (RA​B,RB​C,RA​C)(R_{AB},R_{BC},R_{AC}) agrees on all overlaps in ℛ\mathcal{R}, yet no relation RR on {A,B,C}\{A,B,C\} projects onto all three, so ℛ\mathcal{R} fails the gluing condition. By contrast, in the presheaf that assigns to each scope the assignments satisfying the constraints contained in it, a family of committed assignments sA​B,sB​C,sA​Cs_{AB},s_{BC},s_{AC} that agree on overlaps would satisfy A=B=CA=B=C and A≠CA\neq C at once; no such family exists, so there is no matching family to glue. This distinction is the possibilistic sheaf model of contextuality [2], whose cohomological obstructions are studied in [3]; the connection to acyclic database schemes is made in [4].

C.1.2 A state-level gluing failure: shared resources

Let scopes U1,…,UmU_{1},\ldots,U_{m} be disjoint, let X⁡(Ui)={0,…,B}X(U_{i})=\{0,\ldots,B\} record participant ii’s spend, and let X⁡(U)={s∈{0,…,B}m:∑isi≤B}X(U)=\{s\in\{0,\ldots,B\}^{m}:\sum_{i}s_{i}\leq B\} with restriction s↦sis\mapsto s_{i}. With no overlaps, every tuple in ∏iX⁡(Ui)\prod_{i}X(U_{i}) is a matching family, and ρ:X⁡(U)→∏iX⁡(Ui)\rho:X(U)\to\prod_{i}X(U_{i}) is the inclusion. It is injective, and for m≥2m\geq 2 and B≥1B\geq 1 it is not surjective: the tuple (B,B,0,…,0)(B,B,0,\ldots,0) has no preimage. Now add a ledger scope U0U_{0} whose local state is the spend vector, with local constraint ∑isi≤B\sum_{i}s_{i}\leq B, overlapping each UiU_{i} in the ii-th spend. A matching family must now agree with a ledger state that satisfies the constraint, so every matching family has exactly one global preimage and ρ\rho becomes bijective. This is the formal content of adding an authoritative ledger.

C.1.3 Acyclic relational schemes

The BFMY theorem cited in the main text is classical: acyclicity of the relation-scope hypergraph is equivalent to several desirable local-to-global properties, including forms in which pairwise consistency suffices for global consistency [14, 15]. We use it as a structural boundary, not as an original theorem. Combined with the cyclic example, it says that topology can determine whether local consistency is already globally decisive.

C.2 No universal fixed order of local satisfiability checking

The previous triangle defeats pairwise checks. The next construction shows that merely increasing a fixed locality order does not solve unrestricted global coherence.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a connected graph with n=|V|n=|V|. Associate a binary variable xe∈𝔽2x_{e}\in\mathbb{F}_{2} with each edge. For every vertex vv, impose the parity equation

⨁e∋vxe=cv.\bigoplus_{e\ni v}x_{e}=c_{v}.

Let B∈𝔽2n×|E|B\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n\times|E|} be the vertex-edge incidence matrix and c∈𝔽2nc\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} the charge vector, so the system is B​x=cBx=c.

Proposition C.1 (No fixed kk-local satisfiability test).

For every fixed kk, there exists a finite family of local constraints such that every subfamily of at most kk constraints is jointly satisfiable but the complete family is not.

Proof.

Choose any connected graph with n>kn>k and choose cc with odd total parity. Because each edge touches two vertices, summing all rows of BB gives zero. Hence summing all equations yields

0=⨁v∈Vcv=1,0=\bigoplus_{v\in V}c_{v}=1,

so the full system is inconsistent.

For a connected graph, rank⁡(B)=n−1\operatorname{rank}(B)=n-1. The left nullspace is therefore one-dimensional and is generated by the all-ones vector; equivalently, the only nonzero linear dependence among all nn vertex rows is their total sum. Any proper subset of rows is linearly independent: a dependence among a proper subset, padded with zero coefficients on omitted rows, would produce a nonzero left-null vector not equal to the all-ones vector.

Take any subfamily of j<nj<n equations. Its j×|E|j\times|E| coefficient matrix has row rank jj, so its linear map onto 𝔽2j\mathbb{F}_{2}^{j} is surjective. Consequently every right-hand side on those jj equations is satisfiable, including the restriction of cc. Every subfamily of size at most k<nk<n is therefore satisfiable although the full family is not. ∎

This is a statement about bounded-order joint satisfiability, not about every possible notion of local consistency. Some structured classes admit bounded witness theorems, as Helly’s theorem and acyclic relational schemes demonstrate. The conclusion is only that no fixed universal locality order works across unrestricted constraint semantics.

Globality is not the same as computational hardness.

On an nn-cycle the Tseitin contradiction can require all nn vertex equations before inconsistency appears, yet the graph has constant treewidth and total charge parity can be checked in O⁡(n)O(n) time. Thus “requires a global witness” does not imply “computationally hard.” This distinction is essential when interpreting agent failures.

It also separates subfamily checking from propagation. On the cycle, variables are edges and each vertex constraint is binary, so the primal graph is itself an nn-cycle of treewidth two. Instances whose structure has treewidth less than kk are decided by kk-consistency [22], so 3-consistency, which derives new binary constraints along paths, detects the contradiction although no small subfamily does. Tseitin systems on bounded-degree expanders defeat propagation as well: they require resolution width Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) [16], and resolution width corresponds to the level of consistency needed [5], so kk-consistency fails for every k=o⁡(n)k=o(n).

For a fixed finite constraint language the question “what structure determines the order of globality?” has a precise answer. By the bounded-width theorem of Barto and Kozik, some fixed level of local consistency decides every instance exactly when, for a core language, its algebra of polymorphisms omits tame-congruence types 1 and 2 [13]. Type 1 is an additional obstruction in the general case. Within the Taylor/tractable regime, which already omits type 1, affine equations over nontrivial finite Abelian groups (type 2) are the remaining canonical obstruction; parity is its simplest representative here.

Appendix D Representation, width, and linear obstructions

D.1 Representation synchronization, cycle rank, and verification complexity

Pairwise translations are globally consistent exactly when every loop composes to the identity, and one check per non-tree edge suffices to verify this in linear time.

Let Γ=(V,E)\Gamma=(V,E) be an undirected graph with an arbitrary reference orientation on each edge. Let GG be a group. Each oriented edge i→ji\to j carries gi​j∈Gg_{ij}\in G, with reverse orientation gj​i=gi​j−1g_{ji}=g_{ij}^{-1}. A synchronized representation is a choice of vertex frames hi∈Gh_{i}\in G satisfying

gi​j=hi​hj−1g_{ij}=h_{i}h_{j}^{-1}

for every oriented edge.

Theorem D.1 (Cycle criterion).

A synchronized representation exists iff the ordered product of edge labels around every oriented cycle is the identity.

Proof.

If gi​j=hi​hj−1g_{ij}=h_{i}h_{j}^{-1}, then along a cycle i0→i1→⋯→iℓ=i0i_{0}\to i_{1}\to\cdots\to i_{\ell}=i_{0},

∏r=0ℓ−1gir​ir+1=∏r=0ℓ−1hir​hir+1−1=e\prod_{r=0}^{\ell-1}g_{i_{r}i_{r+1}}=\prod_{r=0}^{\ell-1}h_{i_{r}}h_{i_{r+1}}^{-1}=e

by telescoping.

Conversely, choose a spanning forest TT and one root per component. Set each root frame arbitrarily. Traverse the tree. If tree edge i→ji\to j is traversed away from a vertex whose frame is known, define hj=gi​j−1​hih_{j}=g_{ij}^{-1}h_{i}; if the stored orientation is reversed use the inverse edge label. Because a tree has one simple root path to each vertex, this defines each frame without ambiguity and makes every tree edge satisfy the synchronization equation.

For a non-tree edge i→ji\to j, combine that edge with the unique tree path from jj back to ii. This is its fundamental cycle. The assumed identity product around that cycle is algebraically equivalent to gi​j=hi​hj−1g_{ij}=h_{i}h_{j}^{-1}. Hence all non-tree edges also synchronize. ∎

Corollary D.2 (Spanning-forest verification).

For cc connected components, it suffices to assign frames along |V|−c|V|-c tree edges and verify the β1=|E|−|V|+c\beta_{1}=|E|-|V|+c non-tree edges. With group composition/inversion/comparison cost cGc_{G}, verification takes

O⁡((|V|+|E|)​cG)O((|V|+|E|)c_{G})

time and O⁡(|V|)O(|V|) stored frames in the straightforward implementation.

This is a genuine algorithmic bound only under the declared operation-cost model. For fixed-dimensional rigid transforms cGc_{G} can be treated as constant. For dense d×dd\times d matrix groups, naive multiplication contributes an additional O⁡(d3)O(d^{3}) factor.

D.1.1 Counting coherent labelings

Assume GG is finite. After fixing one root frame in each component, the remaining |V|−c|V|-c frames can be chosen freely. Each choice determines one coherent edge labeling, and distinct choices with fixed roots produce distinct tree-edge labels. Therefore

Ncoh=|G||V|−c.N_{\mathrm{coh}}=|G|^{|V|-c}.

All unconstrained edge labelings number |G||E||G|^{|E|}, so a uniformly random labeling is coherent with probability

|G|−(|E|−|V|+c)=|G|−β1.\boxed{|G|^{-(|E|-|V|+c)}=|G|^{-\beta_{1}}.}

For this model the cycle rank counts independent global coherence conditions. For G=ℤ2G=\mathbb{Z}_{2} this also makes β1\beta_{1} loop checks necessary. A loop check is a linear functional on labelings in ℤ2E\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{E}, and the loops form a cycle space of dimension β1\beta_{1}. Fewer than β1\beta_{1} loops span a proper subspace of it, so some loop γ\gamma lies outside their span, and some labeling has odd sum on γ\gamma yet even sum on every checked loop. That labeling is incoherent but passes every chosen check.

D.1.2 State lower bound for arbitrary relative-transform validation

Fix a graph and define an action query (i,j,g)(i,j,g), for vertices i,ji,j in the same connected component, to be admissible exactly when the true relative transform hi​hj−1h_{i}h_{j}^{-1} equals gg. Distinct synchronized frame configurations modulo one global right action per component induce distinct relative-transform profiles. There are |G||V|−c|G|^{|V|-c} such profiles. Proposition 2.4 therefore implies that an exact validator for arbitrary relative-transform proposals needs at least

(|V|−c)​log2​|G|(|V|-c)\log_{2}|G|

bits in any fixed-length encoding, while storing one group element per non-root tree vertex attains the same information count up to encoding overhead. This bound is task-specific: a validator answering only one fixed relative-transform query can use less state.

D.1.3 Incremental append-only synchronization

When constraints are inserted over time without deletions, weighted union–find (disjoint-set union with group potentials) can maintain component membership and relative frame potentials. Each inserted edge either joins two components or closes a cycle; in the latter case its implied transform is compared with the stored relative potential. Under standard union-by-rank/path-compression assumptions, the data-structure part costs O⁡(α⁡(|V|))O(\alpha(|V|)) amortized per insertion, multiplied by the cost of the necessary group operations. This is a standard dynamic-connectivity specialization; deletions require different machinery and are not covered by the bound.

D.2 Constraint width and bounded local-to-global reasoning

The cost of exact global reasoning is governed by how many variables must be considered together (treewidth), not by the total number of variables or agents.

Consider a finite-domain CSP with nn variables, maximum domain size dd, and a supplied tree decomposition of primal-graph width ww. Each bag contains at most w+1w+1 variables and therefore at most dw+1d^{w+1} local assignments. Standard dynamic programming passes compatibility tables along the decomposition, yielding a running time of the form

O⁡(n​dw+1​p​(n))O(n\,d^{w+1}\,p(n))

where p⁡(n)p(n) captures polynomial bookkeeping and constraint-access costs; under common bounded-arity, constant-time lookup assumptions this is summarized as O⁡(n​dw+1)O(nd^{w+1}) [33]. The crucial qualitative fact is that the exponential cost depends only on interaction width (with domain size as its base), not on the number of variables: exact global consistency can be easy for very large but tree-like systems and difficult for smaller densely entangled systems.

Width is also the right parameter from below. Grohe showed that for a recursively enumerable class of bounded-arity structures, CSP restricted to that class of constraint structures is solvable in polynomial time if and only if the cores of those structures have bounded treewidth, assuming FPT≠W⁡[1]\mathrm{FPT}\neq\mathrm{W}[1] [40]. Marx showed that, under the Exponential Time Hypothesis, no algorithm solves CSP in time f⁡(G)​‖I‖o⁡(tw⁡(G)/log⁡tw⁡(G))f(G)\,\|I\|^{o(\mathrm{tw}(G)/\log\mathrm{tw}(G))} for primal graphs GG of treewidth tw⁡(G)\mathrm{tw}(G) [57]. The exponential dependence on width therefore cannot be removed by a cleverer general algorithm.

For acyclic relational joins, join-tree/semijoin algorithms give an even sharper data-complexity statement. Yannakakis-style evaluation of full acyclic joins can be performed in time linear in input plus output size under standard relational cost assumptions [85]. These classical results justify the paper’s claim that global coherence is not synonymous with global recomputation.

Helly comparison.

Convex feasibility gives another structural bound of a different kind. Helly’s theorem states that for a finite family of convex subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, empty global intersection is witnessed by some subfamily of at most d+1d+1 sets. Thus some state algebras have a bounded local-to-global witness order even though Proposition C.1 rules out a universal order across unrestricted constraints.

D.3 Linear obstruction states, cokernels, and detection versus repair

For linear constraints, a single vector (the syndrome) decides whether local specifications fit, is the smallest state a monitor must keep, and is cheap to compute even though the cheapest repair is hard to find.

Let A:𝔽qn→𝔽qmA:\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}\to\mathbb{F}_{q}^{m} be linear with rank rr. A local specification b∈𝔽qmb\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{m} is globally realizable when A​x=bAx=b has a solution.

Choose a matrix NN whose columns form a basis of ker⁡AT\ker A^{T}. Then NN has m−rm-r columns and define the syndrome

σ⁡(b)=NT​b∈𝔽qm−r.\sigma(b)=N^{T}b\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{m-r}.
Theorem D.3 (Linear obstruction state).

A​x=bAx=b is realizable if and only if σ⁡(b)=0\sigma(b)=0. If the allowed additive updates can realize every syndrome shift, then two current specifications have identical future realizability behavior if and only if they have the same syndrome. Consequently the minimal deterministic temporal monitor for realizability has

qm−rq^{m-r}

states, requiring at least ⌈(m−r)​log2​q⌉\lceil(m-r)\log_{2}q\rceil bits in any fixed-length binary encoding.

Proof.

Because NT​A=0N^{T}A=0, solvability implies NT​b=0N^{T}b=0. Conversely, NT​b=0N^{T}b=0 means bb is orthogonal to ker⁡AT\ker A^{T}. Finite-dimensional linear algebra gives

(ker⁡AT)⟂=im⁡A,(\ker A^{T})^{\perp}=\operatorname{im}A,

so b∈im⁡Ab\in\operatorname{im}A and a solution exists.

If σ⁡(b)=σ⁡(b′)\sigma(b)=\sigma(b^{\prime}), then for every additive update δ\delta,

σ⁡(b+δ)=σ⁡(b)+σ⁡(δ)=σ⁡(b′)+σ⁡(δ)=σ⁡(b′+δ),\sigma(b+\delta)=\sigma(b)+\sigma(\delta)=\sigma(b^{\prime})+\sigma(\delta)=\sigma(b^{\prime}+\delta),

so the two trajectories agree forever on realizability. Conversely, if syndromes s≠s′s\neq s^{\prime} differ and every syndrome shift is realizable by an allowed update, choose δ\delta with σ⁡(δ)=−s\sigma(\delta)=-s. Then b+δb+\delta is realizable while b′+δb^{\prime}+\delta has nonzero syndrome s′−ss^{\prime}-s. Thus different syndromes are future-distinguishable. Myhill–Nerode-style future equivalence therefore has exactly qm−rq^{m-r} classes. ∎

A fixed-length encoding of these states requires

⌈log2⁡qm−r⌉=⌈(m−r)​log2​q⌉\left\lceil\log_{2}q^{m-r}\right\rceil=\left\lceil(m-r)\log_{2}q\right\rceil

bits. When qq is a power of two and the natural field encoding is used, this is exactly (m−r)​log2​q(m-r)\log_{2}q bits.

D.3.1 Cokernel form

Let A:X→YA:X\to Y be a homomorphism of finite Abelian groups. Realizability means b∈im⁡Ab\in\operatorname{im}A. The obstruction is the coset

[b]∈coker⁡A:=Y/im⁡A.[b]\in\operatorname{coker}A:=Y/\operatorname{im}A.

Then bb is realizable iff [b]=0[b]=0. Under updates whose images generate the quotient, two current specifications have identical future realizability behavior iff they lie in the same coset. Thus the cokernel itself is the minimal future-semantic state for this decision problem, with |coker⁡A||\operatorname{coker}A| states.

For a connected Tseitin system, the obstruction quotient has two elements and the semantic state is one parity bit. For Abelian graph synchronization, the obstruction degrees of freedom correspond to independent cycles; the familiar cycle-space dimension β1\beta_{1} reappears.

D.3.2 Random-coherence law

Since |im⁡A|=qr|\operatorname{im}A|=q^{r} among qmq^{m} possible right-hand sides,

Prb∼Unif[Ax=b solvable]=qrqm=q−(m−r).\Pr_{b\sim\mathrm{Unif}}[Ax=b\text{ solvable}]=\frac{q^{r}}{q^{m}}=\boxed{q^{-(m-r)}}.

The exponent is the dimension of the linear obstruction state.

D.3.3 Detection versus minimum repair

Detection is syndrome computation plus a zero test, hence polynomial in the matrix dimensions under standard linear algebra. Minimum Hamming-weight repair asks for

mine⁡‖e‖0s.t.σ⁡(e)=σ⁡(b).\min_{e}\|e\|_{0}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sigma(e)=\sigma(b).

This is the general syndrome-decoding form. Classical coding-theory results show minimum-weight decoding to be NP-hard/NP-complete in standard formulations [17]. Thus a class can admit cheap exact detection while optimal repair is computationally hard. The agent-runtime implication is prevention-oriented: validating an obstruction before commit can be much easier than finding the smallest post-hoc set of local artifacts or assertions to change. The reduction is valid for arbitrary codes because every full-row-rank parity-check matrix HH arises as NTN^{T} for some AA: take the columns of AA to be a basis of ker⁡H\ker H.

D.3.4 Graph homology as the obstruction space

Let Γ=(V,E)\Gamma=(V,E) have cc components and fix an orientation of each edge. For a finite Abelian group AA, the coboundary δ:AV→AE\delta:A^{V}\to A^{E}, (δ​h)i​j=hi−hj(\delta h)_{ij}=h_{i}-h_{j}, has kernel the locally constant functions, so |im⁡δ|=|A||V|−c|\operatorname{im}\delta|=|A|^{|V|-c} and

coker⁡δ=AE/im⁡δ=H1​(Γ,A)≅Aβ1,β1=|E|−|V|+c,\operatorname{coker}\delta=A^{E}/\operatorname{im}\delta=H^{1}(\Gamma;A)\cong A^{\beta_{1}},\qquad\beta_{1}=|E|-|V|+c,

the last isomorphism because H1​(Γ,ℤ)H_{1}(\Gamma;\mathbb{Z}) is free of rank β1\beta_{1} and H0H_{0} is free. Abelian synchronization is realizability of g∈AEg\in A^{E} as δ​h\delta h, so by the cokernel form above its minimal future-semantic state is H1​(Γ,A)H^{1}(\Gamma;A), and a uniformly random labeling is coherent with probability |A|−β1|A|^{-\beta_{1}}, which is the counting law of Appendix D.

Dually, the incidence map ∂:𝔽2E→𝔽2V\partial:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{E}\to\mathbb{F}_{2}^{V} sends an edge to the sum of its endpoints and has rank |V|−c|V|-c. The Tseitin system is realizability of the charge vector as ∂x\partial x, so its obstruction space is

coker∂=H0(Γ;𝔽2)≅𝔽2c,\operatorname{coker}\partial=H_{0}(\Gamma;\mathbb{F}_{2})\cong\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\,c},

one parity bit per component. The two linear obstructions in the paper are therefore the two ends of graph homology. For a cellular sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} of finite-dimensional 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-vector spaces on Γ\Gamma, the sheaf coboundary δℱ:C0​(Γ,ℱ)→C1​(Γ,ℱ)\delta_{\mathcal{F}}:C^{0}(\Gamma;\mathcal{F})\to C^{1}(\Gamma;\mathcal{F}) plays the role of δ\delta, the obstruction space is H1​(Γ,ℱ)=coker⁡δℱH^{1}(\Gamma;\mathcal{F})=\operatorname{coker}\delta_{\mathcal{F}}, and Theorem D.3 applies with m−r=dimH1​(Γ,ℱ)m-r=\dim H^{1}(\Gamma;\mathcal{F}) [43].

D.3.5 Minimum repair for ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} labels

Proof of Proposition 3.6.

Detection is Corollary 3.5 with G=ℤ2G=\mathbb{Z}_{2}. For repair, the coherent labelings are exactly im⁡δ={(hi+hj)i​j:h∈ℤ2V}\operatorname{im}\delta=\{(h_{i}+h_{j})_{ij}:h\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{V}\}, so the minimum number of label changes is

minh∈ℤ2V⁡|{i​j∈E:gi​j≠hi+hj}|.\min_{h\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{V}}\bigl|\{ij\in E:\ g_{ij}\neq h_{i}+h_{j}\}\bigr|.

Given a graph Γ\Gamma, set gi​j=1g_{ij}=1 on every edge. An edge then agrees with hh exactly when hi≠hjh_{i}\neq h_{j}, that is, when the bipartition defined by hh cuts it. The minimum repair therefore equals |E|−maxcut⁡(Γ)|E|-\mathrm{maxcut}(\Gamma), and deciding whether it is at most ℓ\ell is equivalent to deciding whether Γ\Gamma has a cut of size at least |E|−ℓ|E|-\ell. Max-Cut remains NP-complete with unit edge weights (Simple Max Cut, problem ND16 in [34]; the weighted version is in [50]), so minimum repair is NP-hard. ∎

The minimum repair is the frustration index of the signed graph (Γ,g)(\Gamma,g). On planar graphs it reduces to a minimum-weight matching and is polynomial [10, 41].

Appendix E Temporal state and atomic commit

E.1 Temporal semantic state and Myhill–Nerode minimization

A runtime needs to remember only those facts about the past that change which futures are legal; this subsection makes that exact and counts the states for a budget with obligations.

Let Σ\Sigma be an action alphabet and L⊆Σ∗L\subseteq\Sigma^{*} the language of valid finite trajectories. For histories h,h′∈Σ∗h,h^{\prime}\in\Sigma^{*} define future equivalence

h≡Lh′⇔∀u∈Σ∗,hu∈L⇔h′u∈L.h\equiv_{L}h^{\prime}\iff\forall u\in\Sigma^{*},\quad hu\in L\iff h^{\prime}u\in L.

The classical Myhill–Nerode theorem states that a language is regular iff this relation has finitely many classes, and in that case the minimal deterministic automaton has exactly one state per class [46]. In the present interpretation, a temporal fact belongs in authoritative semantic state exactly when forgetting it merges histories with different sets of valid futures.

E.1.1 Budget plus obligations

Let the system have integer budget B≥0B\geq 0 and kk independent Boolean obligations. The alphabet contains unit action spend, idempotent actions marki\texttt{mark}_{i}, and finish. A trajectory is valid when spending never exceeds the budget and finish occurs only after all obligations are marked; after successful finish no further action is legal.

The obvious deterministic monitor has states

(r,S),r∈{0,…,B},S⊆[k],(r,S),\qquad r\in\{0,\ldots,B\},\quad S\subseteq[k],

plus terminal accept and dead/error states. Hence there are (B+1)​2k+2(B+1)2^{k}+2 states.

Theorem E.1 (Exact minimality).

The minimal deterministic monitor for this language has exactly

(B+1)​2k+2\boxed{(B+1)2^{k}+2}

states.

Proof.

Every pair (r,S)(r,S) is reachable by spending B−rB-r units and marking exactly the elements of SS in some fixed order. We show distinct reachable states are Nerode-distinguishable.

If S≠S′S\neq S^{\prime}, choose an obligation in the symmetric difference; without loss take j∈S∖S′j\in S\setminus S^{\prime}. Construct a suffix that marks every obligation missing from SS, does not mark jj, and then finishes. Starting from (r,S)(r,S) this suffix satisfies every obligation (assuming no extra spend is needed), while from (r′,S′)(r^{\prime},S^{\prime}) obligation jj remains unmarked, so the suffix is rejected. The suffix contains no spend, so the budgets r,r′r,r^{\prime} play no role.

If S=S′S=S^{\prime} but r<r′r<r^{\prime}, append exactly r+1r+1 spends, then mark every obligation missing from SS and finish. The run from remaining budget rr enters the dead state on the last required spend, while the run from r′r^{\prime} survives at least that prefix; if r′r^{\prime} may equal r+1r+1, the subsequent marks and finish remain valid. Thus the states are distinguishable.

The accepting terminal state is distinguished from every other state, including the dead state, by the empty suffix under the convention that LL contains exactly successfully terminated histories, or equivalently by any action that is illegal after termination but may be legal before it. The dead state has no accepting continuation and is therefore distinct from every reachable nondead preterminal state, each of which can mark missing obligations and finish. Hence all (B+1)​2k+2(B+1)2^{k}+2 states lie in distinct Nerode classes, matching the explicit monitor upper bound. ∎

The state-count expression is exponential in kk, but the factored memory representation is not: storing rr requires ⌈log2⁡(B+1)⌉\lceil\log_{2}(B+1)\rceil bits and the obligation set requires kk bits, plus constant terminal status. State count, storage bits, and update complexity are distinct quantities and should not be conflated.

E.2 Freshness, atomic commit, and serializability

Each authoritative object carries a version. Transaction TT records a read set R⁡(T)R(T) with the versions used to compute tentative writes W⁡(T)W(T). At commit, validation checks that every recorded version still equals the authoritative version; if so, all writes are installed atomically and their versions advanced.

Proposition E.2 (Commit-order serializability).

Assume (i) R⁡(T)R(T) contains every authoritative state item on which TT’s tentative writes semantically depend, (ii) an unchanged version implies the relevant value is unchanged, and (iii) validation and installation are atomic with respect to competing commits. Then the committed execution is equivalent to serial execution in commit order.

Proof.

Order successful commits T1,…,TmT_{1},\ldots,T_{m} by their atomic commit points. We induct on the prefix length. The empty prefix is trivially equivalent to serial execution. Assume the authoritative state immediately after Tj−1T_{j-1} equals the state produced by serially executing T1,…,Tj−1T_{1},\ldots,T_{j-1}.

Because TjT_{j} commits successfully, immediately before its commit every item in its complete semantic read set has exactly the version, and hence the relevant value, that TjT_{j} used when computing its tentative writes. Therefore the tentative writes are exactly those TjT_{j} would compute if executed against the current serial-prefix state. Atomic installation produces exactly the next serial state. This establishes the induction step and the result. ∎

The completeness of the semantic read set is essential. If a write depends on an undeclared object, that object can change without invalidating the transaction, defeating the argument. Likewise, phantom/range dependencies require a representation capable of versioning the relevant predicate or range; the proposition is not a substitute for the richer machinery of database concurrency control [52].

E.2.1 Complexity under explicit object versions

With O⁡(1)O(1) version lookup, exact validation scans |R⁡(T)||R(T)| recorded versions and installation touches |W⁡(T)||W(T)| explicit writes, giving

O⁡(|R⁡(T)|+|W⁡(T)|)O(|R(T)|+|W(T)|)

work in this model. There is also a matching worst-case query lower bound for the validation subproblem when the only way to learn whether a read object changed is to inspect its independent version counter: a deterministic validator that skips some counter cannot distinguish the all-current world from a world in which exactly the skipped counter changed. Thus exact validation requires Ω⁡(|R⁡(T)|)\Omega(|R(T)|) counter inspections in that explicit-counter model. This lower bound should not be generalized to systems with stronger aggregate freshness summaries.

Appendix F Layer induction, escapes, and separations

F.1 Symmetry quotienting: exact semantic reduction and runtime caveat

Let a finite group GG act on a finite candidate space XX. Suppose feasibility FF and objective JJ are invariant:

F⁡(g​x)=F⁡(x),J⁡(g​x)=J⁡(x).F(gx)=F(x),\qquad J(gx)=J(x).

Then both descend to the orbit space X/GX/G, and

minx:F⁡(x)J(x)=min[x]∈X/G:F⁡([x])J([x]).\min_{x:F(x)}J(x)=\min_{[x]\in X/G:F([x])}J([x]).

If the action is free, every orbit has |G||G| elements and

|X/G|=|X|/|G|.|X/G|=|X|/|G|.

For non-free actions, Burnside’s lemma gives the exact orbit count.

This is an exact reduction in the number of semantically distinct candidates. It is not by itself a wall-clock theorem: a solver must still generate or canonicalize orbit representatives, and equivalence testing may be expensive. A runtime claim of O⁡(|X|/|G|)O(|X|/|G|) therefore requires an explicit model in which representative generation/canonicalization is cheap relative to candidate evaluation.

There is also a categorical reason not to quotient too early. For GG-sets, taking orbits is a left adjoint and therefore preserves colimits, not limits in general. Matching and gluing conditions are limit-like constructions. Objectwise orbit quotients can therefore erase cycle/transition information needed to decide whether local pieces globally realize. Groupoid-valued state retains equivalence morphisms instead of replacing them immediately by coarse orbit labels.

F.2 Separation countermodels for H,𝒞,𝒢,ℱH,\mathcal{C},\mathcal{G},\mathcal{F}, and temporal state

The independence of the operational symbols is best stated through finite countermodels; they form distinct structures rather than a nested hierarchy.

Topology does not determine transformation semantics.

Take identical two-node topology u→vu\to v. System 1 implements v:=uv:=u; System 2 implements v:=1−uv:=1-u. Reachability is identical, but predicted post-state differs. Therefore HH alone cannot recover 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Transformation semantics does not determine realization.

Give three Boolean scopes identical local update operations. In one global semantics require A=BA=B, B=CB=C, and A=CA=C; in another require A=BA=B, B=CB=C, and A≠CA\neq C. Local operations and scope topology can be identical while one matching family is globally realizable and the other is not. A realization condition adds information beyond local transition typing.

Surface identity does not determine semantic equivalence.

Two records may have identical schemas and values while denoting two distinct objects, or may have different schemas while denoting two representations of one object. Neither topology nor syntax determines the groupoid of meaning-preserving translations.

Present values do not determine temporal validity.

Two artifacts can contain identical values while one was derived from current dependency versions and the other from superseded versions. If future admissibility depends on provenance, an abstraction that retains only present payloads merges states with different admissibility profiles and is therefore inexact by Proposition 2.4.

These examples justify distinct semantic responsibilities without asserting set-theoretic containments such as H⊊H+𝒞H\subsetneq H+\mathcal{C}. The structures interact, but none of the counterexamples can be repaired by merely renaming one structure as another.

F.3 From necessity to structure: full proofs

Section 4.3 states these results in words. This subsection gives the formal statements and proofs.

F.3.1 Restriction, translation, and transition

Let ρ⁡(x)=(x|Ui)i\rho(x)=(x|_{U_{i}})_{i} be the family of local views on a declared cover.

Proposition F.1 (Local sufficiency).

A validator that reads only the local views ρ⁡(x)\rho(x) can be exact if and only if ρ⁡(x)=ρ⁡(x′)\rho(x)=\rho(x^{\prime}) implies C⁡(x)=C⁡(x′)C(x)=C(x^{\prime}). It accepts only realizable local families if and only if it rejects every matching family outside ρ⁡(X)\rho(X).

Proof.

If ρ⁡(x)=ρ⁡(x′)\rho(x)=\rho(x^{\prime}) implies C⁡(x)=C⁡(x′)C(x)=C(x^{\prime}), define V⁡(ρ⁡(x),a)=1V(\rho(x),a)=1 exactly when a∈C⁡(x)a\in C(x). This is well defined because states with the same local views share one admissibility profile, and it is exact by construction. Conversely, a validator reading only ρ⁡(x)\rho(x) is a validator for the abstraction ϕ=ρ\phi=\rho, and Proposition 2.4 shows it can be exact only if ρ\rho never merges states with different profiles.

For the second statement, a matching family mm is realizable exactly when m∈ρ⁡(X)m\in\rho(X). A validator that accepts some m∉ρ⁡(X)m\notin\rho(X) therefore accepts an unrealizable family, and one that rejects every such mm accepts only realizable families. When ρ\rho is a bijection onto the matching families, as for a sheaf on the declared cover, the check is automatic; otherwise it is the realization check whose cost Sections 3 and 4 analyze. ∎

The two conditions are the two sheaf axioms, weakened in one useful way. Separatedness is needed only up to admissibility: the runtime needs a sheaf of the admissibility quotient, not of the whole world. Gluing is needed only for families that some participant can actually commit. The topology HH declares which scopes exist, and Section 3 exhibited both failures: aliasing when the cover is too coarse, and the shared budget of Section 3.2 when no scope contains a global constraint.

Participants rarely hold the sufficient state in one format. Let ZZ be the exact semantic state, let participant ii hold ri=ei​(z)r_{i}=e_{i}(z) for an encoding ei:Z→Rie_{i}:Z\to R_{i}, and let a translation ti​j:Ri→Rjt_{ij}:R_{i}\to R_{j} satisfy ti​j∘ei=ejt_{ij}\circ e_{i}=e_{j}.

Proposition F.2 (Translations of an exact state form a groupoid).
  1. (i)

    If eje_{j} is injective, so is eie_{i}: no translation can restore a distinction lost by its source encoding.

  2. (ii)

    If every eie_{i} is a bijection, then ti​j=ej∘ei−1t_{ij}=e_{j}\circ e_{i}^{-1} is uniquely determined, ti​i=idt_{ii}=\mathrm{id}, tj​i=ti​j−1t_{ji}=t_{ij}^{-1}, and tj​k∘ti​j=ti​kt_{jk}\circ t_{ij}=t_{ik}.

  3. (iii)

    Conversely, on a connected graph of participants, a family of bijections that composes to the identity around every cycle arises from bijective encodings of one state, unique up to one global re-encoding.

Proof.

(i) If ei​(z)=ei​(z′)e_{i}(z)=e_{i}(z^{\prime}), then ej​(z)=ti​j​(ei​(z))=ti​j​(ei​(z′))=ej​(z′)e_{j}(z)=t_{ij}(e_{i}(z))=t_{ij}(e_{i}(z^{\prime}))=e_{j}(z^{\prime}), and injectivity of eje_{j} gives z=z′z=z^{\prime}.

(ii) If eie_{i} is a bijection, ti​j∘ei=ejt_{ij}\circ e_{i}=e_{j} forces ti​j=ej∘ei−1t_{ij}=e_{j}\circ e_{i}^{-1}. Then ti​i=ei​ei−1=idt_{ii}=e_{i}e_{i}^{-1}=\mathrm{id}, tj​i∘ti​j=ei​ej−1​ej​ei−1=idt_{ji}\circ t_{ij}=e_{i}e_{j}^{-1}e_{j}e_{i}^{-1}=\mathrm{id}, and tj​k∘ti​j=ek​ej−1​ej​ei−1=ek​ei−1=ti​kt_{jk}\circ t_{ij}=e_{k}e_{j}^{-1}e_{j}e_{i}^{-1}=e_{k}e_{i}^{-1}=t_{ik}. In particular the composite of translations around any cycle of participants is the identity.

(iii) Let the participants form a connected graph whose oriented edges carry bijections ti​j:Ri→Rjt_{ij}:R_{i}\to R_{j}, with tj​i=ti​j−1t_{ji}=t_{ij}^{-1}, composing to the identity around every cycle. Fix a root participant i0i_{0}, set Z=Ri0Z=R_{i_{0}} and ei0=ide_{i_{0}}=\mathrm{id}, and for each ii let eie_{i} be the composite of translations along any path from i0i_{0} to ii. Two paths differ by a cycle whose composite is the identity, so eie_{i} is well defined, and for every edge ti​j∘ei=ejt_{ij}\circ e_{i}=e_{j} because a path to jj may pass through ii. If ei′:Z′→Rie^{\prime}_{i}:Z^{\prime}\to R_{i} is another family of bijections with ti​j∘ei′=ej′t_{ij}\circ e^{\prime}_{i}=e^{\prime}_{j}, then along every path ei′=ei∘σe^{\prime}_{i}=e_{i}\circ\sigma with σ=ei0−1∘ei0′\sigma=e_{i_{0}}^{-1}\circ e^{\prime}_{i_{0}}, so the two families differ by one global re-encoding σ:Z′→Z\sigma:Z^{\prime}\to Z. This is the argument of Theorem 3.4 with the group replaced by the groupoid of bijections between the sets RiR_{i}. ∎

Part (i) is the aliasing theorem at the translation map: a lossy translation merges states. Parts (ii) and (iii) say that the translations of an exact state are exactly a groupoid with trivial holonomy. When encodings are fixed only up to a symmetry of the object—a coordinate frame, a labeling, a unit choice—translations are determined only up to that symmetry, the groupoid acquires nontrivial automorphism groups, and quotienting by the symmetry before checking cycles discards the holonomy that detects the error (Section 3.3).

Let each action aa act on world states by Ta:X→XT_{a}:X\to X, with an absorbing dead state for inadmissible actions, and let a word w=a1⋯anw=a_{1}\cdots a_{n} act by Tw=Tan∘⋯∘Ta1T_{w}=T_{a_{n}}\circ\cdots\circ T_{a_{1}}. A state abstraction ϕ\phi is self-updating if ϕ⁡(x)=ϕ⁡(x′)\phi(x)=\phi(x^{\prime}) implies ϕ⁡(Ta​x)=ϕ⁡(Ta​x′)\phi(T_{a}x)=\phi(T_{a}x^{\prime}) for every action aa. Equivalently, there are update maps faf_{a} with ϕ∘Ta=fa∘ϕ\phi\circ T_{a}=f_{a}\circ\phi, and these compose: fa​b=fb∘faf_{ab}=f_{b}\circ f_{a}.

Theorem F.3 (Coarsest self-updating exact state).

Define x≈x′x\approx x^{\prime} if and only if C⁡(Tw​x)=C⁡(Tw​x′)C(T_{w}x)=C(T_{w}x^{\prime}) for every finite action word ww, including the empty word. Then ≈\approx is exact and self-updating, and every exact self-updating abstraction refines ≈\approx. The coarsest state that is both exact and updatable without re-reading the world is therefore X/≈X/{\approx}.

Proof.

The relation ≈\approx is an equivalence relation because it is defined by equality of the family (C⁡(Tw​x))w(C(T_{w}x))_{w}.

Exact. The empty word gives C⁡(x)=C⁡(x′)C(x)=C(x^{\prime}) whenever x≈x′x\approx x^{\prime}, so ≈\approx refines ∼C\sim_{C} and is exact by Proposition 2.4.

Self-updating. Suppose x≈x′x\approx x^{\prime} and fix an action aa. For every word ww, the word a​waw acts by Ta​w=Tw∘TaT_{aw}=T_{w}\circ T_{a}, so C⁡(Tw​(Ta​x))=C⁡(Ta​w​x)=C⁡(Ta​w​x′)=C⁡(Tw​(Ta​x′))C(T_{w}(T_{a}x))=C(T_{aw}x)=C(T_{aw}x^{\prime})=C(T_{w}(T_{a}x^{\prime})). Hence Ta​x≈Ta​x′T_{a}x\approx T_{a}x^{\prime}.

Coarsest. Let ϕ\phi be exact and self-updating, and suppose ϕ⁡(x)=ϕ⁡(x′)\phi(x)=\phi(x^{\prime}). By induction on the length of ww, self-updating gives ϕ⁡(Tw​x)=ϕ⁡(Tw​x′)\phi(T_{w}x)=\phi(T_{w}x^{\prime}) for every word. Exactness then gives C⁡(Tw​x)=C⁡(Tw​x′)C(T_{w}x)=C(T_{w}x^{\prime}) for every word, so x≈x′x\approx x^{\prime}. Thus ϕ\phi refines ≈\approx.

Update maps. If ϕ\phi is self-updating, fa​(ϕ⁡(x))=ϕ⁡(Ta​x)f_{a}(\phi(x))=\phi(T_{a}x) is well defined on the image of ϕ\phi, and Ta​b=Tb∘TaT_{ab}=T_{b}\circ T_{a} gives fa​b=fb∘faf_{ab}=f_{b}\circ f_{a}. ∎

Relation to Myhill–Nerode.

Let inadmissible actions send every state to an absorbing dead state with C⁡(dead)=∅C(\mathrm{dead})=\varnothing, fix an initial state x0x_{0}, and let LL be the language of histories every action of which is admissible when taken. For admissible histories h,h′h,h^{\prime} with x=Th​x0x=T_{h}x_{0} and x′=Th′​x0x^{\prime}=T_{h^{\prime}}x_{0}, we have x≈x′x\approx x^{\prime} if and only if h≡Lh′h\equiv_{L}h^{\prime}. Indeed, if h​w∉Lhw\notin L then Tw​xT_{w}x is dead; and if h​w∈Lhw\in L, then a∈C⁡(Tw​x)a\in C(T_{w}x) exactly when h​w​a∈Lhwa\in L. Equality of all admissibility sets along all words is therefore equality of all admissible continuations. On reachable states, X/≈X/{\approx} is the minimal monitor of Appendix E.

F.3.2 The components in categorical form

Section 3.1 introduced the sheaf idea in plain terms: ask whether local states that agree on every overlap come from one global state. The refined state model keeps the same logic but allows equivalent representations to be tracked explicitly through a groupoid-valued assignment

𝒮:(𝖴,J)o​p→𝐆𝐩𝐝.\mathcal{S}:(\mathsf{U},J)^{op}\rightarrow\mathbf{Gpd}.

Here 𝖴\mathsf{U} is the collection of local scopes, JJ specifies which families of scopes count as covers of a larger scope, (−)o​p(-)^{op} reverses restriction arrows in the usual presheaf convention, and 𝐆𝐩𝐝\mathbf{Gpd} is the category of groupoids—categories whose every morphism is invertible. Since a groupoid is a category in which every morphism is invertible, 𝒢\mathcal{G} is not a second kind of mathematics beside 𝒞\mathcal{C}. It is the reversible core of representation change, kept as a separate slot so the runtime can tell a genuine change of state (revising a design from 1​m1\,\mathrm{m} to 1.2​m1.2\,\mathrm{m}) from a re-encoding (1​m1\,\mathrm{m} as 100​cm100\,\mathrm{cm}). Descent is the existence-and-coherence condition for gluing those local objects and equivalences into a global object. Noninvertible transformations live in 𝒞\mathcal{C}; formally they are morphisms of a category-valued prestack whose groupoid core is 𝒮\mathcal{S}, and Proposition F.4 shows that, unlike re-representations, they must be checked for realization at commit. Temporal state records only distinctions from the past that can affect current or future admissibility. Neither 𝒮\mathcal{S} nor descent performs optimization by itself; an optimizer, solver, diffusion process, or agent may search over states, while the sheaf/descent structure defines which candidate states count as globally coherent.

F.3.3 Prior art for the same pattern

The bridge of Section 4.3—a necessity for sufficient information, followed by structures chosen to preserve it as it is distributed—recurs in established fields.

Team decision theory.

Whether decentralized decision makers can act well depends on the information structure rather than on individual rationality [56]. Witsenhausen’s counterexample shows that even simple dynamics become intractable under a nonclassical information structure [83]. The partially nested condition of Ho and Chu—if one agent’s action affects what another observes, the second must know what the first knew—restores tractability [45]. The shared-budget ledger is an instance of that condition: every role’s spend affects every other role’s admissible actions, so every role must see the aggregate.

Atlases and fibre bundles.

An object without a global chart is described by local charts on a cover, transition maps between overlapping charts, the cocycle condition on triple overlaps, and gluing [79]. These correspond to HH, 𝒢\mathcal{G}, cycle consistency, and ℱ\mathcal{F}. The impossibility theorem supplies the premise that no participant holds a global chart, and Proposition F.2 is the statement that transition maps of an exact state satisfy the cocycle condition.

Sufficient statistics and filtering.

The admissibility quotient ∼C\sim_{C} is a minimal sufficient statistic for the decision problem in the sense of statistical decision theory [8]. A recursively updatable sufficient statistic, such as the belief state of a filter, is the self-updating state of Theorem F.3, and Kalman’s minimal realization theory is its linear-systems form [44, 49].

Version control.

In the categorical theory of patches, repository states are objects, patches are morphisms, and a merge is a pushout; a merge conflict is a failure of the pushout to exist in the category of files [61]. This is the gluing failure of Section 3.1 in a setting familiar to every software engineer.

F.4 Other ways out of the impossibility, and what each costs

Theorem 2.1 establishes that the missing distinction must come from somewhere and leaves open where. This appendix lists the alternatives, states what each gives up, and says when the theory predicts each one suffices. The comparison locates the proposed runtime within a design space, in the way that the CAP theorem locates distributed databases [37].

Alternative What it gives up When the theory predicts it suffices
Weaken the goal progress a common safe action exists and stalling is acceptable
Obtain the information elsewhere nothing formally, but the authoritative fact must still exist queries or messages can split every aliased fiber within budget
Restructure state so local checks suffice flexibility the invariant is invariant-confluent, or can be split into local quotas
Accept probabilistic success worst-case guarantees the information is in the observation and errors are tolerable
Conventional specialized mechanisms generality across boundaries one mechanism already captures the full relevant state relation
Weaken the goal.

If some action is admissible in every state of an aliased fiber—stop, escalate to a human, do nothing—the fiber intersection is nonempty and Theorem 2.1 no longer bites. The price is progress. Proposition 2.4 makes this precise: a validator that always falls back to the common action is sound, but its progress is limited to that action. Many deployed agents take this route implicitly by asking for confirmation. It is appropriate when stalling is cheap; it is not when the task requires completion under a budget.

Obtain the information another way.

Agents can query tools, broadcast their state, write to a shared blackboard [26], or delegate the decision to one agent that sees everything. Theorem B.4 characterizes exactly when bounded queries suffice, and Corollary 2.2 shows that communication cannot exceed the joint observation, which full communication trivially attains. These are genuine alternatives to exposing state. They share one requirement with the proposed runtime: the queried fact must exist somewhere in authoritative form. A query for “commands used so far” presupposes an accurate counter; a blackboard presupposes that every writer records its spend. The design choice is therefore between agents pulling authoritative state and a runtime pushing or enforcing it, not between having and not having it. Delegating to an all-seeing agent centralizes reasoning as well as state, which the proposed architecture avoids.

Restructure state so that local checks suffice.

The strongest alternative comes from databases. Bailis et al. characterize coordination-free safety relative to an invariant, transaction set, merge operator, common ancestor, and reachable states through invariant confluence [9]. When every pair of invariant-satisfying states reachable from a common ancestor merges to another invariant-satisfying state, those transactions need no global coordination; conflict-free replicated data types can realize suitable cases by construction [70]. In the language of Section 3.1, this is a condition under which the reachable committed local families glue. The independent spend-increment transactions of Proposition 3.3 do not satisfy it under additive merge when m≥2m\geq 2 and B≥1B\geq 1: from the valid common ancestor s=0s=0, one replica commits s1=Bs_{1}=B and another commits s2=Bs_{2}=B; each state satisfies ∑isi≤B\sum_{i}s_{i}\leq B, but their merge has ∑isi=2​B>B\sum_{i}s_{i}=2B>B. Some coordination or restructuring is therefore necessary. Escrow methods split the bound into local quotas BiB_{i} with ∑iBi=B\sum_{i}B_{i}=B [65]. Each quota is a local constraint, so no global check is needed, at the cost of flexibility: one role cannot borrow another’s unused share. Escrow keeps the cover and instead shrinks each local state space to {0,…,Bi}\{0,\ldots,B_{i}\}; every tuple of local states then satisfies ∑isi≤B\sum_{i}s_{i}\leq B, so ρ\rho becomes surjective without a shared ledger scope.

Accept probabilistic success.

A stronger model, or one trained to track state in context, may be right almost always. The theorems concern worst-case guarantees under missing information. When the relevant distinction is present in the observation, nothing is impossible and learning can close the gap; Theorem B.2 bounds only what is achievable when it is absent. The choice is appropriate when occasional violations are tolerable and inexpensive to detect afterward. The detection-versus-repair results, including Proposition 3.6, indicate when afterward is expensive.

Conventional specialized mechanisms.

Transactions, dependency engines, version-aware restarts, residual solvers, and workflow engines already implement parts of the semantics, and Studies III and VI show them tying with the general runtime. Corollary 4.2 predicts this: whenever one mechanism captures the full relevant state relation, it satisfies the required conditions. The general runtime is warranted at boundaries where no single mechanism spans the state, such as a shared budget across roles with different tools, or provenance that crosses artifacts managed by different systems.

Experimental consequence.

These baselines were run as the LH2 escape panel of Study IV. The query baseline still overspent in 4/5 runs; the conservative baseline prevented overspend by stopping at 15; and the escrow baseline (executor 14 + verifier 6) matched the shared ledger at 0/5 violations and improved mean partial score on that panel. The frozen reading is that restructuring the local state spaces suffices for this additive budget; a unique shared-ledger claim is not required.

F.5 Compositional subsystem semantics

A simple categorical composition result makes the local-to-global idea concrete without requiring the full machinery of stacks. Let subsystem state spaces XAX_{A} and XBX_{B} map to a shared interface II through pA:XA→Ip_{A}:X_{A}\to I and pB:XB→Ip_{B}:X_{B}\to I. Their coherent composite state space is the fiber product

XA×IXB={(a,b):pA​(a)=pB​(b)}.X_{A}\times_{I}X_{B}=\{(a,b):p_{A}(a)=p_{B}(b)\}.

Suppose local transitions fA:XA→XA′f_{A}:X_{A}\to X_{A}^{\prime} and fB:XB→XB′f_{B}:X_{B}\to X_{B}^{\prime} induce the same interface transition g:I→I′g:I\to I^{\prime}:

pA′∘fA=g∘pA,pB′∘fB=g∘pB.p_{A}^{\prime}\circ f_{A}=g\circ p_{A},\qquad p_{B}^{\prime}\circ f_{B}=g\circ p_{B}.

Then

(a,b)↦(fA​(a),fB​(b))(a,b)\mapsto(f_{A}(a),f_{B}(b))

is a well-defined map

XA×IXB⟶XA′×I′XB′.X_{A}\times_{I}X_{B}\longrightarrow X_{A}^{\prime}\times_{I^{\prime}}X_{B}^{\prime}.

Indeed, if pA​(a)=pB​(b)p_{A}(a)=p_{B}(b), applying gg and the commuting equations gives pA′​(fA​(a))=pB′​(fB​(b))p_{A}^{\prime}(f_{A}(a))=p_{B}^{\prime}(f_{B}(b)). This elementary pullback argument is the finite-set shadow of the paper’s more general claim: locally valid transitions compose globally when their boundary semantics agree.

Iterating such compositions along a tree of interfaces gives a structural explanation for tree-decomposition algorithms. When interfaces remain small, exact global reasoning can be assembled from local tables whose size is exponential in interface width rather than in total system size.

F.6 Full descent-style coherence-preservation argument

Section 4.2 states this result in words: re-expressions preserve coherence, and state changes must be checked at commit. Here we state it formally, in the language of prestacks and effective descent, and spell out exactly what is assumed and what follows.

Formally, because a groupoid is already a category, one could in principle put every edit and every unit conversion into a single large category. We do not: the groupoid core isolates the invertible, identity-preserving morphisms (𝒢\mathcal{G}), while 𝒞\mathcal{C} carries the remaining, generally noninvertible state-changing actions. The two classes behave differently under descent (Proposition F.4), so the state assignment used for transitions is category-valued, with groupoid core 𝒮\mathcal{S} for the equivalence level. For each scope UU let 𝒮𝒞​(U)\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{C}}(U) be a category of local states and local actions, with restriction functors, whose groupoid core is 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Assume 𝒮𝒞\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{C}} is a prestack: local morphisms glue uniquely, so the comparison functor from 𝒮𝒞​(U)\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{C}}(U) to descent data on a cover is fully faithful. A descent datum is effective when it lies in the essential image of that functor, that is, when it comes from a global state; the coherent states are the effective data.

Why the fibres must be categories.

If the state assignment is groupoid-valued, as in 𝒮:(𝖴,J)o​p→𝐆𝐩𝐝\mathcal{S}:(\mathsf{U},J)^{op}\to\mathbf{Gpd}, then every local morphism fi:xi→yif_{i}:x_{i}\to y_{i} is invertible, so only re-representations can be expressed. State-changing actions such as spending, appending, or overwriting are not invertible. They require a category-valued assignment 𝒮𝒞\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{C}} whose groupoid core is 𝒮\mathcal{S}. And if 𝒮𝒞\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{C}} were assumed to be a stack, every descent datum would be effective and preservation would hold for free, which would say nothing about the non-realizable families of Section 3. The interesting setting is a prestack that need not be a stack.

Fix a cover {Ui→U}\{U_{i}\to U\}. A descent datum consists of objects xix_{i} of 𝒮𝒞​(Ui)\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{C}}(U_{i}) and overlap isomorphisms

ϕi​j:xi|Ui​j​⟶∼​xj|Ui​j\phi_{ij}:x_{i}|_{U_{ij}}\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}x_{j}|_{U_{ij}}

satisfying the cocycle condition on triple overlaps,

ϕj​k∘ϕi​j=ϕi​k.\phi_{jk}\circ\phi_{ij}=\phi_{ik}.

A morphism of descent data (xi,ϕi​j)→(yi,ψi​j)(x_{i},\phi_{ij})\to(y_{i},\psi_{ij}) is a family fi:xi→yif_{i}:x_{i}\to y_{i} with ψi​j∘fi|Ui​j=fj|Ui​j∘ϕi​j\psi_{ij}\circ f_{i}|_{U_{ij}}=f_{j}|_{U_{ij}}\circ\phi_{ij}. Restriction defines a comparison functor κ:𝒮𝒞​(U)→DD⁡({Ui})\kappa:\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{C}}(U)\to\mathrm{DD}(\{U_{i}\}). The assignment is a prestack for the cover when κ\kappa is fully faithful, equivalently when morphisms glue uniquely, and a stack when κ\kappa is moreover essentially surjective. A datum is effective when it is isomorphic to κ⁡(x)\kappa(x) for some xx.

With 𝒮𝒞\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{C}} a prestack, let (xi,ϕi​j)(x_{i},\phi_{ij}) be effective with global realization xx. Suppose local actions fi:xi→yif_{i}:x_{i}\to y_{i}, together with target overlap isomorphisms ψi​j\psi_{ij} satisfying the cocycle law, form a morphism of descent data:

ψi​j∘fi=fj∘ϕi​j.\psi_{ij}\circ f_{i}=f_{j}\circ\phi_{ij}.
Proposition F.4 (Coherence preservation and its limit).
  1. (i)

    If every fif_{i} is an isomorphism, the target datum (yi,ψi​j)(y_{i},\psi_{ij}) is effective and the family glues to a unique global isomorphism f:x→yf:x\to y.

  2. (ii)

    If the target datum is effective with realization yy, the family glues to a unique global transition f:x→yf:x\to y.

  3. (iii)

    For non-invertible fif_{i} the target datum need not be effective: there are prestacks, effective data, and locally valid actions whose combined result has no global realization.

Proof.

Assume 𝒮𝒞\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{C}} is a prestack, (xi,ϕi​j)≅κ⁡(x)(x_{i},\phi_{ij})\cong\kappa(x), and (fi)(f_{i}) is a morphism of descent data to (yi,ψi​j)(y_{i},\psi_{ij}).

(i) If every fif_{i} is an isomorphism, then (fi−1)(f_{i}^{-1}) is also a morphism of descent data, since ψi​j∘fi=fj∘ϕi​j\psi_{ij}\circ f_{i}=f_{j}\circ\phi_{ij} gives fj−1∘ψi​j=ϕi​j∘fi−1f_{j}^{-1}\circ\psi_{ij}=\phi_{ij}\circ f_{i}^{-1}. Hence (fi)(f_{i}) is an isomorphism in DD\mathrm{DD} and (yi,ψi​j)≅(xi,ϕi​j)≅κ⁡(x)(y_{i},\psi_{ij})\cong(x_{i},\phi_{ij})\cong\kappa(x), so the target is effective, realized for instance by y=xy=x. Full faithfulness of κ\kappa gives a unique f:x→yf:x\to y with κ⁡(f)\kappa(f) equal to the composite isomorphism, and ff is an isomorphism because κ\kappa reflects isomorphisms.

(ii) If (yi,ψi​j)≅κ⁡(y)(y_{i},\psi_{ij})\cong\kappa(y), then (fi)(f_{i}) determines a morphism κ⁡(x)→κ⁡(y)\kappa(x)\to\kappa(y) in DD\mathrm{DD}, and full faithfulness gives a unique f:x→yf:x\to y inducing it.

(iii) Take disjoint scopes U1,…,UmU_{1},\ldots,U_{m} with m≥2m\geq 2 and a budget B≥1B\geq 1. Let 𝒮𝒞​(Ui)\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{C}}(U_{i}) be the poset {0,…,B}\{0,\ldots,B\} viewed as a category, with a unique morphism s→s′s\to s^{\prime} when s≤s′s\leq s^{\prime} (spending never decreases). Let 𝒮𝒞​(U)\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{C}}(U) be the poset {s∈{0,…,B}m:∑isi≤B}\{s\in\{0,\ldots,B\}^{m}:\sum_{i}s_{i}\leq B\} under the componentwise order, with restriction s↦sis\mapsto s_{i}. With no overlaps, descent data are arbitrary tuples and morphisms of descent data are componentwise inequalities. A global morphism s→ts\to t exists exactly when si≤tis_{i}\leq t_{i} for every ii, and it is unique, so κ\kappa is fully faithful and 𝒮𝒞\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{C}} is a prestack. The datum x=(0,…,0)x=(0,\ldots,0) is effective. The local actions f1:0→Bf_{1}:0\to B, f2:0→Bf_{2}:0\to B, and identities elsewhere form a morphism of descent data, each fif_{i} is a legal local transition, and the target (B,B,0,…,0)(B,B,0,\ldots,0) is not effective because 2​B>B2B>B.

For the trajectory statement, let XcohX_{\mathrm{coh}} be the class of effective data and assume the initial state is effective. If every committed step is either a family of isomorphisms, covered by (i), or has a target that the runtime has checked to be effective, covered by (ii), then each step maps an effective state to an effective state and glues to a global transition. Induction on tt proves that every finite committed prefix remains coherent. ∎

The counterexample in (iii) is the shared budget of Section 3.2. Each role’s local transition is legal, every overlap condition holds vacuously, and the combined state is not a global state. A runtime that checks only local legality and overlap squares accepts it; a runtime that checks effectiveness, here the ledger constraint, rejects it.

The proposition is a preservation theorem. Whether local models are scientifically correct, whether the selected action is useful, whether a coherent target exists for every proposal, and whether the runtime allows sufficient progress are separate questions, corresponding respectively to local truth, planning/objective quality, realizability, and the soundness/progress/completeness distinctions of Appendix B.2.

Why atomicity appears in the systems formulation.

The descent proof is extensional: it describes one compatible before/after family. A runtime that commits only part of that family can expose an intermediate state not represented by either descent datum. Atomic commit, or another mechanism that prevents observers from treating the partial family as authoritative, is therefore an execution-level condition for implementing the mathematical transition as one semantic step.

F.7 Task-dependent semantic-state size: decision, construction, and validation

The phrase “minimal semantic state” is meaningful only relative to the task the runtime must perform. The same physical constraint system can require radically different state sizes for three interfaces: deciding whether some global realization exists, constructing one, or validating arbitrary proposed realizations.

Tseitin systems give a clean example. Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be connected with n=|V|n=|V| and charge vector c∈𝔽2nc\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}.

Decision only.

Global realizability is equivalent to even total charge,

⨁v∈Vcv=0.\bigoplus_{v\in V}c_{v}=0.

Thus one maintained parity bit is sufficient for exact coherence decision. It is also necessary whenever updates may flip arbitrary single charges, because the even and odd classes have different future acceptance behavior.

Constructing a solution.

Among the 2n2^{n} charge vectors, exactly 2n−12^{n-1} have even parity. An edge assignment xx satisfies exactly one charge vector, namely c=B​xc=Bx, so no single edge assignment serves two distinct coherent charge vectors. If the runtime must be able to recover a satisfying edge assignment for every coherent charge vector, it must distinguish at least these 2n−12^{n-1} input classes, requiring at least n−1n-1 bits in a lossless fixed-length state representation of the charge class. Storing n−1n-1 independent charges attains this count, with the final charge determined by parity.

Validating arbitrary proposed edge assignments.

Now the action is a candidate x∈𝔽2|E|x\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|E|} and admissibility means B​x=cBx=c. For every coherent cc the admissible set is the affine solution set {x:B​x=c}\{x:Bx=c\}; distinct cc have disjoint admissibility profiles, while every incoherent cc has the empty profile. Hence there are

2n−1+12^{n-1}+1

distinct profiles. By Appendix B.2, an exact arbitrary-proposal validator needs at least

⌈log2⁡(2n−1+1)⌉=n\left\lceil\log_{2}(2^{n-1}+1)\right\rceil=n

bits for every n≥1n\geq 1.

The same underlying system therefore has a one-bit decision state, roughly n−1n-1 bits for full constructive input identity, and nn bits for exact arbitrary proposal validation. This is why the paper avoids equating “the global state” with one universal storage object: semantic sufficiency is defined relative to the action/query interface.

Appendix G Benchmark constructions, future tests, and boundaries

G.1 Causal benchmark constructions implied by the theorems

The theory is intended to generate experiments, not merely explain completed ones. The following synthetic constructions can be embedded inside public agent benchmarks without changing the foundation model.

G.1.1 Aliasing intervention

Study I realizes this construction and the next one on revision logs. Create paired task instances x,x′x,x^{\prime} with identical model-visible prompts, tool descriptions, and local artifacts but different hidden authoritative state such that the required actions are disjoint. Example: the visible task requests a resource-consuming operation while an authoritative shared ledger differs between the two instances. Under the aliased condition, Theorem 2.1 predicts that no deterministic observation-only policy can be correct on both, and Theorem 2.3 bounds randomized success for larger aliased families. The causal intervention exposes exactly the missing ledger field, leaving model, tool set, prompt wording, and inference budget fixed. Success should jump only after the observation partition is refined.

G.1.2 Reasoning-budget falsification test

Within the aliased condition, increase chain-of-thought budget, number of self-reflection passes, number of agent roles, and communication rounds while keeping the joint observation unchanged. These changes may improve other task components but cannot remove the constructed impossibility. If performance on the aliased decision approaches certainty without new information, then either the instances are not truly aliased, their admissible sets are not actually incompatible, or the system has an unintended information channel. The experiment is therefore a direct test of the theorem’s assumptions as well as the agent architecture.

G.1.3 Local-consistency order stress test

Embed parity constraints across a variable number of artifacts or agents. Construct instances for which every subset of at most kk local constraints is satisfiable while the complete family is not, as in Appendix C.2. Compare validators that inspect only fixed-size neighborhoods against a global parity/linear-algebra validator. Scaling nn with fixed kk tests the claim that no universal fixed local-check order suffices for unrestricted semantics.

G.1.4 Representation-cycle stress test

Study VII realizes this construction on ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} labels. Represent one latent object in several coordinate/schema views connected by reversible transforms. Generate coherent instances from random vertex frames and incoherent instances by corrupting one non-tree edge. A spanning-forest validator should detect every corruption that creates nontrivial cycle product in O⁡(|V|+|E|)O(|V|+|E|) group operations. This experiment directly exercises H+𝒢H+\mathcal{G} without requiring a domain-specific engineering representation.

G.1.5 Detection-versus-repair stress test

For a linear obstruction system, first measure exact detection cost through syndrome computation. Then ask the system to find a minimum-cardinality set of local edits that restores coherence. The theory predicts a qualitative separation: exact detection remains polynomial while optimal repair inherits the hardness of minimum syndrome decoding in the general case. Approximation or heuristic repair can still be practically useful; the claim concerns worst-case exact optimality.
