These constructions give a cleaner empirical program than simply adding more benchmarks. Each benchmark task should identify which theorem assumption it instantiates, what intervention changes that assumption, and what outcome would falsify the predicted mechanism.

G.2 Future benchmark program

G.2.1 Interventions for the remaining theorems

Studies I–IX test the aliasing theorem, the shared-budget and ownership results, the cycle certificate, and the conservative-extension prediction. The table lists interventions that would test the remaining results; each could fail empirically.

Theoretical statement Empirical intervention Predicted signature
Exact semantic abstraction remove one state field at a time failures appear precisely when merged states have different admissible-action profiles
Acyclic vs cyclic gluing matched tasks with join-tree vs cyclic overlap structure pairwise reconciliation suffices on the acyclic class but admits false positives on cyclic instances
Treewidth dependence families matched for size but varying interaction width exact coherence cost tracks width more strongly than raw agent/object count
Temporal Nerode state budget/obligation tasks with matched reasoning budget explicit minimal ledger removes targeted failures; more dialogue without the ledger need not
Detection vs repair inject linear/global inconsistencies before vs after commit detection remains cheap; minimum post-hoc repair can dominate cost

G.2.2 τ2\tau^{2}-bench revision panel

This panel has been run; Section 5.6 reports it. As executed, it injected stale reads, authority changes, and silent reverts into 12 deterministic tasks (four per family) and compared three arms: unguarded, conventional current-state preconditions, and the coherence runtime. The frozen design did not include the separate “normal conversational workflow” arm of the original outline; the stock τ2\tau^{2} agent serves as the unguarded arm. The remaining extensions are uninjected frequency measurement, more models, and a redesign of the two tasks in which agents re-read before acting.

G.2.3 BixBench3 for scientific-artifact coherence

BixBench3 is attractive because it operates at research-study scale and grades multiple structured outputs derived from public raw data [25]. The coherence experiment should not ask whether the model “knows biology” better. It should inject controlled changes to an upstream datum, parameter, or method choice and measure whether dependent tables, figures, intermediate analyses, and conclusions are correctly invalidated and regenerated. This directly tests H+𝒞+ℱ+DH+\mathcal{C}+\mathcal{F}+D in a domain whose local truth mechanism is the released analysis and deterministic grader. The model can remain responsible for interpretation and tool use; the experiment measures whether the surrounding state semantics keeps the derivation current.

G.2.4 Representation-equivalence and cycle benchmarks for 𝒢\mathcal{G}

Studies VII and VIII already close the deterministic cycle suite and a multi-year real-data prevalence check, and Study IX covers both full-view and split-view agents. Remaining work: repair routing for split-view merges, and agent-facing metamorphic tasks built from known semantics-preserving transforms (schema rename, units, frames, serialization, identifier renaming, harmless reorderings, behavior-preserving refactors) and from the concrete holonomy failures Study VIII found, with non-equivalent near-neighbors so that collapsing every change into one class cannot pass. For equivalent states x≃x′x\simeq x^{\prime}, evaluate invariance or equivariance

x≃x′⟹f⁡(x)≃f⁡(x′)x\simeq x^{\prime}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x)\simeq f(x^{\prime})

as appropriate, or f⁡(g​x)=f⁡(x)f(gx)=f(x) / f⁡(g​x)∼g⁡(f⁡(x))f(gx)\sim g(f(x)) when the task asks for invariant decisions versus equivariant outputs. Paid agent runs require a frozen model, budget, and task set before any scoring.

G.2.5 General computer and software agents

SWE-bench and OSWorld are valuable future tests because they provide persistent executable environments, not because every task is inherently a coherence task. Select or construct subsets with explicit dependency closure, cross-file or cross-application invariants, version changes, or terminal commit requirements. The theory predicts little or no gain on tasks that are purely local and one-shot. That negative prediction should be tested rather than hidden.

G.4 Additional boundaries, summaries, and agent-specific consequences

G.4.1 Incremental global summaries

Explicit global semantics can be maintained incrementally, without rescanning the entire world after every action. If an invariant factors through an Abelian aggregate

S=⨁isi,S=\bigoplus_{i}s_{i},

then replacing one contribution sis_{i} by si′s_{i}^{\prime} updates the authoritative summary via

S′=S⊕(−si)⊕si′S^{\prime}=S\oplus(-s_{i})\oplus s_{i}^{\prime}

using a constant number of group operations. For a general associative monoid without inverses, a balanced aggregation tree supports O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) point updates and O⁡(1)O(1) root-summary queries. The global/local distinction concerns semantics, not necessarily computational centralization.

G.4.2 Partial-order reduction

If two enabled actions preserve each other’s enabledness and commute on state, then swapping their order leaves the final semantic state unchanged. Classical trace theory identifies schedules related by adjacent swaps of independent actions. Thus kk mutually independent actions have k!k! sequential interleavings but only one trace class. This is a trajectory-level analogue of symmetry quotienting: explicit semantics can remove redundant schedules without conflating genuinely interacting actions.

G.4.3 Theory-to-AI consequences

The main impossibility result has a particularly direct interpretation for agent design.

  1. 1.

    Adding an agent role whose initial view is a deterministic function of already available information cannot refine the joint observation partition. Such a role may improve computation but cannot remove an aliasing impossibility.

  2. 2.

    Longer chain-of-thought or more sampling can improve proposal quality inside one information state, but Theorem 2.3 gives families where success remains information-limited.

  3. 3.

    External tool calls can remove impossibility only if they return genuinely new state information or change the world so that a common valid action emerges; Theorem B.4 states exactly when a bounded number of queries suffices. Merely reformatting or re-reasoning over the same evidence cannot.

  4. 4.

    A semantic runtime need not expose all authoritative state to the model. It may maintain compressed sufficient statistics, version vectors, obstruction syndromes, or equivalence frames outside the prompt and use them at validation/commit time.

  5. 5.

    Safety-only evaluation is incomplete. A reject-all runtime is sound. Agent systems should separately measure soundness, progress, and completeness, plus task quality conditional on admissible execution.

G.4.4 Scope of the claims

The theory proves targeted statements: certain information deficits make correct action impossible; certain structural classes admit local-to-global reconstruction while unrestricted classes do not; certain representation-consistency problems have efficient exact certificates; and temporal/action semantics determine a minimum amount of state that cannot be removed without changing legal futures. These are deliberately more precise than blanket claims that every global property is hard, that every local agent architecture fails, that explicit semantic state guarantees optimality, or that one formalism dominates all domains.

These boundaries are part of the contribution: the theory tells an AI systems designer when more model intelligence can help and when the bottleneck lies elsewhere.
